📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dana White’s Power Slap has threatened legal action against a parody competition called Power Spank, which sees women slap each other on the backside.

Released in January 2023, Power Slap is a combat sports promotion founded and co-owned by UFC boss Dana White, in which competitors take turns delivering unprotected slaps to each other’s faces.

In a recent development, in October, the Lingerie Fighting Championships (LFC) debuted Power Spank in Clearwater, Florida, as a parody of White’s competition. The inaugural event featured eight women, including MMA fighters and exotic dancers, competing for a $500 grand prize, which was won by a contestant known as Bebe.

According to USA Today, attorneys representing Power Slap sent LFC a cease-and-desist letter in late October, demanding that the organization stop using the Power Spank name.

According to recent reports, however, LFC CEO Shaun Donnelly has refused to comply, arguing that the competition constitutes parody protected under the First Amendment. “We respect Power Slap and its founders, but we will not be bullied into abandoning protected speech,” he stated in an official statement.

“We will defend our right, and the right of every American, to free speech, and if that takes us to the Supreme Court, we are prepared to go,” he continued.

Industry observers note that donnelly also explained that Power Spank was conceived after an LFC athlete was reportedly hospitalized following an appearance in Power Slap. “Power Spank is our answer: same energy, same theatrics, none of the brain damage. And let’s be honest, a spank is a lot more fun to watch than a slap.”.

LFC has confirmed it intends to continue running Power Spank at its US events while reviewing its legal options. At the time of writing, no formal lawsuit had been filed, and White had not publicly commented on the dispute.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a fresh way to power the future of computing.
  • According to recent reports, ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J.
  • Recent findings suggest that electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eighty years after the creation of ENIAC, the world's first general-purpose electronic computer, researchers at the University of Pennsylvania are exploring a fresh way to power the future of computing. Instead of relying entirely on electrons, which have formed the backbone of computers since the 1940s, scientists are now turning to light.

According to recent reports, ENIAC, developed by Penn researchers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, helped launch the modern computing era by using streams of electrons to solve complex mathematical problems. That same electronic approach still powers today's computers, smartphones, and AI systems. But as artificial intelligence grows more demanding, the limits of electron-based hardware are becoming harder to ignore.

Why Electrons Are Reaching Their Limits.

Recent findings suggest that electrons carry an electrical charge, which creates several challenges inside modern computer chips. As they move through materials, they generate heat and face resistance that wastes energy. Those problems become even more difficult as chips grow more complex and process enormous amounts of data for AI applications.

Researchers led by Penn physicist Bo Zhen in the School of Arts & Sciences believe photons, the particles that make up light, could help solve some of these issues.

"Because they are charge-neutral and have zero rest mass, photons can carry information quickly over long distances with minimal loss, dominating communications technology," explains Li He, co-first author of a paper published in Physical Review Letters and a former postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab. "But that neutrality means they barely interact with their environment, making them bad at the sort of signal-switching logic that computers depend on.".

In other words, light is excellent for carrying information rapidly and efficiently, but it struggles with the switching operations needed for computing.

Combining Light and Matter for AI Computing.

To overcome that problem, Zhen's team developed a special quasiparticle called an exciton-polariton. The particle forms when photons are strongly linked with electrons inside an atomically thin semiconductor material. This combination allows light to interact much more effectively, making it capable of performing the signal switching required for computing tasks.

The breakthrough could be especially crucial for artificial intelligence systems, which consume enormous amounts of power.

It has been revealed that many experimental photonic AI chips already use light to handle certain calculations at high speed. However, when these systems need to perform nonlinear activation steps, such as decision-making operations, they usually must convert light signals back into electronic ones. That conversion slows the process and increases energy use, reducing the benefits of photonic computing.

Sources indicate that using exciton-polaritons, the Penn researchers demonstrated all-light switching while using only about 4 quadrillionths of a joule of energy. That amount is extraordinarily small, far below the energy needed to briefly power a tiny LED light.

Toward Faster and More Efficient AI Chips.

If the technology can be successfully scaled, it could lead to photonic chips capable of processing information directly from cameras without repeated conversions between light and electricity. The approach could also lower the massive energy demands of large AI systems and potentially support basic quantum computing functions on future chips.

Bo Zhen is the Jin K. Lee Presidential Associate Professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the School of Arts & Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.

Li He was a postdoctoral researcher in the Zhen Lab in Penn Arts & Sciences. He is at the moment an assistant professor at Montana State University.

Additional authors on the study include Zhi Wang and Bumho Kim from the University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences.

The research was supported by the US Office of Naval Research (N00014-20-1-2325 and N00014-21-1-2703) and the Sloan Foundation.

Materials provided by University of Pennsylvania. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#11459. Scientists are seriously asking if bees and ChatGPT are conscious

📅 05 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (941 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists are seriously asking if bees and ChatGPT are conscious

📅 05 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common.
  • Industry observers note that there are many different ways of studying consciousness.
  • But two latest papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You might think a honey bee foraging in your garden and a browser window running ChatGPT have nothing in common. But recent scientific research has been seriously considering the possibility that either, or both, might be conscious.

Industry observers note that there are many different ways of studying consciousness. One of the most common is to measure how an animal – or artificial intelligence (AI) – acts.

But two latest papers on the possibility of consciousness in animals and AI suggest new theories for how to test this – one that strikes a middle ground between sensationalism and knee-jerk skepticism about whether humans are the only conscious beings on Earth.

Questions around consciousness have long sparked fierce debate.

According to recent reports, that’s in part because conscious beings might matter morally in a way that unconscious things don’t. Expanding the sphere of consciousness means expanding our ethical horizons. Even if we can’t be sure something is conscious, we might err on the side of caution by assuming it is – what philosopher Jonathan Birch calls the precautionary principle for sentience.

The recent trend has been one of expansion.

For example, in April 2024 a group of 40 scientists at a conference in New York proposed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. Subsequently signed by over 500 scientists and philosophers, this declaration claims consciousness is realistically possible in all vertebrates (including reptiles, amphibians and fishes) as well as many invertebrates, including cephalopods (octopus and squid), crustaceans (crabs and lobsters) and insects.

In parallel with this, the incredible rise of large language models, such as ChatGPT, has raised the serious possibility that machines may be conscious.

Sources indicate that five years ago, a seemingly ironclad test of whether something was conscious was to see if you could have a conversation with it. Philosopher Susan Schneider suggested if we had an AI that convincingly mused on the metaphysics of consciousness, it may well be conscious.

Industry observers note that by those standards, today we would be surrounded by conscious machines. Many have gone so far as to apply the precautionary principle here too: the burgeoning field of AI welfare is devoted to figuring out if and when we must care about machines.

Yet all of these arguments depend, in large part, on surface-level behavior. But that behavior can be deceptive. What matters for consciousness is not what you do, but how you do it.

A newly introduced paper in Trends in Cognitive Sciences that one of us (Colin Klein) coauthored, drawing on previous work, looks to the machinery rather than the behavior of AI.

Recent findings suggest that it also draws on the cognitive science tradition to identify a plausible list of indicators of consciousness based on the structure of information processing. This means one can draw up a useful list of indicators of consciousness without having to agree on which of the current cognitive theories of consciousness is correct.

Some indicators (such as the need to resolve trade-offs between competing goals in contextually appropriate ways) are shared by many theories. Most other indicators (such as the presence of informational feedback) are only required by one theory but indicative in others.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the useful indicators are all structural. They all have to do with how brains and computers process and combine information.

The verdict? No existing AI system (including ChatGPT) is conscious. The appearance of consciousness in large language models is not achieved in a way that is sufficiently similar to us to warrant attribution of conscious states.

Yet at the same time, there is no bar to AI systems – perhaps ones with a very different architecture to today’s systems – becoming conscious.

Sources indicate that the lesson? It’s possible for AI to behave as if conscious without being conscious.

Biologists are also turning to mechanisms – how brains work – to recognize consciousness in non-human animals.

In a new paper in Philosophical Transactions B, we propose a neural model for minimal consciousness in insects. This is a model that abstracts away from anatomical detail to focus on the core computations done by simple brains.

Our key insight is to identify the kind of computation our brains perform that gives rise to experience.

This computation solves ancient problems from our evolutionary history that arise from having a mobile, complex body with many senses and conflicting needs.

According to recent reports, importantly, we don’t identify the computation itself – there is science yet to be done. But we show that if you could identify it, you’d have a level playing field to compare humans, invertebrates, and computers.

The problem of consciousness in animals and in computers appear to pull in different directions.

For animals, the question is often how to interpret whether ambiguous behavior (like a crab tending its wounds) indicates consciousness.

For computers, we have to decide whether apparently unambiguous behavior (a chatbot musing with you on the purpose of existence) is a true indicator of consciousness or mere roleplay.

Yet as the fields of neuroscience and AI progress, both are converging on the same lesson: when making judgement about whether something is consciousness, how it works is proving more informative than what it does.

Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Colin Klein and Andrew Barron. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs highlights it.
  • According to recent reports, that button is easy to add.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

When an LLM app gives a wrong answer, nothing in your logs highlights it. The request returns 200, the JSON is valid, and no exception fires. Usually the user is the only one who notices. A thumbs-down button records that moment, on the exact trace that went wrong, while the user still remembers why.

According to recent reports, that button is easy to add. The hard part is what comes after: turning the thumbs-down into a reviewed test case, a judge score, and a better prompt.

Industry observers note that we ran that loop in TypeScript in four tools: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. All four handled the first four steps, which are user feedback, reviewer comments, a dataset and an LLM judge. Only AcruxCore rewrote the prompt from TypeScript. On 15 support tickets that no tool had seen, the rewritten prompt routed 13 correctly, against 7 for the original.

It has been revealed that our test app is a support-ticket router. It reads a ticket and returns JSON with a category (account, billing, bug or feature_request) and a priority (P0, P1 or P2). The first version of the prompt describes only the output format:.

The support team has a policy that this prompt never states. Sign-in problems are always account. A customer who can't use the product at all is P0. Any billing error is P1, even when the customer states there is no rush. Feature requests are P2, however angry the customer sounds.

Without that policy, the model guesses priority from the customer's tone. Here are three real replies from the first version:.

Recent findings suggest that every reply is valid JSON, so no schema check catches the mistake. A person has to read the reply and say it is wrong. The loop in this article takes that judgement and turns it into a better prompt.

All four tools cover evaluation. We compared the self-hosted ones on tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent, and on prompt registries in Prompt Management in TypeScript. For a broader comparison of self-hosted options, see this LangSmith alternatives roundup. This article covers the feedback loop only.

According to recent reports, we wrote 30 tickets. Fifteen are the "production traffic" that each tool's app processed. The other 15 are a holdout set. No tool saw them, and we used them only for the final before-and-after check.

Each tool ran the same sequence from one TypeScript script:.

The reviewer comments follow one template, so the wording is identical in every tool:.

According to recent reports, the comments name one rule each. The full policy appears nowhere in the data any tool received.

Sources indicate that the app model isn't fully deterministic at temperature 0. Each tool's run got between 6 and 8 of the 15 traffic tickets right, so the tools received 7 to 9 thumbs-down each. The holdout check below repeats every measurement three times.

All four tools accept feedback on a trace from TypeScript. They differ in how a second person, the reviewer, adds the correct answer.

Sources indicate that langSmith stores both as feedback on a run. The thumbs-down runs go into an annotation queue, where a reviewer adds feedback with a comment:.

Industry observers note that langfuse stores both as scores. An annotation queue needs a score config first:.

It has been revealed that phoenix stores both as span annotations. The reviewer's comment goes in explanation:.

Sources indicate that phoenix stores spans asynchronously. Our first run annotated a span before Phoenix had stored it, and the API returned a 404. The script now waits until all 15 spans are visible.

Industry observers note that acruxCore stores both as feedback rows on the trace. The source field separates the end user from the reviewer:.

This is the first step where the code differs a lot. Each tool can make a dataset, but only one builds it from feedback in one call.

Sources indicate that in LangSmith, a run query finds the thumbs-down runs. Then createExamples copies them into a dataset. You decide where the reviewer's comment goes. We put it in the reference output:.

LangSmith can also do this without code. An automation rule in the UI can add runs that match a filter to a dataset.

It has been revealed that in Langfuse, the scores API finds the thumbs-down traces. Two details cost us a run each. A boolean score is filtered with value: "false", not 0. And the trace ID is returned only when you ask for the subject field group:.

In Phoenix, getSpans can't filter by annotation. So the script lists the app's spans, reads their annotations, and keeps the ones with a thumbs-down. Then createDataset takes the examples. We kept the source span ID in the metadata.

In AcruxCore, buildFromFeedback takes the reviewer's feedback IDs. Each comment becomes that example's grading criteria, and the input comes from the variables captured on the trace:.

Sources indicate that each tool scored the first version of the prompt on its own dataset. The judge read the reviewer's comment and the router's reply, and returned 1 for a match and 0 for a mismatch.

LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix each have an experiment runner that takes your evaluator function, and we gave all three the same judge prompt. AcruxCore grades with its built-in judge inside the optimize run. All four used the same judge model.

The first version fails almost every reviewed case. That is expected, because these are the cases people marked wrong. A score of 1 means the app model got that case right on the second call, or the judge accepted a wrong reply. We didn't check which.

Sources indicate that the judge can also run without your code. Besides the in-code evaluator we used, Langfuse has a managed LLM-as-a-judge that runs on production traces and on experiments, with your own judge prompt. LangSmith has online evaluators, which you set up in its UI, for the same job.

According to recent reports, an optimizer reads the failing cases and the reviewer comments, writes latest versions of the prompt, and scores each one with the judge. This is the step that turns feedback into a better prompt, and it's where the four tools differ most.

LangSmith's API reference lists an optimize prompt job (POST /api/v1/repos/optimize-job). It takes a prompt name, a dataset name, evaluator IDs and an algorithm, promptim or demo. No method in the TypeScript SDK wraps it, so we called it with fetch. We gave it a code evaluator that checks the reply against the reviewer's correct answer.

Sources indicate that the job was accepted and reported successful about ten seconds later. It ran no experiment on the dataset. With auto_commit set to true, it added no fresh commit to the prompt. We found no guide for this endpoint, so we may have configured it wrongly, but the job record and its logs gave no error to act on.

LangSmith's documented route to prompt optimization is promptim, which its README calls an experimental library. It is a Python package with a CLI, and it can add a human review step through LangSmith annotation queues.

According to recent reports, langfuse has no optimizer. Its blog demonstrates a workflow with Claude Code agent skills that reads Langfuse data and edits the prompt. That workflow runs in a coding agent, not in your app's code.

Sources indicate that phoenix's Optimize Prompts Automatically tutorial uses Arize's prompt-learning package, which you clone from GitHub and install with pip. The Phoenix TypeScript client has no optimizer export, and the tutorial runs outside Phoenix. Arize's commercial platform, Arize AX, has prompt optimization built in.

For Python teams, there are more options: Opik's Agent Optimizer and DSPy both rewrite prompts from a dataset and a metric. This article covers TypeScript.

Its optimize run takes the dataset and drafts three rewrites of the production prompt. It runs each rewrite and the current production version on every example, and the judge grades all of them:.

The run finished with this report:.

The three rewrites tied, so we took candidate A. Its rationale: "Added explicit priority rules for each category and clarified that access-blocking challenges are P0, billing errors are P1, and feature requests are P2, overriding tone/urgency." The Improve a prompt from feedback guide covers the dashboard version of this step.

According to recent reports, A rewrite that passes the cases it was built from can still fail on new tickets. So we ran both prompts on the 15 holdout tickets, three times each, outside every tool. The script calls the model directly and checks the category and the priority against the expected answer. No judge is involved.

The two misses are worth reading:.

Recent findings suggest that both come from one line in the rewrite: "P1 for bugs without workaround." That rule isn't in the team's policy, and no reviewer wrote it. The optimizer made it up to explain the examples it had. There was also no outage in the traffic set's thumbs-down cases, because the first version routed that one correctly. So no comment ever stated that a full outage is P0.

It has been revealed that the optimizer learns only from what customers marked wrong. Anything they never marked stays a guess, and the rationale won't tell you which rules are guesses. Read the rewritten prompt before you promote it.

Sources indicate that in LangSmith, Langfuse and Phoenix, shipping a newly introduced version is a tag or label move. We indicated those calls in the prompt-management article. Here there was no rewrite to ship, so the step didn't apply.

Recent findings suggest that in AcruxCore, promotion commits the candidate as a new prompt version and moves the production alias to it. Nothing else moves:.

The app renders production on every call, so the next ticket used version 2 without a deploy.

Use LangSmith if your team already works in it and writes Python. Feedback, queues, datasets and experiments all work from TypeScript, and promptim covers optimization from Python.

Use Langfuse if you want a managed judge that runs on live traces with your own prompt. Plan to write the dataset glue code and the rewrite step yourself.

In a recent development, use Phoenix if you already trace with OpenTelemetry and annotate spans. Strategy to move to Python, or to Arize AX, for optimization.

Use AcruxCore if you want all six steps from TypeScript in one tool, including the rewrite. Keep a human on the promote button.

#11454. A classic brain test exposed AI's biggest weakness

📅 10 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (749 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A classic brain test exposed AI's biggest weakness

📅 10 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, artificial intelligence systems can write essays, answer questions, and solve complex problems.
  • Researchers led by Suketu Patel put several leading AI models through a well-known psychology experiment called the Stroop task.
  • The Stroop task is a classic psychological test that has been used for decades to study attention, concentration, and self-control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, artificial intelligence systems can write essays, answer questions, and solve complex problems. But latest research suggests they may struggle with something humans do every day: staying focused on the task at hand when distractions get in the way.

Researchers led by Suketu Patel put several leading AI models through a well-known psychology experiment called the Stroop task. The results revealed a significant difference between how AI systems process information and how the human brain manages attention.

The Stroop task is a classic psychological test that has been used for decades to study attention, concentration, and self-control.

In the test, color words such as "red," "blue," or "green" are displayed in colored ink. Sometimes the word and the ink color match. For example, the word "red" might appear in red ink. Other times they conflict, such as the word "red" printed in blue ink.

Participants are asked to name the color of the ink rather than read the word itself.

That sounds simple, but it creates a challenge because reading words is an automatic habit for most people. The brain must suppress the urge to read the word and instead focus on identifying the ink color.

Psychologists often use the task to measure what is known as executive control, a set of mental processes that helps people regulate attention, resist distractions, and stay focused on goals.

The researchers wanted to see whether modern large language models (LLMs) handle this challenge in the same way humans do.

LLMs are the AI systems behind tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. They are trained on enormous amounts of text and learn patterns in language, allowing them to generate responses that often appear remarkably human.

When given short lists containing five color words, the AI systems generally performed well, even when the words and colors did not match.

However, the picture changed dramatically as the lists became longer.

It has been revealed that GPT-4o achieved 91% accuracy when working with five words. At ten words, its accuracy fell to 57%. When the list expanded to forty words, accuracy dropped to just 15%.

Claude 3.5 Sonnet maintained stable performance through lists of twenty words but then experienced a sharp decline, falling to 24% accuracy with forty-word lists.

The researchers observed similar patterns in GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, and Gemini 2.5.

The challenge became even more difficult when matching and mismatched color words appeared together in the same list.

In a recent development, under those conditions, performance deteriorated further. Accuracy for the mismatched items dropped to nearly zero in some cases.

It has been revealed that according to the researchers, the AI models had trouble maintaining the instruction to identify ink colors. Instead, they increasingly defaulted to reading the words themselves.

In other words, the systems appeared unable to consistently suppress the response they had been most heavily trained to produce.

In a recent development, this finding is particularly interesting because humans face a similar conflict. People are generally much better at reading words than naming ink colors. Yet despite this bias, most individuals can maintain high accuracy and stable performance even when confronted with long lists of conflicting words and colors.

According to recent reports, human Attention vs. Machine Attention.

The study highlights an important distinction between human and artificial intelligence.

Although modern AI systems can produce impressive language and reasoning capabilities, their underlying mechanisms differ from the attention processes found in biological brains.

Humans can often sustain focus on a specific goal while filtering out competing information. The results suggest that current AI models may struggle with this type of cognitive control when tasks become increasingly demanding.

The researchers argue that the performance collapse seen in these experiments points to fundamental limitations in today's large language models. While AI can sometimes mimic human behavior, its ability to maintain attention appears to operate very differently from the way people do.

The findings offer a reminder that even the most advanced AI systems still have weaknesses, particularly when tasks require them to resist distractions and stay focused over extended sequences of information.

#11452. Brain-inspired chip runs near absolute zero and could transform quantum computing

📅 12 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (557 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Brain-inspired chip runs near absolute zero and could transform quantum computing

📅 12 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions.
  • The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang.
  • Quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) have unveiled a significant advance in cryogenic electronics that could help overcome key challenges in quantum computing and support future deep space missions. The team, from HKU's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Centre for Advanced Semiconductors and Integrated Circuits (CASIC), developed a programmable neuromorphic hardware platform capable of operating at temperatures near absolute zero.

The research was led by Professor Yuhao Zhang and PhD student Xin Yang. Their work introduces a new method for generating and controlling negative differential resistance (NDR) in industry standard Silicon Carbide (SiC) MOSFETs. Using this approach, the researchers demonstrated for the first time that a single transistor can reproduce the energy efficient "spiking" activity of biological neurons at temperatures as low as 10mK.

Brain-Inspired Hardware for Quantum Computing.

Quantum computers depend on sophisticated control electronics to manage qubits, which are highly sensitive and must be kept at millikelvin temperatures. Existing silicon based control systems consume considerable power and produce unwanted heat, making it necessary to position them away from the qubits themselves. That distance creates extensive wiring requirements that can hinder performance and make large scale quantum computers more difficult to build.

"Our work introduces a hardware platform that can be integrated alongside quantum processors," said Professor Zhang. "By using the unique carrier dynamics in silicon carbide, we can create circuits that are thousands of times more energy-efficient than conventional electronics, significantly reducing the thermal load on cryogenic systems.".

Silicon Carbide Reveals Unique Cryogenic Behavior.

The team found that SiC MOSFETs display a strong "S-shape" NDR effect when cooled below 2K. This behavior is driven by electron-donor impact ionization (EDII). Unlike other technologies that depend on heat generated within a device, the newly observed mechanism arises directly from the material's atomic properties. As a result, it remains highly stable and can be reproduced consistently across different manufacturing batches.

"This is a robust and scalable approach," said Mr. Yang. "Because SiC is already used globally in electric vehicles and power grids, we can leverage existing industrial foundries to manufacture these cryogenic chips on 300-mm wafers.".

From Artificial Neurons to Deep Space Missions.

According to recent reports, the study also demonstrated that these artificial neurons can be linked together, or "cascaded," into larger networks. This capability could enable advanced local data processing at cryogenic temperatures and improve notable quantum computing functions such as quantum error correction and real time quantum control.

Recent findings suggest that the potential applications extend well beyond quantum computing. Because the circuits are designed to operate reliably in extremely cold environments, they could also be valuable for deep space exploration. Future systems may be able to function in the harsh conditions found on the Moon's surface or in the distant regions of our solar system.

The findings were published in Nature Communications in a paper titled "Cryogenic neuromorphic circuits using gate-controlled negative differential resistance in silicon carbide.".

Industry observers note that there are plenty of people out there who, after falling out with friends, family, and partners, want to get their own back in some way. Plenty go on social media and make posts about the situation, while others are happy to throw clothes and other items away.

In the case of Joseph Gerard Cancellare Jr., the 68-year-old was arrested on November 12, more than a year after he allegedly sent a card full of peanut butter to a former friend.

According to reports, the woman – who hasn’t been named – admitted to being a former friend of the 68-year-old and had spent time socially with him over the last two decades.

Additionally, some reports state that Cancellare Jr. blamed the woman for being the reason why his ex-wife decided to divorce him, hence wanting to get some payback.

He was taken into custody by the Plantation Police Department and now faces charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and culpable negligence exposing another person to harm.

The woman told police that the 68-year-old was “well aware” of the allergy, and that even breathing in air around peanuts is “life-threatening” to her.

#11448. SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

📅 19 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1409 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

SpaceX wants to build AI data centers in space. Will it work?

📅 19 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, imagine if one tech giant could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy.
  • Recent findings suggest that among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers.
  • Industry observers note that the logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, imagine if one tech giant could become the railroad, electric utility and cloud-computing provider of the emerging space economy. That potential fueled excitement around the long-anticipated initial public offering of SpaceX. Investors are not simply betting on rockets anymore. They are betting on an entire orbital ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that among the most ambitious and challenging ideas riding this wave of enthusiasm is something that sounds almost like science fiction: orbital data centers. SpaceX may be one of the most well-known companies seeking to build them, but it is not the only one.

Industry observers note that the logic is seductive: Launch the data centers into orbit, where solar energy is abundant and land, water and local power grids are no longer constraints. As artificial intelligence drives an explosion in computing demand, companies are pitching orbital data centers as a way to escape the growing environmental and infrastructure pressures of Earth-based computing. Data centers often also face backlash from the public at having these centers located in their communities.

But there is a vast difference between launching satellites and operating an industrial-scale computing infrastructure in orbit. Space is unforgiving. Radiation damages electronics. The electronics generate enormous amounts of heat, and getting rid of that heat is surprisingly difficult in space. Repairs are extraordinarily expensive, and every pound launched into orbit still carries a significant cost.

We are engineering professors who study data center design and space systems engineering. Building a space-based data center will involve considerations from both sides.

First off, consider what goes into an Earth-based data center, like those that you’ve probably begun to see pop up everywhere. These facilities power cloud computing, video streaming, online banking, scientific computing and, increasingly, artificial intelligence. But a data center is much more than a room full of servers.

It has been revealed that A data center needs several things to operate reliably. The first is electric power. Servers, networking equipment and storage devices consume large amounts of electricity, and that power demand is growing rapidly with AI.

Sources indicate that the second is cooling. Almost all the electricity consumed by servers eventually becomes heat. If that heat is not removed quickly and reliably, equipment performance drops, failures increase and the data center can shut down. Cooling systems often include air handling units, chillers, cooling towers, pumps and, increasingly, liquid-cooling equipment. In many facilities, cooling is the largest energy consumer after the computing equipment itself.

The third is physical infrastructure, including the necessary land, buildings, structural support, backup power, water systems, communication networks and maintenance access. Data centers also need to be close enough to consumers and network backbones to provide fast digital services.

In short, Earth-based data centers are large electrical and thermal infrastructure systems built around computing hardware.

So what would it take to build these data centers in space, and why are companies finding this possibility such an interesting business proposition?

As on Earth, these data centers would require massive amounts of power. In space, this power would come from solar panels. The Sun always shines in space and can’t be blocked by clouds. However, depending on the orbit the solar panels are put in, the Earth may shadow them for some portion of the orbit.

And even the best solar cells available today can convert only about half the sunlight that hits them to electricity.

According to recent reports, another potential advantage found in space is cooling. The cold background of space (near minus 455 degrees Fahrenheit, or minus 270 degrees Celsius) creates an opportunity: waste heat from the data center could escape into space through radiators, keeping the electronics cool.

In principle, that design could eliminate some of the bulky and water-intensive cooling infrastructure used on Earth. However, those thermal radiators would require a large amount of surface area, and that would be in addition to the area required by the solar panels.

In a recent development, in space, there is no air to blow across hot equipment and help heat escape. The heat has to leave as infrared radiation, which is a relatively slow process. As a result, removing 10 megawatts of waste heat can require radiator surfaces comparable to the size of two football fields.

Sources indicate that space-based data centers could also avoid some of the local conflicts that come with building large data centers on the ground. Many communities resist new data center developments because of their land use, energy and water demand, and noise and environmental impact.

A space-based system would avoid competing for local land and water resources, and it would not generate neighborhood noise or require local zoning approval in the same way.

According to recent reports, however, space is already getting crowded, and launching thousands of large orbital data centers would accelerate this problem. Orbital debris and micrometeorites are hazards because they can puncture the space data center, and a worst-case collision could destroy it and create even more space debris.

The frequency of space debuts necessary to send all the equipment to orbit may also become a concern for some communities. SpaceX has had protests at its launch complex in Boca Chica, Texas, from local activists who argue that its rocket testing and launches damage the surrounding environment.

All that data would need to be sent between Earth and these data centers – and between the data centers themselves – using radio waves or laser communications systems. Although satellite constellations such as Starlink and Amazon Leo have demonstrated that doing this is possible, the amount of data sent to and from space would balloon.

Recent findings suggest that these data centers, along with their solar panels and radiators, cannot be launched in one piece and would need to be assembled in space. This process would require latest equipment for in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing.

Sources indicate that another key challenge is the refresh cycle of computing hardware. Data center servers are not built to last forever. Operators on Earth usually replace or upgrade hardware every three to five years as chips improve, workloads change and equipment ages.

Sources indicate that and equipment failures can require replacing components. The refresh and repair processes are relatively straightforward on Earth, where workers can physically remove and replace servers.

Sources indicate that in space, refresh and repair becomes much harder. Hardware sent to orbit may be difficult or too expensive to upgrade. If the computing platform cannot be updated, or too many components fail, it may become obsolete long before the surrounding infrastructure reaches the end of its useful life.

In a field where performance improves so rapidly and demand from computing continues to increase, this hurdle could prove a major economic and operational challenge.

Then there is the harshness of space. These data centers would be in a near vacuum, with constant radiation hitting them. And depending on their orbit, they would go from hot when in the sunlight to cold in Earth’s shadow many times a day. All of these challenges, and more, are concerns that will need to be addressed.

Despite these challenges, companies are moving forward with designing space-based data centers. SpaceX just confirmed the design for its AI1 Compute Satellite, which it hopes to use as an orbital data center spacecraft. However, this satellite is 100 to 1,000 times less capable than current Earth-based data centers.

Not every computing task makes sense to do in space. Many data center applications depend on fast response times and close connections to users on Earth. Financial transactions, interactive AI services and most cloud applications are extremely sensitive to delay.

More feasible early applications may be those that are less latency-sensitive and more tightly connected to space operations. Examples could include processing Earth observation data from satellites, military or intelligence data processing, scientific computing related to space missions, or specialized computing for satellites and other space assets.

In other words, the first viable space data centers may serve space-based customers before they compete with mainstream cloud data centers on Earth.

Friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

Recent findings suggest that in this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Industry observers note that friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge showed up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

It's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it claims first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

So why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:.

Most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

Here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

It has been revealed that mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

Two storage rules save you pain later:.

Recent findings suggest that the good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:.

Then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:.

In a recent development, the psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

For digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

The cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

According to recent reports, use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:.

It has been revealed that store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

Keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

According to recent reports, the pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:.

Recent findings suggest that the verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

Sources indicate that the hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only shows how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand upcoming on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

Chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

According to recent reports, one endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:.

Industry observers note that the tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

Industry observers note that on top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

If you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:.

It has been revealed that that evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Industry observers note that automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

According to recent reports, card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

In a recent development, the threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:.

It has been revealed that if you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Sources indicate that always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

The code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

It has been revealed that PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

It has been revealed that here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:.

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code problems the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

Then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:.

Industry observers note that eaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

Don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

Sources indicate that if you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

Sources indicate that true fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

It has been revealed that mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Recent findings suggest that partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

According to recent reports, no. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

Industry observers note that nearly 20 years after she died in 2006 at the age of 97, Yuan’s gravestone is attracting widespread attention in China. According to the South China Morning Post, before her death, Yuan asked her son to engrave a selection of her herbal formulas on her grave so they would remain publicly available.

While her name, date of birth, and date of death are still featured on her grave, Yuan’s grave is also filled with rows of ingredients and measurements for various medicinal remedies.

It has been revealed that 100 prescriptions carved on a tombstone. But why? ❤️In Henan, China, the tombstone of a TCM doctor named Yuan Shufang has become a destination for people seeking traditional medicine knowledge.All 100 prescriptions include the names of the herbs and their dosages — something… pic.twitter.com/WRjFTqJGKd.

Since a local outlet covered the findings in November 2026, many visitors have travelled to her resting spot and photographed the inscriptions and copied them by hand.

One traditional Chinese medicine practitioner who visited the grave three times told SCMP that experienced doctors often share which ingredients they use, but leave students to work out the quantities themselves, which makes this practice quite rare.

Recent findings suggest that “Master Yuan revealed the exact amounts she used. We only need to make some adjustments based on her work when treating our patients. Few doctors could match her generosity and open-mindedness,” Duan said.

Tech Report: Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a latest technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.
  • Sources indicate that published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances.
  • It has been revealed that type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a latest technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.

Sources indicate that published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances. Unlike many current approaches, the method relies mainly on imaging data rather than expensive spectroscopic observations. The advance is expected to help astronomers take full advantage of the enormous datasets that will soon arrive from next generation sky surveys, particularly those conducted by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

It has been revealed that type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode. Because these explosions reach nearly the same intrinsic brightness, astronomers use them as "standard candles": by comparing their actual brightness with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can calculate their distance.

According to recent reports, these measurements played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Scientists attribute that acceleration to dark energy, one of the most significant unsolved questions in modern physics.

Sources indicate that however, there is an important complication. Type Ia supernovae are not perfectly identical.

How Host Galaxies Affect Supernova Measurements.

It has been revealed that over the past 20 years, astronomers have found that a supernova's observed brightness is influenced by the galaxy where it occurs. Supernovae found in older or more massive galaxies can appear slightly different from those occurring in younger or less massive galaxies.

According to recent reports, researchers have typically accounted for these differences using relatively simple correction methods. While useful, these approximations can limit the accuracy of distance measurements and, in turn, the precision of cosmological studies.

A Unified Model of Supernovae and the Universe.

Industry observers note that the new framework addresses this challenge by modeling multiple factors simultaneously. Rather than treating each component independently, the researchers built a single, integrated model that includes the supernova explosions themselves, their host galaxies, the dust that alters their light, changes in supernova rates throughout cosmic history, and even the expansion of the Universe.

By connecting all of these ingredients within one statistical and physical framework, the team can capture relationships that are often overlooked when the pieces are analyzed separately.

"A powerful way of modelling the Universe is to simulate it ab initio in the computer using Bayesian inference," says Raúl Jiménez (ICREA-ICCUB), co-author of the study. "This provides a way to vary all possible parameters at the same time to predict what Universe we live in. Furthermore, by having this capacity, one can look into possible 'unknown unknown' systematics to understand their effect. The impact of these systematics in our inference is arguably the most crucial missing ingredient in current approaches to model the Universe.".

Using Artificial Intelligence To Analyze the Cosmos.

Building such a comprehensive model would normally require enormous computing power. To make the approach practical, the researchers turned to a modern technique called simulation-based inference.

The process begins with scientists generating large numbers of simulated universes based on physical models. A neural network (a type of artificial intelligence) then learns how the simulated observations relate to the physical properties that produced them. Once trained, the system can compare real astronomical observations with its simulations and determine the most likely underlying parameters.

This strategy makes it possible to analyze tens of thousands of supernovae simultaneously, a task that would be impractical using traditional techniques.

Accurate Galaxy Distances From Images Alone.

One of the study's most significant findings is that the framework can determine galaxy distances (redshifts) with high accuracy using only imaging data.

Redshift measures how much a galaxy's light has been stretched as the Universe expands. It provides information about both the galaxy's distance and how far back in time we are observing it.

According to the researchers, the newly introduced method delivers redshift estimates with precision comparable to spectroscopic measurements, but without requiring spectra. This capability is especially important because upcoming surveys are expected to identify millions of supernova candidates, while only a small percentage can realistically receive spectroscopic follow-up observations.

Ready for the Rubin Observatory Data Deluge.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, currently being built in Chile, is expected to begin a decade long survey of the sky in the near future. During that mission, it will discover an unprecedented number of supernovae. Roughly 99% of those objects will be observed only photometrically, meaning through images taken in different colors rather than detailed spectra.

The CIGaRS framework was specifically developed with this challenge in mind.

"Unlike other frameworks, which require analytic simplifications, our no-compromise end-to-end simulation-based inference approach is uniquely capable of extracting the full cosmological and astrophysical information from the Rubin Observatory's hard-earned data, while avoiding the pitfalls of selection and modelling biases," claims Konstantin Karchev (ICCUB-SISSA Trieste), lead author of the study.

Insights Into How Supernovae Form.

According to recent reports, the benefits extend beyond measuring dark energy. The framework also provides newly introduced information about the origins of Type Ia supernovae themselves.

By reconstructing how supernova occurrence rates vary with the ages of stars in different galaxies, the model helps scientists investigate long standing questions about the systems that eventually produce these explosions.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that combining physics based simulations with artificial intelligence can overcome several limitations of current cosmological methods. They estimate that the approach could improve cosmological constraints by as much as a factor of four compared with traditional techniques that depend only on a relatively small sample of spectroscopically observed supernovae.

As the Rubin Observatory prepares to usher in a upcoming era of astronomical discovery, tools such as CIGaRS could help scientists extract the maximum amount of information from its observations and gain a deeper understanding of the Universe.

A man in South Korea has apologized after admitting to cheating to get the top score on his certified tax accountancy exam, all because he wanted to make his parents proud again.

Over the years, plenty of people have found ways to cheat on their exams and get away with it. However, in the case of Han Won-seok, he has become the target of a viral investigation into South Korea’s certified tax accountancy exam.

According to recent reports, the 34-year-old, from Seoul, came out as the top scorer in the test’s first round, only getting one of the 160 questions wrong. He scored 397.5 out of a possible 400 points, raising suspicions about the result.

After some backlash, Won-seok joined his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, on his YouTube channel, admitting to the cheating after using a mini-camera and generative AI.

“I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI,” Won-seok said.

“I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating.”.

Sources indicate that the 34-year-old apologised to other exam takers who have now come under investigation because of him. He also added that he wanted a high score in order to make his parents proud of him again by getting a well-paid job.

As per Yonhap in Korea, Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency have also placed a number of it’s investiatiors onto the case after receiving a “written confession” from Won-seok and his lawyer about the incident.

South Korea files first criminal lawsuit over exam cheating with AI smart glasses.

University professor refuses to grade homework as students keep using AI.

Students are using smart glasses to cheat on tests at school.

Sources indicate that the 34-year-old’s certificate from the exam has been revoked, and he may face criminal charges over it. It wouldn’t be the first time either as, back in July, South Korea filed its first criminal case over the use of AI-powered smart glasses as a man was caught cheating.

Recent findings suggest that the rise in popularity of smart glasses has given students additional power in cheating on exams. Over in China, services are being run so that test takers can rent smart glasses solely for their exams.

However, in the United States, one university professor is now refusing to grade work completed by students due to the fear of AI assistance. “Grading for correctness just adds a huge incentive for them to use AI for homework instead of doing it themselves, and penalizes students for honesty,” professor Richard Borcherds said.

Tech Report: Quantum mechanics once baffled scientists. Now it's changing the world

📅 05 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science.
  • In a upcoming perspective article published in Science, Dr.
  • Sources indicate that "Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," remarked Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science. The theory challenged conventional thinking and left even leading physicists struggling to make sense of its implications. A century later, it has become the foundation of technologies that influence daily life, including lasers, microchips, secure communications, and emerging quantum computers.

In a upcoming perspective article published in Science, Dr. Marlan Scully of Texas A&M University reflects on the remarkable evolution of quantum mechanics, from an abstract theory about tiny particles to a powerful framework helping researchers tackle some of the most difficult questions in science.

Sources indicate that "Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," remarked Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University. "Now it's driving innovations that were unimaginable just a generation ago.".

Scully has played a major role in advancing the field. He co-authored the influential textbook Quantum Optics, a resource that has educated generations of physicists. His research in coherent nanoscale laser spectroscopy helped make it possible to study molecules with atomic-scale precision. He has also developed groundbreaking concepts involving quantum heat engines, which challenge traditional assumptions about thermodynamic efficiency and may one day lead to newly introduced energy technologies.

From Schrödinger's Cat to Quantum Technology.

One of the most famous illustrations of quantum mechanics came in 1935, when Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat paradox. The thought experiment suggested that a cat could exist in a state that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Schrödinger introduced the idea to highlight how strange quantum theory appeared.

Today, those once-bizarre concepts have moved far beyond philosophical debates.

In a recent development, "That 'quantum weirdness' is no longer just a philosophical puzzle," noted Scully. "It's the foundation of quantum computing, quantum cryptography and even gravitational wave detection.".

The foundations of quantum mechanics were built by pioneers including Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg. They developed two different mathematical approaches, wave mechanics and matrix mechanics, to describe quantum systems. Over time, these approaches were unified and contributed to the development of quantum field theory, which explains how particles interact through electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

In a recent development, their work expanded on Niels Bohr's early atomic model, which pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus much like planets orbit the sun. While later discoveries refined that picture, Bohr's model helped pave the way for modern quantum theory.

Quantum Coherence and the Rise of Lasers.

According to recent reports, among the most important concepts in quantum mechanics is quantum coherence. This phenomenon allows particles such as atoms and photons to remain linked in a coordinated state, even across significant distances.

Quantum coherence led directly to the development of the laser, a technology that many once believed could never work. Today, lasers are used throughout modern society, from supermarket barcode scanners to vision correction procedures and advanced scientific instruments.

Coherence is also closely tied to quantum entanglement, the phenomenon that prompted Albert Einstein to describe it as "spooky action at a distance.".

According to recent reports, entanglement enables particles to share information through uniquely quantum properties. These effects form the basis of quantum encryption systems and improve the sensitivity of sophisticated instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which detects tiny ripples in spacetime.

Quantum Heat Engines Challenge Classical Limits.

One of the more surprising applications of quantum physics involves quantum heat engines.

It has been revealed that traditional engines are constrained by the Carnot Limit, which defines the maximum efficiency allowed by classical thermodynamics. Researchers have found that by exploiting quantum coherence, it may be possible to create engines that exceed those classical limits.

"It's a striking example of how quantum principles can rewrite the rules of classical physics," Scully noted.

Quantum Biology, Gravity, and Turbulence.

The influence of quantum mechanics now extends far beyond physics.

In biology, techniques such as coherent Raman spectroscopy allow researchers to examine viruses and other structures at the nanoscale, providing valuable insights into the microscopic world.

Quantum ideas are also shaping efforts to understand the universe itself. Scientists working on concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity are attempting to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein's theory of relativity, one of the biggest unsolved problems in modern physics.

Sources indicate that researchers are even applying quantum concepts to the long-standing challenge of understanding turbulence. The chaotic motion of air and fluids affects weather patterns, climate systems, and aircraft performance. By studying superfluid helium, a substance that displays unusual quantum behavior, scientists are uncovering patterns that could improve climate modeling, storm prediction, and aviation safety.

The Next Century of Quantum Discovery.

Despite a century of success, quantum mechanics continues to raise profound questions.

Can gravity be quantized (i.e., does gravity behave like other forces at the quantum level)? Could quantum computers transform medicine and materials science? What latest insights about the universe might emerge from future quantum technologies?

Scully believes the search for answers is only beginning.

Recent findings suggest that "At the start of the 20th century, many thought physics was complete," he said. "Now, in the 21st century, we know the adventure is just beginning.".

Five Ways Quantum Mechanics Affects Everyday Life.

#11437. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought
