Introducing Falcon-H1-Arabic: Pushing the Boundaries of Arabic Language AI with Hybrid Architecture

📅 05 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discover more in our official blogpost, featuring an interactive experience.
  • Industry observers note that the journey of building world-class Arabic language models has been one of continuous learning and iteration.
  • It has been revealed that when we rolled out Falcon-Arabic a few months ago, the response from the community was both humbling and enlightening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discover more in our official blogpost, featuring an interactive experience.

Industry observers note that the journey of building world-class Arabic language models has been one of continuous learning and iteration. Today, we're excited to announce Falcon-H1-Arabic, our most advanced Arabic language model family to date, representing a significant leap forward in both architecture and capabilities. This release embodies months of research, community feedback, and technical innovation, culminating in three powerful models that set newly introduced standards for Arabic natural language processing.

It has been revealed that when we rolled out Falcon-Arabic a few months ago, the response from the community was both humbling and enlightening. Developers, researchers and students across the Arab world used the model for real use cases, pushing them to its limits and providing invaluable feedback. We learned where the model excelled and, more importantly, where it struggled. Long-context understanding, dialectal variations, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific knowledge emerged as key areas requiring deeper attention.

We didn't just want to make incremental improvements, we wanted to fundamentally rethink our approach. The result is Falcon-H1-Arabic, a model family that addresses every piece of feedback we received while introducing architectural innovations that were previously unexplored in Arabic language modeling.

Falcon-H1-Arabic 3B, 7B, 34B models outperforming all SOTA models of similar sizes and sometimes bigger.

Falcon-H1-Arabic is built on the Falcon-H1 hybrid architecture, which integrates State Space Models (Mamba) and Transformer attention within every block. Both components run in parallel and their representations are fused before the block’s output projection. This design provides the linear-time scalability of Mamba for extremely long sequences while preserving the precise long-range modeling capabilities of attention. For Arabic, with its rich morphology and flexible sentence structures, this approach significantly improves coherence and reasoning across extended text. We've deployed this architecture across three scales (3B, 7B, 34B parameters), each balancing capacity, efficiency, and deployability for different use cases from edge devices to enterprise applications.

According to recent reports, falcon-H1 architecture. Attention and SSM run in parallel within each block; their outputs are concatenated before the block’s output projection. The number of SSM/Attention heads depends on the model size. More details on the Falcon-H1 technical report.

We've dramatically increased context capabilities from Falcon-Arabic's 32K limit to 128K tokens for the 3B model and 256K tokens for both the 7B and 34B models. At 256K tokens (~200,000 words), these models can process several novels or hundreds of pages of technical documentation enabling applications in legal analysis, medical records, academic research, and extended conversations that were previously impractical. Our post-training specifically addresses "lost in the middle" challenges to ensure models effectively utilize their full context range, not just accept long inputs.

According to recent reports, we rebuilt our pre-training data pipeline from the ground up to better reflect the complexity of Arabic. This began with a multi-stage quality filtering process tailored to Arabic orthography, morphology, diacritics, and syntactic patterns. Instead of heuristic filtering, we used deep linguistic analysis to isolate coherent, well-structured text and remove noise commonly found in open-web corpora. The result is a significantly cleaner, more stylistically consistent Arabic dataset.

Dialect coverage was another key priority. Arabic is not monolithic; Modern Standard Arabic coexists with dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, and Maghrebi, each with distinct vocabularies and grammatical constructions. We expanded dialectal sources substantially so the models would understand and generate the full spectrum of real-world Arabic rather than leaning disproportionately toward formal MSA. To maintain global reasoning and domain diversity, we also preserved the multilingual capabilities of Falcon-H1 by training the Arabic models on an almost equal mix of Arabic, English, and multilingual content totalling around 300 Billion Tokens. This ensures strong performance in code, STEM, and cross-lingual reasoning. The following figure illustrates the distribution of the pre-training data across languages and categories. All values are expressed in billions of tokens.

Sources indicate that after pre-training, Falcon-H1-Arabic undergoes a focused post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). During SFT, we expose the models to high-quality Arabic instructions, curated long-context examples, and structured reasoning tasks that teach them to follow directives, maintain coherence over extended sequences, and ground their responses in relevant information. This stage is crucial for ensuring that the models can actually use their large context windows which does not emerge automatically from architecture alone.

According to recent reports, we follow SFT with a targeted DPO phase to refine alignment, conversational quality, and preference consistency. DPO helps the models balance long-context reasoning with general linguistic competence, improving helpfulness and reducing common failure modes such as drifting, overuse of context, or neglecting earlier information. Throughout both stages, we carefully monitor for catastrophic forgetting and maintain a controlled curriculum so gains in long-context behavior do not come at the expense of core reasoning or factual accuracy. The result is a family of models that handles extended documents and dialogue with ease while preserving strong performance on everyday language tasks.

It has been revealed that beyond benchmark-oriented optimization, our post-training process deliberately strengthens areas that traditional evaluations do not fully capture, including conversational faithfulness, rhetorical organization, structured follow-ups, and discourse coherence. These enhancements significantly boost the model’s practical usefulness, making Falcon-H1-Arabic more dependable in real multi-turn dialogue, instruction execution, and long-context conversational flows.

According to recent reports, numbers tell an vital part of the story. On the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard (OALL), a comprehensive benchmark evaluating Arabic language understanding across diverse tasks, Falcon-H1-Arabic achieves state-of-the-art results at every scale we tested. Note that our scores may vary slightly from those reported on the leaderboard, as we used vLLM as the backend instead of the leaderboard’s Accelerate-based implementation. These differences are typically under one point while offering significantly faster runtime.

Beyond OALL, we also report results on the 3LM benchmark for STEM-related tasks on both synthetic and native splits; Arabculture for Arabic culture assessment; and AraDice for Arabic dialect coverage across Levantine, and Egyptian varieties as well as Arabic culture across 6 countries. The reported AraDice score is the average of all the 3 scores.

In a recent development, starting with the 3B model, the performance is exceptional. It reaches approximately 62% on OALL, outperforming all small-scale models, including Gemma-4B, Qwen3-4B, and Phi-4-mini by roughly ten points. On 3LM, the main Arabic STEM benchmark, it scores around 82% on the native split and 73% on the synthetic split. It also achieves about 62% on the ArabCulture benchmark and around 50% across AraDice dialect evaluation (Egyptian, Gulf, and Levantine). This makes Falcon-H1-Arabic-3B a high-quality, highly efficient model suitable for edge deployments, real-time applications, and agentic systems where latency and cost matter.

Sources indicate that the 7B model continues this upward trajectory. With a score of 71.7% on OALL, it surpasses all models in the ~10B class, including Fanar-9B, Allam-7B*, and Qwen3-8B. On 3LM, it reaches about 92% on the native split and 85% on the synthetic one. AraDice scores rise into the mid-50s across all dialects, and ArabCulture results approach 80%. This model strikes an ideal balance between capability and deployability, making it the most practical choice for general-purpose Arabic NLP in production environments.

The 34B model represents our flagship system and establishes a upcoming state of the art for Arabic language modeling. It reaches approximately 75% on OALL, outperforming not only models of similar size but even much larger systems such as Llama-3.3-70B and AceGPT2-32B. Its 3LM scores reach about 96% on the native split and 94% on the synthetic one. On ArabCulture it scores close to 80%, and on AraDice it reaches around 53 across dialects. The fact that a 34B hybrid model surpasses the performance of 70B-scale transformers demonstrates the effectiveness of the Falcon-H1 architecture, the quality of the data, and the strength of the post-training pipeline.

These benchmark results validate our approach but also highlight an important reality: the frontier of Arabic language modeling is advancing rapidly. Each percentage point on these benchmarks represents countless hours of engineering effort, careful dataset curation, and architectural refinement. The margins by which Falcon-H1-Arabic leads aren't just statistical artifacts, they translate to meaningfully better user experiences in real-world applications.

Each model in the Falcon-H1-Arabic family is suited to different deployment scenarios. The 3B model is optimized for speed, cost-efficiency, and high-throughput systems, making it ideal for agentic workflows, on-device applications, low-latency chat, and environments with strict resource constraints. The 7B model serves as the general-purpose workhorse for most production applications, powering document understanding systems, chatbots, summarization pipelines, and content generation tools. The 34B model is designed for high-stakes domains where accuracy and long-range reasoning matter most, including legal analysis, medical summarization, academic research, and large-scale enterprise automation. Its extended context window makes it uniquely capable of analyzing hundreds of pages of text in a single pass while maintaining precise coherence.

Like all language models, Falcon-H1-Arabic may reflect biases from training data and can produce hallucinated information. Model outputs should not be used as sole authorities for medical, legal, or financial decisions without professional verification. Long-context performance may degrade at extreme ranges. We recommend task-specific evaluation and appropriate guardrails before deployment in production or sensitive applications.

According to recent reports, this work stands on the shoulders of many. We extend our gratitude to the Arabic NLP research community, whose open sharing of benchmarks, datasets, and methodologies enables progress across the field. Special thanks to our colleagues at TII: Ilyas Chahed, Younes Belkada, Dhia Eddine Rhaiem, Puneesh Khanna, Jingwei Zuo, Mikhail Lubinets, Slim Frikha, Maksim Velikanov, Kacper Piskorski, and Suhail Mohmad for their invaluable support during this project.

Sources indicate that impressive milestone for Arabic language AI. Falcon-H1-Arabic’s hybrid architecture is a strong step toward closing the performance gap in high-quality Arabic understanding and generation. Exciting to see innovation that’s not just scaling models, but rethinking architecture to better capture the richness and complexity of Arabic. Looking forward to seeing real-world applications and benchmarks. https://soch.sindhwildlife.com.pk/.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA today released Cosmos Reason 2, the latest advancement in open, reasoning vision language models for physical AI. Cosmos Reason 2 surpasses its previous version in accuracy and tops the Physical AI Bench and Physical Reasoning leaderboards as the #1 open model for visual understanding.

According to recent reports, since their introduction, vision-language models have rapidly improved at tasks like object and pattern recognition in images. But they still struggle with tasks humans find natural, like planning several steps ahead, dealing with uncertainty or adapting to new situations. Cosmos Reason is designed to close this gap by giving robots and AI agents stronger common sense and reasoning to solve complex problems step by step.

It has been revealed that cosmos Reason 2 is a state-of-the-art, open reasoning vision-language model (VLM) that enables robots and AI agents to see, understand, blueprint, and act in the physical world like humans. It uses common sense, physics, and prior knowledge to recognize how objects move across space and time to handle complex tasks, adapt to fresh situations, and figure out how to solve problems step by step.

Improved spatio-temporal understanding and timestamp precision.

Optimized performance with flexible deployment options from edge to cloud with 2B and 8B parameters model sizes.

Support for expanded set of spatial understanding and visual perception capabilities — 2D/3D point localization, bounding box coordinates, trajectory data, and OCR support.

Improved long-context understanding with 256K input tokens, up from 16K with Cosmos Reason 1.

Adaptable to multiple use cases with easy-to-use Cosmos Cookbook recipes.

Industry observers note that video analytics AI agents — These agents can extract valuable insights from massive volumes of video data to optimize processes. Cosmos Reason 2 builds on the capabilities of Cosmos Reason 1 and now provides OCR support, as well as 2D/3D point localization and a set of mark understanding.

Developers can jumpstart development of video analytics AI agents by using the NVIDIA blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Salesforce is transforming workplace safety and compliance by analyzing video footage captured by Cobalt robots with Agentforce and VSS blueprint with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

According to recent reports, data annotation and critique — Enable developers to automate high-quality annotation and critique of massive, diverse training datasets. Cosmos Reason provides time stamps and detailed descriptions for real or synthetically generated training videos.

Uber is exploring Cosmos Reason 2 to deliver accurate, searchable video captions for autonomous vehicle (AV) training data, enabling efficient identification of critical driving scenarios. This co-authored Reason 2 for AV Video Captioning and VQA recipe demonstrates how to fine-tune and evaluate Cosmos Reason 2-8B on annotated AV videos. Across multiple evaluation metrics, measurable improvements were achieved: BLEU scores improved 10.6% (0.113 → 0.125), MCQ-based VQA gained 0.67 percentage points (80.18% → 80.85%), and LingoQA increased 13.8% (63.2% → 77.0%). These gains demonstrate effective domain adaptation for AV applications.

According to recent reports, robot planning and reasoning — Act as the brain for deliberate, methodical decision-making in a robot vision language action (VLA) model. Cosmos Reason 2 now provides trajectory coordinates in addition to determining next steps.

Encord provides native support for Cosmos Reason 2 in its Data Agent library and AI data platform, enabling developers to leverage Cosmos Reason 2 as a VLA for robotics and other physical AI use cases.

Companies like Hitachi, Milestone and VAST Data are using Cosmos Reason to advance robotics, autonomous driving, and video analytics AI agents for traffic and workplace safety.

Try Cosmos Reason 2 on build.nvidia.com and experience the latest features with sample prompts for generating bounding boxes and robot trajectories. Upload your own videos and images for further analysis.

Industry observers note that download Cosmos Reason 2 models (2B and 8B) on Hugging Face or use Cosmos Reason 2 in the cloud. The model will be available soon on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. To get started, check out Cosmos Reason 2 documentation and the Cosmos Cookbook.

Cosmos Predict is a generative AI model that predicts future states of the physical world as video, based on text, image, or video inputs.

Cosmos Transfer is our lightest multicontrol model built for video to world style transfer.

NVIDIA GR00T N1.6 is an open reasoning vision language action (VLA) model, purpose-built for humanoid robots, that unlocks full body control and uses NVIDIA Cosmos Reason for better reasoning and contextual understanding.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Chinese influencer has sparked backlash after using AI to digitally recreate his late grandfather and continue posting videos to their popular fashion account, which has nearly six million followers.

The social media account, known as “Kang Kang and Grandpa,” became a viral sensation thanks to videos showing Grandpa Kang modeling stylish outfits, streetwear, and accessories alongside his grandson.

However, in September 2026, Kang Kang unveiled that his grandfather had died peacefully in his sleep, leaving fans devastated.

The account had built an audience of approximately 5.8 million followers, with viewers praising Grandpa Kang’s fashion sense and positive attitude toward aging.

In a recent development, in October, the account unexpectedly returned with new videos featuring the deceased influencer, but there was a catch. His grandson had used artificial intelligence to bring him back digitally.

According to the South China Morning Post, Kang Kang uploaded several AI-generated videos, including one showing his grandfather interacting with him as a baby.

Another depicted Grandpa Kang lining up to buy designer sneakers and asking fellow elderly shoppers whether they were fans of K-pop star G-Dragon.

One particularly unusual video demonstrated the pair together across different historical periods, including as cavemen and even prehistoric fish.

While some fans supported Kang Kang’s decision to keep his grandfather’s memory alive, others questioned whether it was appropriate to use AI to depict someone who could no longer consent.

As Chinese outlet The Paper reported, supporters argued that the technology offered grieving families a upcoming way to remain connected to their loved ones. Critics, however, accused the account of exploiting the deceased.

Grandmas in China are captivated by their AI grandsons in viral trend.

Robin Williams’ family revives his Instagram account to combat AI recreations.

AI resurrects DMX and 2Pac for “mind-blowing” new viral song.

On November 8, Kang Kang addressed the controversy, explaining that he wanted to recreate moments with his grandfather that they never had the opportunity to film.

He said the videos were intended to share previously untold stories and allow his grandfather to continue bringing joy to viewers.

However, Kang Kang acknowledged the criticism and said he would reconsider using AI if the content made people uncomfortable.

By November 11, the account had removed the controversial AI videos, along with Kang Kang’s response. Its Xiaohongshu profile had also reportedly been cleared of posts.

The controversy comes as AI-generated personalities continue to divide audiences. In October, a Chinese AI K-pop group faced backlash after its creators announced that one of its virtual members was pregnant, later admitting they invented the storyline to write her out of the group.

MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes.
  • Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them.
  • According to recent reports, researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a new approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

According to recent reports, researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a new approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

"We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

Sources indicate that chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

Sources indicate that the team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

Sources indicate that to solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

Sources indicate that "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates latest capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How claims.

Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers.

Recent findings suggest that the first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can plan difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each upcoming flip under the proper conditions.

"If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How claims.

It has been revealed that the researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate quickly enough for real-time flight.

A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

"The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

According to recent reports, experiments revealed that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

"This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up newly introduced opportunities for multimodal locomotion," says Hsiao.

Recent findings suggest that the team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a new position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

"This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen says.

Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

Industry observers note that one major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

The team also looks to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

"For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a upcoming control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," notes Chen.

This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

#11369. Latest Update: The European Commission's fresh Digital Fairness Act could change monetisation in games forever - and not just in Europe

Latest Update: The European Commission's fresh Digital Fairness Act could change monetisation in games forever - and not just in Europe

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1404 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the European Commission has published its proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has the potential to change how video games are monetised - worldwide - forever.
  • And note that while the Digital Fairness Act isn't about video games exclusively - it's much broader than that - it does mention video games specifically, highlighting both their increased importance to society now, and that policy-shaping bodies like the European Commission are prepared to take them seriously.
  • The Digital Fairness Act is set to become European law, probably sometime between 2028 and 2029, once everyone's discussed it and made whatever amendments they're going to make to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the European Commission has published its proposed Digital Fairness Act, which has the potential to change how video games are monetised - worldwide - forever. A draft of the Act was leaked yesterday and what's been published today appears to be, to my eye, the same, though there's now also a mini-site accompanying it that explores the Act in more detail and uses more understandable language.

And note that while the Digital Fairness Act isn't about video games exclusively - it's much broader than that - it does mention video games specifically, highlighting both their increased importance to society now, and that policy-shaping bodies like the European Commission are prepared to take them seriously.

The Digital Fairness Act is set to become European law, probably sometime between 2028 and 2029, once everyone's discussed it and made whatever amendments they're going to make to it. And at that point, breaching the regulations will come with potentially steep fines (up to six percent of a organization's worldwide annual turnover, or up to €2m where an annual turnover isn't available).

The biggest things in the Digital Fairness Act relating to video games are regulations around loot boxes (sometimes referred to as "variable reward systems" or systems with "uncertainty-based rewards") and virtual currencies, particularly with regard to "minors" - anyone under 18 years old.

It has been revealed that the Act stipulates paid-for virtual currencies must be disabled in a game by default for minors, then activated by parental and guardian approval, and that paid loot boxes "shall not" be offered to minors at all. Moreover, games must provide a way for everyone to disable paid loot boxes completely, and clearly show the probability of receiving items from them.

Industry observers note that it's these changes that have the potential to overhaul how loot boxes work everywhere going forwards, and whether companies use them at all. To understand why, I talked to games business expert George Osborn, who runs the excellent Video Games Industry Memo newsletter, and who's been following the Act closely.

Osborn sees this as a "really substantial" regulatory change and believes that companies like EA, Xbox, Activision Blizzard, PlayStation, and other big gaming companies, both in console gaming and mobile gaming, will be "really concerned" by this. That's partly because a lot of these things being outlined are not necessarily easy to implement.

It has been revealed that for starters, a company now needs a way to work out who's a minor playing its game and who isn't, and it needs to provide "a master switch", as Osborn calls it, for people to switch paid loot boxes off with. These things require not just design changes but perhaps entire alterations to a game's approach; it means theoretically being able to turn paid card packs off in EA Sports FC Ultimate Team, example, and their not being able to be sold to minors at all.

"EA might be looking at it and going, 'This isn't great news for [EA Sports FC] Ultimate Team because people can switch it off,'" Osborn added, "but Ultimate Team is at least hived off in a box." EA could potentially age-gate Ultimate team as a mode and deal with it that way. But what if you're a card game where random paid rewards are central to your premise? "What that now means is you're possibly going to have to find a way to just completely turn that off for consumers, and it is very difficult to do that when they're embedded into the design of the game.".

In a recent development, the virtual currency issue is potentially easier to tackle because existing parental controls can control spending, so those tools could expand to cover it. But another proposal brought forward in the Digital Fairness Act states that a game must clearly show, in a region's local currency, how much an item costs when bought with virtual currency, which adds another layer of complication when considering different currencies and people moving between countries with their devices.

According to recent reports, these changes require investment and thought, and they sit alongside broader changes that affect things like subscription services, such as Xbox Live and PlayStation Plus and Nintendo Online, to make them easier to cancel and less able to obfuscate prices and hidden extras. There's even a stipulation that people be able to talk to a human in customer service rather than a chat bot. There are more technicalities for game-making companies to consider.

Recent findings suggest that but why should people outside of the European Union care? These rules are only enforceable there. Because: if a firm is selling a game into the European Union, which I expect every game company will want to do - "you don't just want to rule out a market of a few hundred million consumers; it's not a light thing to cut that out", Osborn says - then it will have to comply by these rules. And if it does, how many different versions of a game will it be prepared to make?

In a recent development, think about the recent global move towards all devices using USB-C chargers: that was a movement started by a European Commission ruling. Think of the new Switch 2s with removable battery packs: that was another change instigated by the European Commission. "Because that market is significant enough, you design for it," Obsorn claims, "and then your logic becomes, 'Well, we'll just do this for the rest of the world.' You're not going to produce one with the battery sealed in and the battery without. You're just going to find one way to produce things.

"That's likely to be the biggest impact in the UK and the rest of the world," he adds, "as people adjust the designs of their games to follow these rules. There's going to be a strong likelihood that some of the design features will remain within the games because it's easiest to work off a single universal version.".

It has been revealed that the other thing, which Osborn thinks is more key, is that policy makers around the world are "desperate" for solutions to problems and don't know where to look for them. "So if someone comes up with an answer to a question that's been annoying everybody, like 'what do we do about loot boxes?'," he states, "and it provides a particularly strong - or perceived to be effective - solution, it'll be copied. And it'll be copied because a major regulatory bloc like the European Union, which is known for protecting consumers particularly well, has decided this is a good thing. People trust it.".

Then, because companies have already developed a way to comply with those rules, it becomes difficult for them to argue that they can't do it elsewhere. "Because those regulators go, 'Well why not?'" Osborn claims. "Because if you build the solution in one place, you can build it elsewhere.".

Whether or not this will be the end of loot boxes as we know them, Osborn isn't sure. "My guess would be this will continue to push loot boxes into the fringes of video game monetisation. It was already starting to happen," he states. "I know some really high-profile games have them very prominently, which makes people feel like is there really any change here? But I know a lot of companies behind the scenes started to quietly move away from them in the last few years when they were a reputational problem. If you move to a world in which you're meant to have a massive off-switch in your game for them, that's a world in which fewer companies will go in that direction.".

It has been revealed that some will stick with it. "If you're an EA, it's going to be very difficult to move away from the model that has supported your business for years," Osborn claims. And card-based deck-building games will struggle to avoid it. "But overall, we're going to see a shift away from it," he adds. "And more broadly what this marks is a much wider crackdown on the way that video games monetise their players. As you start to see that crackdown come into force, game developers are going to have to think much more carefully about how the design decisions they make don't just interact with ethical practices, but actually with legal practices too.".

Newly introduced leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

According to recent reports, the base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at upcoming hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a upcoming 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing consumers of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.

Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe, but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera looks we’ve seen to date.

In a recent development, personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. Cutting lenses and skimping out on upgrades (again) doesn’t help matters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hello! This idea started as a single theme week, which we thought we might run in the lead up to Grand Theft Auto 6's launch. Then it turned into a pair of theme weeks. Then we realised we had so much stuff - and that, frankly, GTA 6 would be so dominating it'll be around for far more than a week itself - that we couldn't really fit it into two weeks either.

Sources indicate that so, allow me to introduce a whopping three-and-a-bit-ish weeks of specialist GTA- and not-GTA-themed coverage on Eurogamer! (Insert celebratory car horn toots here.).

Recent findings suggest that with GTA 6 launching next Thursday, we'll start with a week of coverage dedicated to the series, beginning today with a reader competition (more on that shortly!) and running until next weekend. We'll be covering GTA from all angles here - retrospectives, features, launch day coverage and beyond - across the series as a whole, as well as the major one we've got coming up. You can see that in one place at our GTA Week hub, which will populate as stories go live.

Sources indicate that however! If that - coupled with the inevitable wave of coverage that already comes from an enormous moment in video games like this - sounds like the last thing you want from us, well frankly, we get it. Matching big games with big coverage is a part of the brief at a site like Eurogamer, but it's also far from the only thing we want to be about. And we know it's far from the only thing you're going to want to read about for the rest of November, either.

To counteract that, then: we're also running a solid two weeks of counterprogramming, beginning on Monday 23rd November after GTA 6's launch. Expect all things not-GTA: coverage of lesser-known games, smaller-budget efforts, in-depth features on games and stories that are thematically opposed to it, have nothing to do with it, or take it for inspiration but go in an entirely different direction. All of our special counterprogramming can be found at our Not-GTA hub here as it goes live.

Those of you who've been coming back to Eurogamer for a few years might remember our "Games That Got Away" theme week from a few years back - we're bringing that back in a modified form here, too. Look forward to dedicated write ups - some labelled as reviews, some as broader reflective essays and criticism - on some of the great games we haven't quite found the time for so far this year, as we look to clear our own pile of shame.

Amongst all this, rest assured that normal service is also continuing here as ever. All the essential reporting, criticism, guides and the rest - across all things video games, whether or not that includes the Major One - will carry on as usual.

Ultimately, our hope is to offer something for everyone with this period - both the people who look to us to be comprehensive across gaming's biggest moments, and those who see us as a place for deep, nuanced, or simply fun stories on the medium's lesser-known corners.

It has been revealed that thank you as ever for reading - we really do appreciate it. And on that note, here's a link to Bertie's blog on our readers' competition, where you can win yourself your very own copy of GTA 6.

Tech Report: Open Responses: What you need to know

📅 15 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Open Responses is a latest and open inference standard.
  • It has been revealed that the era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads.
  • In a recent development, this mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open Responses is a latest and open inference standard. Initiated by OpenAI, built by the open source AI community, and backed by the Hugging Face ecosystem, Open Responses is based on the Responses API and is designed for the future of Agents. In this blog post, we’ll look at how Open Responses works and why the open source community should use Open Responses.

It has been revealed that the era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads. Developers are shifting toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act over long-time horizons. Despite this shift, much of the ecosystem still uses the Chat Completion format, which was designed for turn-based conversations and falls short for agentic use cases. The Responses format was designed to address these limitations, but it is closed and not as widely adopted. The Chat Completion format is still the de facto standard despite the alternatives.

In a recent development, this mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard. Over the coming months, we will collaborate with the community and inference providers to implement and adapt Open Responses to a shared format, practically capable of replacing chat completions.

Open Responses builds on the direction OpenAI has set with their Responses API introduced in March 2025, which superseded the existing Completion and Assistants APIs with a consistent way to:.

Open Responses extends and open-sources the Responses API, making it more accessible for builders and routing providers to interoperate and collaborate on shared interests.

It has been revealed that we’ll briefly explore the core changes that impact most community members. If you want to deep dive into the specification, check out the Open Responses documentation.

Recent findings suggest that client requests to Open Responses are similar to the existing Responses API. Below we demonstrate a request to the Open Responses API using curl. We're calling a proxy endpoint that routes to Inference Providers using the Open Responses API schema.

Industry observers note that clients that already support the Responses API can migrate to Open Responses with relatively little effort. The main changes involve how reasoning content is exposed:.

Recent findings suggest that openAI models used to only expose summary and encrypted_content. With Open Responses, providers may expose their raw reasoning via the API. Clients migrating from providers that previously returned only summaries and encrypted content will now have the opportunity to receive and handle raw reasoning streams when supported by their chosen provider.

Industry observers note that for Model Providers, implementing the changes for Open Responses should be straightforward if they already adhere to the Responses API specification. For Routers, there is now the opportunity to standardize on a consistent endpoint and support configuration options for customization where needed.

Over time, as Providers continue to innovate, certain features will become standardized in the base specification.

In summary, migrating to Open Responses will make the inference experience more consistent and improve quality as undocumented extensions, interpretations, and workarounds of the legacy Completions API are normalized in Open Responses.

You can see how to stream reasoning chunks below.

Here’s the difference between getting an Open Response and using OpenAI Responses for reasoning deltas:.

Open Responses distinguishes between “Model Providers” — those who provide inference — and “Routers” — intermediaries who orchestrate between multiple providers.

Clients can now specify a Provider along with provider-specific API options when making requests, allowing intermediary Routers to orchestrate requests between upstream providers.

Recent findings suggest that open Responses natively supports two categories of tools: internal and external. Externally hosted tools are implemented outside the model provider’s system. For example, client side functions to be executed, or MCP servers. Internally hosted tools are within the model provider’s system. For example, OpenAI’s file search or Google Drive integration. The model calls, executes, and retrieves results entirely within the provider's infrastructure, requiring no developer intervention.

Open Responses formalizes the agentic loop which is usually made up of a repeating cycle of reasoning, tool invocation, and response generation that enables models to autonomously complete multi-step tasks.

image source: openresponses.org.

For internally-hosted tools, the provider manages the entire loop; executing tools, returning results to the model, and streaming output. This means that multi-step workflows like "search documents, summarize findings, then draft an email" use a single request.

Clients control loop behavior via max_tool_calls to cap iterations and tool_choice to constrain which tools are invocable:.

The response contains all intermediate items: tool calls, results, reasoning.

In a recent development, open Responses extends and improves the Responses API, providing richer and more detailed content definitions, compatibility, and deployment options. It also provides a standard way to execute sub-agent loops during primary inference calls, opening up powerful capabilities for AI Applications. We are looking forward to working with the Open Responses team and the community at large on future development of the specification.

Breaking: Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
  • Industry observers note that scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
  • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," remarked Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the fresh study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a new way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

Industry observers note that scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

"We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," remarked Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the fresh study published in Nature.

A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

It has been revealed that quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

To fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The latest results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

Recent findings suggest that "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," remarked Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

Sources indicate that ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

Recent findings suggest that these anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a new type of particle with its own unusual rules.

"The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen said.

Industry observers note that each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

That experiment indicated that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

"In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," said Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

For the new study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

The S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

By combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

"It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," stated Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

The experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

According to recent reports, "So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen mentioned.

In a recent development, the next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on new techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

In a convoluted 90s way, one friend had taken their PC to another friend's house, where the three of us had assembled to play it. We'd take it in turns to burn around the top-down city, and when we weren't at the controls, we'd still be active in the experience, with the huge paper map unfolded, looking for spray shops the player could nip into when chased by the police. It was like being the passenger in a car. I can picture now, almost 30 years later, vividly.

The other distinct GTA memory I have is of playing Vice City and San Andreas one summer after I'd broken my arm and leg. I jumped off a roof in Australia when I was drunk; I wouldn't recommend it. Anyway, upon returning home, there wasn't a lot I could do - the breaks were both on one side so I'd crutch around (they gave me a wooden crutch in Australia) like a pirate - so a friend and I spent that summer taking turns playing GTA. It's all those shared moments laughing at Tommy Vercetti driving up staircases on vintage scooters that I remember, or CJ flapping his wooden-block hands around like paddles while gesticulating in cutscenes. Us just messing around. Friendship. That's what remembering Vice City and San Andreas conjures for me.

Industry observers note that but what about you - what do you remember about playing GTA games? Let your mind wander, let your mind remember, and thank you in advance for sharing your stories with us and everyone else. Have a lovely weekend.

Ask anyone selling an old chain or a broken ring what they want to know, and it's one thing: what is this worth? A small calculator can answer that in a second, but most of the ones you find online get the details wrong. They ignore troy ounces, treat 14K as 58.5% one day and 58.3% the next, or show a "value" that no buyer will ever pay.

According to recent reports, in this tutorial, we'll build a gold value calculator that gets those details right. It runs on plain HTML and JavaScript, updates as the user types, works with a screen reader, keeps its state in a shareable URL and pulls a live spot price through a small Node.js endpoint. The calculation lives in one pure function, so we can test it in a few lines.

Every gold calculator comes down to three inputs: how much the item weighs, how much of that weight is actually gold, and what pure gold is trading for today.

Purity is measured in karats, out of 24. A 14K ring is 14 parts gold and 10 parts other metals, so it's 14 ÷ 24 = 58.3% gold. You'll also see 14K stamped as "585", which is the hallmark many manufacturers use for the same alloy. For a calculator, the karat fraction is the safer default:.

According to recent reports, the second detail most tutorials miss is the unit. Gold spot prices are quoted in USD per troy ounce, which is 31.1035 grams, not the 28.35-gram ounce on a kitchen scale. Jewelers also use pennyweight (dwt), which is 1.5552 grams. If your calculator multiplies grams by a per-ounce price without converting, every result is wrong by a factor of 31.

Put together, the formula looks like this:.

For example, with gold at $2,400 per troy ounce, 10 grams of 14K gold contains 5.83 grams of pure gold, which is worth $449.85 at melt.

That $449.85 is the value of the gold content alone. Refiners and buyers pay a percentage of it, because refining, assaying and handling cost money. Depending on the buyer, the item and the market, the payout can sit well below melt value.

That gap is why good production tools separate the two numbers. A dedicated scrap jewelry gold calculator, like the one The Alloy Market offers, lets sellers estimate what their gold is worth from its weight and karat before they send anything in. Our calculator does the same job with a payout field: leave it at 100% to see melt value, or enter a buyer's rate to see a realistic offer.

Start with real form controls and a visible for each one. Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears as soon as the user types, and screen readers handle it inconsistently. The W3C forms tutorial covers the rules in detail.

A few choices here matter more than they look:.

Recent findings suggest that A little CSS gives touch-friendly controls. Keeping inputs at 16px (1rem) also stops iOS Safari from zooming in when a field gets focus.

It has been revealed that the biggest problem with most calculator snippets is that the math is buried inside an event handler, mixed with getElementById calls. You can't test it, and you can't reuse it on a server. Put the calculation and validation in their own module instead:.

Both functions take plain values and return plain values. They don't know a DOM exists, which means the same file can run in the browser, in Node.js and in your test runner.

Industry observers note that notice that we don't round inside the calculation. Rounding happens once, at display time. Rounding in the middle of a chain of multiplications is a classic way to end up a few cents off.

Industry observers note that now connect the form to the module. Listening for the input event on the form itself catches changes from every field, including the dropdowns, so there's no need to wire up each control separately.

With the markup, CSS and script in place, here's the finished calculator showing our 10 g, 14K example with an 80% buyer payout:.

It has been revealed that asking people to type the spot price works, but prefilling it is friendlier. Don't call a metals price API straight from the browser, though. Your API key would be visible to anyone who opens DevTools, and every visitor would spend one of your API calls.

Recent findings suggest that instead, put a small endpoint in front of your price provider and cache the result. This example uses Express and the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later:.

Three things keep this endpoint dependable:.

It has been revealed that on the page, the loadSpot() function from Step 3 fills the field and shows the time of the price. The field stays editable, so a seller who has a quote from a specific buyer can type that instead.

It has been revealed that A seller comparing offers might want to send their numbers to a family member, or come back to them tomorrow. Because every input has a name, turning the form into a query string is one line with URLSearchParams.

Industry observers note that the syncUrl() function in Step 3 runs on every change and uses history.replaceState instead of pushState, so typing doesn't fill the back button with dozens of entries. On load, restoreFromUrl() puts the values back. A link like this opens with the form already filled in:.

It has been revealed that because goldValue() is a pure function, testing it needs no browser and no mocks. Node.js ships with a built-in test runner, so there's nothing to install:.

Run it with node --test. (Add "type": "module" to your package.json so Node treats the files as ES modules.) The troy ounce test is the one worth keeping forever: if anyone "simplifies" the conversion later, it fails immediately.

The same pattern of a pure calculation module, a thin DOM layer and a cached server endpoint works for any calculator where the price depends on several inputs, from shipping estimates to currency conversion.

In a recent development, let the user choose. Most people weigh jewelry in grams, but spot prices are quoted per troy ounce, so the calculator should accept either and convert internally.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you thought raisins in muffins were bad, you haven’t seen anything yet. Sixteen students were hospitalized after muffins containing small batteries were served at an elementary school bake sale in Germany, sparking a massive emergency response.

The incident occurred on November 12 at Fröbel Elementary School in Coswig, where a student had brought homemade muffins to sell during a school event.

According to German broadcaster MDR, two students discovered small objects inside their muffins while eating them.

The objects were identified as button-cell batteries, prompting fears that other children might have unknowingly swallowed them.

Police subsequently recovered three batteries from two muffins, while 16 students who had eaten the baked goods were sent to nearby hospitals as a precaution.

According to an official statement from Wittenberg district authorities, at least 35 emergency responders and 12 ambulances were dispatched to the school.

However, just one child was transported to the hospital by ambulance, while the remaining 15 were taken by their parents or other private transportation.

Fortunately, none of the students suffered injuries, and medical examinations confirmed that no batteries had been swallowed.

Ten students treated at Dessau Municipal Hospital were even given free ice cream following their examinations.

As for how the batteries ended up inside the muffins, police believe they were accidentally mixed into the batter during preparation.

Recent findings suggest that investigators mentioned witness accounts supported the explanation and found no evidence of deliberate wrongdoing. In other words, the school didn’t do muffin.

The incident did, however, raise serious concerns because swallowing button-cell batteries can cause potentially life-threatening internal burns, particularly if they become lodged in the esophagus.

It comes just weeks after a school in Oregon was sued for nearly $1 million after students were served pretzels seasoned with crushed oven cleaner.

Earlier in 2026, another school apologized after accidentally serving students baked dirt that had been prepared for a science experiment.

In the German muffin incident, police confirmed that all 16 children had returned home safely by November 13.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago. And now onward!

Sources indicate that my favourite thing so far about Ocarina of Time is the judgement plastered on little Link's face when he encounters, well, almost everyone. Whether he means to or not, he serves sass all over town, and in Kakariko Village, and I am very much here for it.

In a recent development, also, I wasn't prepared to come face-to-face with a monster's butt cheeks. At all. Imagine the scene: I'm enjoying the tunes of the Lost Woods, processing the changes that have happened to Hyrule in the last seven years, all while making my way to the Forest Temple. Then the Moblin's turn their backs to reveal... Well, everything.

Industry observers note that this week I've spent an ungodly amount of time playing World of Warcraft: Forever (you may have read my preview on the website) and have been essentially glued to it during every minute of free time I've had away from work. I've got both my main professions above the level 225 mark and I'm firmly in the thick of it now. Levels take longer, items are actually getting good, and I've had to make a second alt character for extra bank space.

Sources indicate that as a result, I've not been to the gym in a while. I actually got one of those emails asking why I've fallen off, offering some tips to get back into the routine. Sorry Nuffield Health, my sleep schedule is ruined and I've substituted proper workouts for squats and basic at-home cardio. Surely, this can't go wrong...

I don't have the same level of nostalgia for Ocarina of Time that my peers do, but that has not stopped me from enjoying every minute of running around Hyrule smashing pots and trying not to cry over the touching cutscenes and, well, Saria.

In a recent development, the game feels like Dark Souls for children (endearing) and that is completely my jam. It's magical, satisfying, and often sad. There's creepy enemies as well as cute ones, trap floors and doors, mysterious NPCs... and my heart just feels so warm whenever I'm playing it. My fingers are now crossed that there's a Majora's Mask remake in the pipeline over at Nintendo. (As well as a Super Mario 64 remake, which I admit, is pushing it. But for what it’s worth, I'd probably sell my soul to see it get the Ocarina treatment.).

It takes me a while to settle with games; it takes me a while to settle full stop. I suppose in Fire Emblem's case I'm out of touch, seeing as the last instalment I played was on 3DS. But I struggled with the garish enthusiasm early on and the whole thing seemed overly simple. Nevertheless, I've settled a bit now, and now that the game's layering on more strategy and Intelligent System's expertise is coming to the fore, I'm beginning to enjoy myself much more.

In a recent development, I wasn't expecting it to be quite so boobsy, though. Was Fire Emblem always this way? Perhaps it's my fault for picking the scantily clad queen Theodora, though that sort of presentation isn't reserved only for her. She's no wallflower, though. My favourite moment so far was when she got off her elephant during a parade - yes, her elephant - and walked over to punch a teenage boy in the face for halting proceedings. Apparently she was doing him a favour.

According to recent reports, the relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence. Samsung is Android’s physical emissary, powering a plurality of all its handsets globally. But Google, and in particular its services, is the glue that holds Samsung’s smartphone experience together.

It has been revealed that the back and forth is over a decade old; back in early 2014, Samsung shipped a refreshed magazine-style skin with its Galaxy tablets that eschewed many of the design tenets Google had been pushing its partners to adhere to. Not only was Samsung willfully defying its most important partner, but it made a point of barely mentioning Android during its press conferences.

Around the same time, it transitioned its smartwatches from Android Wear to Tizen and began shipping duplicative apps on its devices (many of which persist to this day). The goal was to distance itself from Google as much as possible.

While we don’t know exactly what happened behind closed doors, we saw the outcome quite clearly: Magazine UX lasted one product cycle, and the two companies signed a 10-year cross-license patent deal, which may have helped Samsung prevent any future lawsuits with Apple. Google then sold Motorola to Lenovo, clearing the way for Samsung to continue building its burgeoning hardware business on the back of Google’s mobile ecosystem.

Since then, the two companies have grown even closer. In 2021, they co-confirmed a upcoming Wear OS along with an overarching wearables partnership that has since grown to include Android XR as well. And Google is still the default search engine for Samsung devices, despite reported inroads made by Microsoft in 2023 to convince the Korean giant to switch to a ChatGPT-powered version of Bing Search. (Samsung’s ongoing relationship with Microsoft, which bundles its Office suite on most Galaxy devices, could be seen as a point of leverage for negotiations with Google, too.).

Sources indicate that this brings us to today, and to AI. Samsung was among the first companies to adopt Google’s full suite of Gemini Intelligence products, and its phones often get new AI features before anyone else. But like a decade ago, when Samsung shipped Bixby to kind-of-sort-of compete with Google Assistant, it still wants to offer its own services alongside Google’s.

So a rumor that Samsung may launch a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription next year for $5/month piqued my interest for the same reason Magazine UX did 12 years ago. Galaxy AI features today are a blend of first-party and third-party capabilities, but none of them are especially useful, particularly when compared to Google’s own Android equivalents powered by Gemini Intelligence. Now Bar and Now Brief, two heavily promoted features in Samsung’s marketing, are wildly disappointing.

Sources indicate that at I/O this past May, Google announced Spark, an agent that goes out and performs actions on your behalf. And while it’s since been somewhat eclipsed by more capable mobile options like Meta’s Muse, it’s obvious that Google is working on a follow-up that will perform functions both on the phone and inside apps.

That’s exactly what Samsung is rumored to be working on with Bixby Action, a spiritual successor to its namesake that, when it debuted, prioritized on-device tasks like turning on Wi-Fi over web-based actions Google Assistant did better.

According to leaks from SamMobile, Galaxy AI Premium will offer agentic upgrades for phone users to “create commands triggers and system routines for daily tasks” or “automate routine daily tasks using Galaxy AI.” Gen Video will reportedly “convert static photos into dynamic video clips,” while a fresh Daily Briefing likely does what it indicates on the tin.

Will Samsung users see enough value in this hodgepodge of features paywalled only because they use a surfeit of compute? And what models will power them on the backend?

Right now, Google is in the enviable position of being able to offer its AI at three distinct layers: the model itself, which is invisible to the user; the OS level, which can promulgate Gemini across every Android phone that runs Google services; and the hardware level, where Pixel lets it specialize and optimize.

In a recent development, samsung, not particularly known for its software prowess, will likely need to step gingerly around Google’s AI shadow while also justifying the cost to shore up its much-needed services revenue. Based on this leaked roadmap, though, I’m not confident it will work out.

It has been revealed that instead, Samsung may want to acquire one of the many up-and-coming AI agent startups whose valuations are rising more quickly than their user bases. While Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have taken up most of the recent conversation, I’ve been using Hark, Town, and Instinct pretty regularly for a month or so and could see them being brought in-house by Samsung and offered either as standalone products or customized for Galaxy devices. As Google is doing with its own AI plans, Samsung could provide Galaxy consumers a year of free service, after which they would be expected to pay.

Samsung doesn’t have a great history of building software, but many of its acquisitions, from SmartThings to Viv Labs (which became “next-gen” Bixby) to LoopPay (which became Samsung Pay) to Whisk (which became Samsung Food), have proven successful. Given the current urgent state of mobile AI, I’d forgo the hodgepodge and bring in some outside expertise.

Whether Huang can survive the impending investigation by Nvidia’s board remains to be seen, but the CEO has been a stalwart in the tech space for 33 years, and there is no clear successor to his position should he be forced to resign.

Damien reviewed DroidDeck, which I wrote about last week as part of a broader look at Android’s gaming renaissance.

Over the last few days, things have become even more preposterous: the Ocarina of Time remake, which was released on Thursday, has already been recompiled to run natively on Android (though it runs better on PC), largely with the help of frontier AI models.

All of these AI-powered shenanigans come after Anthropic said it would stop making it possible to recreate copies of games, claiming that “recreating someone else’s specific game using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.” Good thing there are no other models capable of doing the same thing.
