💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an enhancement, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090.
  • In a recent development, once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity.
  • Industry observers note that he built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A lawyer with a private AI server built on eight used Nvidia V100 GPUs returned with an enhancement, moving about 80% of its work up from 2-bit to 4-bit NVFP4 precision and bringing in 1TB of RAM and an RTX 3090. The server uses DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with a legal harness, the workflows and checks he wraps around the model, for his law practice. The cost? Performance, with code output dropping from 160–215 to 150–180 tokens per second, although the crashes that hit the new build are gone. The culprit behind the crashes, originally blamed on PCIe, was likely a bad PSU.

In a recent development, once a random hardware nerd lawyer on Reddit, the lawyer's responses to the original breaking story illuminated his identity. He’s a trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina. ProprietaryLegalAI commented on our first story three times, linking to a code repository, site, and LinkedIn that identify him as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai. His other firm, PLI, is a technology consultancy, not a law firm, and now lists private, on-prem LLM serving as a service.

Industry observers note that he built the software side with AI, specifically Claude Code, which wrote the kernels and ran the benchmarks with his direction. The Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 models handled the optimizations, custom kernels, and re-quantizing; he noted he was surprised at how well Fable built custom Volta kernels, and how it re-quantizes the experts his legal harness triggers. From about February to July, he built a legal harness around Claude that worked, while his attempts at a local-model version failed, but then DeepSeek V4.1 Flash arrived, and he was able to port it successfully, even if he says it’s not as good as frontier.

Sources indicate that he reaffirms that “the documents never leave the office” and upgraded the system from 256GB to 1TB of RAM and tossed in a newer GPU, even as the V100s stay on “borrowed time” with R580, the last Nvidia driver branch to support them. The project’s intentions, as listed last time, suggested he wanted the system to be able to offload more of his workload, so this and the precision change are a reasonable upgrade. His previously stated goal of wanting the system to handle more than one request at a time has also been met.

In a recent development, the original “Volta sPLIt” build we covered has transformed into the “Volta Max uPLIft,” still with the clever lettering as his company’s initials are PLI — Proprietary Legal Intelligence. He now claims “near-NVFP4 precision,” having described NVFP4 on our forum earlier this week as “essentially full precision.” NVFP4 is Nvidia’s 4-bit floating-point format, and Nvidia publishes its own NVFP4 version of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash; the project’s README indicates that version matches the precision of the model’s official weights at 4.25 bits per weight.

It has been revealed that deepSeek V4.1 Flash is built from “experts,” the parts of the model that do most of the work for each word. This model didn’t fit at that precision before, as 384 routed experts, in each of 40 layers, counts to 15,360 in all. At official precision, this comes out to about 269 GiB, by his estimate, and eight 32GB V100s have 256 GiB in total before anything else is loaded. With the 2-bit build, the weights were 248.8GB; the latest build’s Hugging Face package is about 556GB.

In a recent development, the workaround is to keep every expert on the cards at 2-bit and swap the most-used ones up until the cards are full, which in this case came out to about 38.7%, or 5,949 experts, at precisely NVFP4. “Most-used,” in this context, refers to a count from a mix of four kinds of text, which are weighted equally, one of which is his own legal harness traffic.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The payoff is that those experts do most of the work. In testing with one request at a time, between 80% and 86% of decode routes, the calls to an expert made while the model writes, land on the NVFP4 experts, lowest for general text and highest for source code. The prediction for the two-request setup he runs is 78% to 85%. The remaining 15% to 22% of calls would still go to a 2-bit expert.

In a recent development, measured against Nvidia’s own version of the model as the reference, he was able to get good results. Same next token, or how often a build picks the same next token as the reference, went up to 95.1% from 92.2%. For KL divergence, which measures how far a build’s probabilities are from the reference’s, it went down to 0.079 nats from 0.196. In measuring multiple-choice answers that change, across 513 questions from a standard multiple-choice knowledge test, it went from 79 different to just 8.

This does not measure accuracy — which was about the same across all three cases — but fidelity. Those tests ran on the build’s first release, but not on the upcoming two-request setup he now runs.

According to recent reports, the result of the changes: higher fidelity but at a lower level of performance. Code output is 3% to 30% slower, depending on the prompt length, and legal writing is 9% to 23% slower. Before the build, he hoped to maintain about 80 tokens per second on legal and prose; the bench came in at 86 to 106 for legal and 78 to 86 for prose. The upside is that running two requests at once raises total output to 159.0 tokens per second, versus 118.9 with a sole request. The first token also arrives sooner at every prompt length, 108.4 seconds versus 118.7 seconds at 256K tokens.

Each request needs a “slot,” though, and this comes at a cost. Every slot keeps its own state on the cards, which leaves room for fewer NVFP4 experts: 6,215, 5,949, 5,663 for one, two, and three slots, respectively. This means each added slot may push another one to two points of the calls back to 2-bit, which could reduce output quality.

According to recent reports, the move to more RAM came this week with eight 128GB modules at 2,933 MT/s, originally eight 32GB modules that had to be run at DDR4-2666 due to ECC errors. After the RAM upgrade, the host reports two NUMA nodes, and two boots hung at the first transfer between the boards, so he reordered the cards in software. The GPUs remain capped at 1,522 MHz, as before.

As for the PSU, he took the common approach of chasing PCIe slots, cards, and cables to narrow down the cause, finally concluding it was “probably one bad PSU.” He also added more fans, but with no temperature changes, this only indicated that airflow was not the problem. He changed the power delivery, and nine of nine long chats read clean afterward. Also, don’t judge his cable management skill; any “advice [there] is welcome and will be ignored,” which is the only comment to make in that situation.

Recent findings suggest that he also already has two DGX Sparks running the same model at 1M context for agent work, and three or four sessions at once, and he isn’t stopping there. Now it comes down to scaling. Eight more V100s and a second server, with 512GB of 3,200 MT/s ECC RAM, are waiting in the wings. The second box would run another high-precision DeepSeek, used as an extra agent or to run tasks in parallel. The initiative is also to move DeepSeek’s small draft model off the V100s and onto the RTX 3090, which hasn’t happened yet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AssetOpsBench is a comprehensive benchmark and evaluation system with six qualitative dimensions that bridges the gap for agentic AI in domain-specific settings, starting with industrial Asset Lifecycle Management.
  • According to recent reports, while existing AI benchmarks excel at isolated tasks such as coding or web navigation, they often fail to capture the complexity of real-world industrial operations.
  • AssetOpsBench is built for asset operations such as chillers and air handling units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AssetOpsBench is a comprehensive benchmark and evaluation system with six qualitative dimensions that bridges the gap for agentic AI in domain-specific settings, starting with industrial Asset Lifecycle Management.

According to recent reports, while existing AI benchmarks excel at isolated tasks such as coding or web navigation, they often fail to capture the complexity of real-world industrial operations. To bridge this gap, we introduce AssetOpsBench, a framework specifically designed to evaluate agent performance across six critical dimensions of industrial applications. Unlike traditional benchmarks, AssetOpsBench emphasizes the need for multi-agent coordination—moving beyond `lone wolf' models to systems that can handle complex failure modes, integrate multiple data streams, and manage intricate work orders. By focusing on these high-stakes, multi-agent dynamics, the benchmark ensures that AI agents are assessed on their ability to navigate the nuances and safety-critical demands of a true industrial environment.

AssetOpsBench is built for asset operations such as chillers and air handling units. It comprises:.

Experts helped curate 150+ scenarios. Each scenario includes metadata: task type, output format, category, and sub-agents. The tasks designed span across:.

AssetOpsBench evaluates agentic systems across six qualitative dimensions designed to reflect real operational constraints in industrial asset management. Rather than optimizing for a single success metric, the benchmark emphasizes decision trace quality, evidence grounding, failure awareness, and actionability under incomplete and noisy data.

Each agent run is scored across six criteria:.

Across early evaluations, we observe that many general-purpose agents perform well on surface-level reasoning but struggle with sustained multi-step coordination involving work orders, failure semantics, and temporal dependencies. Agents that explicitly model operational context and uncertainty tend to produce more stable and interpretable trajectories, even when final task completion is partial.

This feedback-oriented evaluation is intentional: in industrial settings, understanding why an agent fails is often more valuable than a binary success signal.

A central contribution of AssetOpsBench is the explicit treatment of failure modes as first-class evaluation signals in agentic industrial workflows. Rather than treating failure as a binary outcome, AssetOpsBench analyzes full multi-agent execution trajectories to identify where, how, and why agent behavior breaks down under realistic operational constraints.

Failure analysis in AssetOpsBench is implemented through a dedicated trajectory-level pipeline (TrajFM), which combines LLM-based reasoning with statistical clustering to surface interpretable failure patterns from agent execution traces. This pipeline operates in three stages: (1) trajectory-level failure extraction using an LLM-guided diagnostic prompt, (2) embedding-based clustering to group recurring failure patterns, and (3) analysis and visualization to support developer feedback and iteration.

Across industrial scenarios, recurrent failure modes include:.

Sources indicate that importantly, AssetOpsBench does not rely solely on a fixed, hand-crafted failure taxonomy. While a structured set of predefined failure categories (e.g., verification errors, step repetition, role violations) is used for consistency, the system is explicitly designed to discover fresh failure patterns that emerge in practice. Additional failure modes identified by the LLM are embedded and clustered automatically, allowing the taxonomy to evolve as new agent designs and behaviors are evaluated.

To preserve industrial confidentiality, raw execution traces are never exposed. Instead, agents receive aggregated scores across six evaluation dimensions together with clustered failure-mode summaries that explain why an agent failed, without revealing sensitive data or intermediate reasoning steps. This feedback-driven design enables developers to diagnose weaknesses, refine agent workflows, and iteratively resubmit improved agents.

This failure-aware evaluation reflects the realities of industrial asset management, where cautious, degradation-aware reasoning—and the ability to recognize uncertainty, defer action, or escalate appropriately—is often preferable to aggressive but brittle automation.

Recent findings suggest that assetOpsBench-Live is designed as an open, competition-ready benchmark, and we welcome submissions of agent implementations from the community. Agents are evaluated in a controlled, privacy-preserving environment that reflects real industrial asset management constraints.

In a recent development, to submit an agent, developers first validate their implementation locally using a provided simulated environment, which includes representative sensor data, work orders, alerts, and failure-mode catalogs. Agents are then containerized and submitted for remote execution on hidden evaluation scenarios.

According to recent reports, submitted agents are evaluated across six qualitative dimensions—task completion, accuracy, result verification, action sequencing, clarity, and hallucination—using a consistent, reproducible evaluation protocol. Execution traces are not exposed; instead, participants receive aggregated scores and structured failure-mode feedback that highlights where and why an agent’s reasoning or coordination broke down.

This feedback-driven evaluation loop enables iterative improvement: developers can diagnose failure patterns, refine agent design or workflow structure, and resubmit updated agents for further evaluation. Both planning-focused and execution-focused agents are supported, allowing researchers and practitioners to explore diverse agentic designs within the same benchmark framework.

According to recent reports, this is an exceptionally key and well-executed benchmark. The shift in focus from "did the task succeed?" to "how and why did the process fail?" is precisely what's needed to move AI agents from research demos into high-stakes industrial environments.

It has been revealed that the six-dimensional evaluation framework and the TrajFM pipeline for analyzing failure modes are standout contributions. The data you've shared is striking—particularly that no tested model, including the top performers, could meet the 85-point deployment readiness threshold. This honest result highlights a critical maturity gap and sets a clear, high bar for the community.

In a recent development, the findings around multi-agent coordination are especially valuable. The significant accuracy drop from single-agent (68%) to multi-agent (47%) workflows quantifies a major challenge many have anecdotally observed but rarely measured so clearly.

Congratulations to the team on this crucial work. By providing a rigorous, feedback-driven, and privacy-preserving evaluation platform, AssetOpsBench doesn't just measure progress—it actively guides the field toward building more robust and trustworthy industrial agents.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials.
  • The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa.
  • The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a fresh approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters.

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

It has been revealed that human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

Sources indicate that scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work reveals that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality.".

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin.

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Industry observers note that physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

In a recent development, "It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself.".

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he remarked. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature.".

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

Industry observers note that "This gives us a completely newly introduced tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," stated Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications.

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

Industry observers note that one particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

According to recent reports, communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

Recent findings suggest that "The implications are wide-ranging," stated Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a newly introduced generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed.

Recent findings suggest that for decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," stated Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen.".

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

Waze is officially rolling out alerts for cyclists along your route that leverages location data from Garmin trackers.

It has been revealed that in an effort to “boost driver awareness” of nearby bicycle riders, Waze will start showing real-time alerts for nearby cyclists to drivers in the area. The feature shows both a location on the map ahead as well as a visible alert on screen.

Waze knows the location of a nearby cyclist through a partnership with Garmin, with “LiveTrack” location sharing from the Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatches users to share location data with the Google-owned navigation app.

Cyclists need to opt-in to the feature to have their location shown, and the alerts drivers see are temporary and anonymous. When cyclists end their ride, Waze alerts also go away.

This feature is completely opt-in and built with privacy in mind. Drivers only see a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby — never information about a specific cyclist or route. Plus, alerts automatically turn off the moment a cyclist ends their ride on their Garmin device.

This is rolling out starting today to the Waze apps on both Android and iOS.

Unlocking Agentic RL Training for GPT-OSS: A Practical Retrospective

📅 27 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that agentic reinforcement learning (RL) extends traditional LLM training by optimizing not just a single-turn response, but an entire decision-making process learned through direct interaction with an environment during training.
  • Sources indicate that linkedIn is an AI-first tech giant that's built agents to help professionals be more successful.
  • The GPT-OSS model has shown comparable performance to OpenAI o3-mini and o4-mini [ref], but its suitability for agentic reinforcement learning training has not yet been validated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that agentic reinforcement learning (RL) extends traditional LLM training by optimizing not just a single-turn response, but an entire decision-making process learned through direct interaction with an environment during training. Unlike traditional single-turn reinforcement learning or offline preference-based methods that rely on static datasets, agentic RL trains policies by actively collecting on-policy data as the agent prepares actions, invokes tools, observes outcomes, and adapts its behavior over multi-step trajectories in either simulated or real environments. This interaction-driven optimization assigns credit across long-horizon decisions, where intermediate choices such as query reformulation, tool selection, and execution order directly influence downstream success. Training follows an iterative closed loop in which the agent interacts with the environment to collect rollout trajectories, computes rewards over these trajectories, updates the policy based on observed outcomes, and then uses the updated policy to drive the next round of interaction and data collection such as GRPO or PPO algorithms..

Sources indicate that linkedIn is an AI-first tech giant that's built agents to help professionals be more successful. In this setting, models must reason over incomplete information, interact with structured services, and adapt to evolving user intent across multiple steps rather than produce a single static response. These capabilities are especially critical for agents that support the goals of recruiters, job and knowledge seekers, and learners end customers, such as retrieving information, refining queries, coordinating tools, and executing multi-step workflows. By learning robust decision policies through interaction, agentic RL provides a principled foundation for building scalable, reliable, and adaptable AI systems through end-to-end optimization.

The GPT-OSS model has shown comparable performance to OpenAI o3-mini and o4-mini [ref], but its suitability for agentic reinforcement learning training has not yet been validated. Most recent work focuses on fine-tuning without tool calling, such as: Fine-tuning with gpt-oss and Hugging Face Transformers and unsloth tutorial: how to fine-tune gpt-oss. This blog explores the journey to unlock agentic RL training for GPT-OSS as a potential backbone model for agentic applications.

Sources indicate that in our experiments, we use verl as our training framework since it is one of the most popular adopted frameworks in the open source community. We use gsm8k, Retool task, verifiable instruction following task, which are commonly used in RL training. We focus on presenting experimental results for the GPT-OSS-20B model, and our attention-sink fix also works for GPT-OSS-120B. The Qwen-2.5-32B model is additionally used to benchmark standard metric trends during RL training.

It has been revealed that verl has been an OSS framework used by the team, and the team has previously collaborated and contributed to it to help democratize agentic reinforcement learning training. With the introduction of the fresh Harmony chat template in GPT-OSS, the first step is to ensure that the training framework fully supports the updated message format and conversation semantics required by Harmony. This step helps rollout generation, trajectory construction, and tool parsing remain consistent and correct under the new template.

The team uses ReTool as a representative example to verify code correctness. ReTool is an agentic coding task in which the model is asked to solve a math problem with the assistance of a code compiler tool. This setup allows the model to focus on core reasoning and algorithmic logic, while delegating the actual arithmetic and execution to the tool. During an episode, the model interacts with the code tool multiple times, using execution results as feedback to refine its solution. At the end of the trajectory, the model produces a final answer, on which the reward is computed.

During the initial training runs, we observed exploding KL divergence and entropy, along with non-increasing rewards, indicating underlying concerns in the GPT-OSS training setup, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Left: Qwen32b has significantly higher rewards compared to GPT-OSS 20B; Right: The gradient norm exploded as training progressed.

Sources indicate that figure 2. Non-zero importance sampling clip value even for on-policy training.

We focus on on-policy methods because they provide greater stability and more reliable convergence. The foundation of pure on-policy Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) mandates that the importance sampling ratio must be exactly 1. The mathematical definition of the importance ratio is:.

ratio=π(a∣s)πold(a∣s) \text{ratio} = \frac{\pi(a \mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)} ratio=πold​(a∣s)π(a∣s)​.

This requirement ensures that the policy update is executed only on the data generated by the current policy π(a | s) = πold(a | s), preventing unintended clipping.

We have observed the non-zero clipping value in our ReTool training, as shown in Figure 2, stemming from a mismatch between the two log-probabilities:.

Root Cause: The Dual Forward Pass and MoE Architecture.

Prior to verl 0.3.0, the implementation relied on two separate forward passes (one to compute the current log_prob and one to retrieve the stored old_log_prob) for the same state-action pair.

In a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture like GPT-OSS, the gating network routes the input to different experts. Due to implementation factors (e.g., subtle floating-point differences or explicit stochasticity), the expert routing can differ slightly between the two passes. Readers who are interested can further read Stabilizing MoE Reinforcement Learning by Aligning Training and Inference Routers.

This difference in routing leads to:.

log⁡(π(a∣s))≠log⁡(πold(a∣s)) \log(\pi(a \mid s)) \neq \log(\pi_{\text{old}}(a \mid s)) log(π(a∣s))=log(πold​(a∣s)).

The resulting ratio deviates from 1, falsely triggering the PPO clip and violating the core on-policy assumption.

Solution: Enforcing Ratio = 1 via Log-Probability Substitution.

The fix resolves the problem by logically overriding the flawed computation when the environment is known to be on-policy (i.e., when the minibatch size equals the global batch size):.

By setting old_log_prob equal to the newly computed log_prob (detached to prevent gradient flow through the reference value), the importance ratio is mathematically forced back to 1. This strategy bypasses the instability caused by MoE's non-deterministic routing and guarantees strict on-policy behavior during PPO training.

Although fixing the log-probability mismatch reduced the importance-sampling clip ratio to zero, gradient norms continued to explode and rewards failed to improve. To isolate the issue, we simplified training to GSM8K, a single-step task without agentic tool use. The same instability persisted, as shown in the green curves in Figure 3, indicating a fundamental issue in basic RL training with GPT-OSS under verl.

We hypothesize that training–inference mismatch could be a potential cause: discrepancies between inference-time execution—where engines such as vLLM and SGLang aggressively optimize for throughput—and training-time execution under FSDP, which prioritizes numerical precision and stability, can effectively turn otherwise on-policy RL into off-policy optimization.

Sources indicate that this blog details why such mismatches lead to unstable gradients and non-improving rewards. Figure 3 compares training runs with and without rollout correction (see this verl blog for details). After applying rollout correction, training dynamics improve significantly, with gradient norms remaining stable rather than exploding.

However, as shown in the left plot of Figure 4, the reward increases only modestly, and convergence on the simple GSM8K task remains substantially slower compared to smaller dense model variants.

In a recent development, figure 3. Gradient norm behavior under different training configurations. Green: Training without rollout correction, exhibiting unstable gradients. Red: Training with the attention layer frozen to isolate the glitch to the attention mechanism, resulting in partial stabilization. Blue: Training with rollout correction enabled (sequence-level importance sampling), yielding stable gradient norms.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4. Left: Reward improvement on GSM8K remains slow even after applying rollout correction, with performance comparable to runs where the attention layer is frozen during training. Right: A substantial log-ppl mismatch is observed between the inference engine (SGLang with Triton kernels supporting attention-sink forward passes) and the training stack (FSDP with FlashAttention-v2), indicating a large training–inference inconsistency.

Sources indicate that to further isolate the root cause, we freeze the attention layers during training and observe reward dynamics similar to those of runs without freezing (blue curve vs yellow curve in Figure 4). This indicates that learning is primarily driven by the MoE layers, while the attention mechanism contributes less effectively than expected. In addition, we observe a substantial token-level probability mismatch between the inference engine and the distributed training stack which are using different attention kernels. Together, these observations motivate a deeper investigation into the attention mechanism.

Attention sinks used in GPT-OSS are learnable scalar parameters (one per attention head) that act as "virtual tokens" in the softmax computation. They allow the model to allocate attention mass to a learned sink rather than forcing all attention to content tokens, which has been shown to improve attention stability in streaming inference and training with sliding-window attention.

After a deeper investigation, we identified several major complications:.

Key difference: The sink participates in softmax normalization but doesn't contribute to the output.

The attention weight for content token j in row i is defined as:.

Pij=exp⁡(Sij)∑j′=1Nkexp⁡(Sij′)+exp⁡(Sh) P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(S_{ij})} {\sum_{j'=1}^{N_k} \exp(S_{ij'}) + \exp(S_h)} Pij​=∑j′=1Nk​​exp(Sij′​)+exp(Sh​)exp(Sij​)​.

The sink probability is computed but not used in the output:.

Pi,h=exp⁡(Sh)∑j′=1Nkexp⁡(Sij′)+exp⁡(Sh) P_{i,h} = \frac{\exp(S_h)} {\sum_{j'=1}^{N_k} \exp(S_{ij'}) + \exp(S_h)} Pi,h​=∑j′=1Nk​​exp(Sij′​)+exp(Sh​)exp(Sh​)​.

The gradient of the loss L with respect to the sink parameter Sh is:.

∂L∂Sh=−∑iPi,h(∂L∂Si,h−∑j∈{1,…,Nk}Pij∂L∂Sij) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_h} = - \sum_i P_{i,h} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{i,h}} - \sum_{j \in \{1,\ldots,N_k\}} P_{ij} \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}} \right) ∂Sh​∂L​=−i∑​Pi,h​​∂Si,h​∂L​−j∈{1,…,Nk​}∑​Pij​∂Sij​∂L​​.

Since the sink is computed but not used in the output, its gradient ∂L/∂Si,h = 0.

Therefore, the backward equation simplifies to:.

∂L∂Sh=−∑iPi,h(∑j∈{1,…,Nk}Pij∂L∂Sij) \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_h} = - \sum_i P_{i,h} \left( \sum_{j \in \{1,\ldots,N_k\}} P_{ij} \frac{\partial L}{\partial S_{ij}} \right) ∂Sh​∂L​=−i∑​Pi,h​​j∈{1,…,Nk​}∑​Pij​∂Sij​∂L​​.

In a recent development, the forward pass was adapted from vLLM's FlashAttention fork, and we implemented the backward pass to compute gradients for the sink parameters. The implementation will be released following the internal review process.

According to recent reports, after applying the fix in FlashAttention v3, we observe substantially faster convergence for GPT-OSS-20B across a range of reinforcement learning tasks. These include single-turn RL on math reasoning (GSM8K — red curve in Figure 5), instruction following (VerifyIf, evaluated on an out-of-domain multi-if benchmark — Figure 6), and multi-turn agentic RL with tool use (ReTool — Figure 7).

Across all settings, training becomes stable and exhibits steady reward improvement.

Figure 5.. Single Turn GSM8K, the red curve converges much faster than the rest without the fix.

Figure 6. On verifiable instruction following the task, the run without the fix collapsed (blue), and the run with fix showed steady reward improvement.

In a recent development, figure 7. On the Retool task, the run with fix revealed steady reward improvement and no gradient exploding (fa2 is the flash attention 2 without the fix while fa3 is the flash attention 3 with the fix). After the fix, the validation accuracy score goes up now.

One issue we consistently encountered was excessive memory allocation during the FSDP forward pass, which led to repeated out-of-memory (OOM) failures when training GPT-OSS-20B bf16 models on 16 H200 nodes (max response length: 16k, prompt length: 8k). This behavior is highly unexpected for a 20B-parameter MoE model.

We identified the concern as originating from two different implementations of the MoE forward path in Hugging Face Transformers. This issue has also been reported by other users: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/complications/40073; When verl computes log-probabilities under FSDP, the inference forward path is triggered. In the current Hugging Face implementation, this path duplicates hidden states for all experts and performs batched matrix multiplication, materializing extremely large tensors in GPU memory. By contrast, the training forward path uses a for-loop to process each expert sequentially and then combines the results. While slower, this approach is significantly more memory efficient.

We patched the Hugging Face implementation to use a more memory-efficient execution path, avoiding repeated materialization of experts.

According to recent reports, agentic RL requires the agent to interact with the environment over multiple steps while maintaining an ever-expanding context. Observations and environment feedback from each step are appended to the context and used as input for subsequent decision-making, which introduces significant challenges for memory efficiency and scalability during training.

Industry observers note that under fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), model parameters, optimizer states, and gradients are sharded across the entire world size (i.e., all GPUs in the training cluster). Each GPU stores and updates only its assigned parameter shards, while rollout data are replicated across all GPUs—meaning every GPU processes the full agent interaction history for each rollout.

Industry observers note that during the forward pass, when computation reaches a layer whose parameters are not locally available, an all_gather operation is triggered to materialize the full parameters across GPUs. During the backward pass, a corresponding reduce_scatter operation aggregates gradients and ensures that each GPU retains only its local shard. This provides a degree of scaling: as the number of GPUs increases, the per-GPU memory footprint decreases.

FSDP provides model-level scaling by sharding model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs. Sequence parallelism (or context parallelism) further reduces per-GPU memory consumption by partitioning the input sequence across devices, thereby lowering the peak activation memory on each GPU.

As the number of sequence-parallel dimensions increases, the maximum activation memory per GPU correspondingly decreases. We have implemented sequence parallelism to be attention-sink-aware and compatible with FlashAttention v3 (Figure 8, right).

Figure 8. Left: Inference without sequence parallelism. Right: Inference with sequence parallelism, where additional all-to-all communication is performed before and after the attention layer. This partitions the sequence across parallel workers and reduces the peak memory footprint of attention computation by a factor proportional to the sequence-parallelism degree.

Sequence parallelism scales along the sequence dimension to reduce the per-GPU activation footprint. Input tokens from all sequences are packed into a single contiguous list by removing padding tokens, while position IDs are used to distinguish tokens belonging to different sequences. This design naturally benefits from FlashAttention’s variable-length support. For sequence parallelism, layers other than the attention layer do not have inter-position dependencies; therefore, they do not require each GPU to hold a complete sequence shard, and no additional communication is needed for these layers.

The attention layer, however, requires all tokens belonging to the same sequence to be present on the same GPU in order to compute attention weights correctly. To satisfy this constraint, an all-to-all communication is performed to gather sequence elements, with the split performed at the attention-head level. This design avoids communication within the attention computation itself, which would otherwise be prohibitively expensive. After the attention layer, a single all-to-all communication redistributes the outputs back to their original sequence-parallel layout, after which the remaining non-attention layers can proceed without further synchronization.

Our journey to enable agentic RL training for the GPT-OSS backbone model was a practical retrospective, highlighting that unlocking advanced capabilities in open-source LLMs requires meticulous, deep-dive engineering.

We made contributions that transformed the viability of GPT-OSS for agentic applications, specifically by:.

Stabilizing PPO: We contributed a fix to restore on-policy integrity, overriding the log-probability mismatch caused by the MoE architecture’s non-determinism (Figure 2).

Enabling Attention Sink Support: We successfully implemented and integrated the attention sink backward pass into FlashAttention v3, correcting the catastrophic training–inference mismatch that had previously caused instability and slow convergence (Figures 5, 6, and 7).

Scaling Memory Efficiency: We introduced crucial memory optimizations, including patching the MoE materialization process and integrating sequence parallelism with the upcoming attention sink support, enabling training with the long context windows essential for multi-step agents (Figure 8).

These engineering efforts validate GPT-OSS as a scalable and high-performance backbone for building the next generation of intelligent, multi-step decision-making agents.

Mathematical Clarification on Attention Sink Gradient.

It has been revealed that regarding the attention sink backward pass derivation (Section 4), I'd appreciate clarification on the notation and justification. The article presents the general formula: ∂L/∂S_h = -Σ_i P_{i,h} (∂L/∂S_{i,h} - Σ_{j∈{1,...,N_k}} P_{ij} ∂L/∂S_{ij}). I believe the final formula is correct, but the notation ∂L/∂S_{i,h} is unclear. If this refers to the gradient of the loss with respect to the sink's contribution to the output at position i (i.e., ∂L/∂(P_{i,h} V_sink)), then indeed it would be zero since there's no V_sink term. However, the sink parameter S_h itself does affect the output through softmax normalization: P_{ij} = exp(S_{ij}) / (Σ_{j'} exp(S_{ij'}) + exp(S_h)). When S_h changes, all P_{ij} change, affecting O_i = Σ_j P_{ij} V_j. The gradient ∂L/∂S_h is non-zero and flows through this normalization.

On-Policy Fix: Clarification Needed.

Sources indicate that the solution for the MoE log-probability mismatch (Section 2) sets old_log_prob = log_prob.detach() when on_policy=True. The article mentions that "The implementation will be released following the internal review process." Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers plan around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

Recent findings suggest that actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It highlights how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Industry observers note that historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

Carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

According to recent reports, interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production problems. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

These records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual issue could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

Historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating new tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

It has been revealed that for example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the new estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The latest integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying issue.

Research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

Start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

It has been revealed that suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

Sources indicate that for example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

Avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

It has been revealed that A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

According to recent reports, the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

For example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

Suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook vital differences.

A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

In such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

Industry observers note that however, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

According to recent reports, historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

It has been revealed that if several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

In a recent development, production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

Sources indicate that historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as vital inputs to sprint forecasting.

When you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

According to recent reports, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

Sources indicate that however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

According to recent reports, timeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

According to recent reports, timeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

According to recent reports, however, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

Industry observers note that apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

Sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a initiative, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

In a recent development, sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

According to recent reports, 2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

Bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

Sources indicate that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

Recent findings suggest that **3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

According to recent reports, teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

Recent findings suggest that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

According to recent reports, 4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Recent findings suggest that time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Recent findings suggest that technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Drive will soon prompt consumers to switch to Adobe Acrobat while viewing PDFs, and Gemini will get a few new tricks powered by the tech giant’s creative suite.

The pipeline from PDFs opened in Google Drive and Gmail to Adobe Acrobat is notoriously strained. That goes for any PDF viewer, but as soon as certain tools are necessary, a large number of people rely on Adobe’s products to edit and store documents.

Google announced prepares to ease the process. According to a press release today, Google will be adding a “direct pathway” from Google Drive and Gmail in Adobe Acrobat. Acrobat will be suggested to users within the services, which will likely act as a quick transfer sort of feature. It doesn’t seem to indicate users will see any Adobe PDF editing tools within Google Drive. Google Drive has notoriously fallen short in this regard.

Industry observers note that the partnership announcement also means Gemini will get access to some of Adobe’s creative tools. Further detail isn’t clear, but that includes Gemini, Gemini Enterprise, and Google AI Mode in Search. It sounds like the integration will allow users to edit or manage PDFs and other files straight from Google’s AI interfaces.

Industry observers note that it’s not just PDFs and Google Drive; Adobe’s Photoshop gets a shout, too. Expected sometimes in the future, we may see more powerful image editing powered by Gemini within Adobe Photoshop, as opposed to the current models and limitations within. Gemini Nano Banana models are right now in use, but AI generation and editing could go further with a more focused effort. Google claims the push “could enable near-real-time edits,” but there’s no concrete timeline set for when we could see that.

That goes for each of these byproducts of the new partnership. Google Drive and Gmail integration with Adobe Acrobat will likely be the first to roll out, with Gemini features to follow shortly after.

AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
  • Industry observers note that as artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading people, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common.
  • Latest research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

Industry observers note that as artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading people, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

Latest research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness.

According to recent reports, published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," states Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," notes Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural.".

Sources indicate that to investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that highlighted different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness.

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

Recent findings suggest that however, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," indicates Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical.".

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an vital insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Sources indicate that awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Sources indicate that because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

Industry observers note that "Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, prepares, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study indicates is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important.".

Weeks after shipment was swiped by China, Pentagon ‘struggles to account for’ $31 billion in missing F-35 aircraft parts

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week.
  • Recent findings suggest that inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source.
  • Chief among the issues that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Pentagon is struggling to track an astonishing 26 million F-35 warfighter parts, worth an estimated $31 billion, according to analysis published by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) this week. In its report — published just weeks after China purportedly swiped a classified shipment of F-35 parts diverted through Hong Kong — the GAO criticized the current inventory system as “outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete.” Possible solutions were also provided by the GAO; however, the implications are that the most advanced and costly fighter jets in U.S. history may not be ready and reliable due to inventory management deficiencies.

Recent findings suggest that inventory problems have been a long-standing feature of the deployment of the F-35, notes the source. The F-35 program is estimated to cost $1.9 trillion over its lifecycle. It is the most costly weapon system in history, says the GAO. But the Department of Defense (DOD) has “long-standing and ongoing deficiencies related to the accountability and financial reporting of F-35 parts,” asserts the watchdog.

Chief among the issues that need to be addressed is the headlining massive unmonitored pool of roughly 26 million spare parts. These are spread among 700 government and contractor facilities worldwide, but the technology for managing massive inventories has existed for decades.

According to recent reports, we might have seen a telling symptom of the inadequate F-35 parts tracking system back in September. A communications and/or accountability breakdown resulted in a UPS worker routing top-secret parts through Hong Kong to save time. They were allegedly swiped by China after an employee is thought to have missed an email warning not to divert the parts.

Frustratingly, this is the third report since 2019 from the GAO, and the latest published report complains that the DOD has “made minimal progress” in implementing past recommendations. For example, in a 2022 report, periodic physical inventories of F-35 parts were recommended but have not been implemented yet, notes Stars and Stripes. There is also no reliable procedure for verifying data from prime contractors, which can be “inaccurate and incomplete.”.

Currently, it is believed that there are over 1 million parts, worth more than $85 million, that are lost or missing. Moreover, about 17,000 parts that have been sent in for repair, worth as much as $42.5 billion, aren’t tracked.

Stars and Stripes mentions that the Pentagon is working on “a live connection” for the F-35 Joint Program Office (JPO), bridging its inventory software and that of prime contractors with F-35 parts. The JPO asserts that it is now modernizing its infrastructure with direct real-time interfaces. “This integration directly addresses previous system gaps to ensure seamless accountability of F-35 spare parts,” remarked a JPO spokesperson, quoted by Breaking Defense.
