💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles.
  • According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a latest type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost.
  • Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a latest type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring notable health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

Sources indicate that the researchers believe their latest design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A Newly introduced Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision.

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

It has been revealed that "The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another crucial advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare.

It has been revealed that to evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

Recent findings suggest that when used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

Industry observers note that the healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

Sources indicate that the researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," noted Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment.".

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough.

Recent findings suggest that the new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

Recent findings suggest that the Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

In a recent development, "This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," stated Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible.".

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices.

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is at the moment practical.

Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

Sources indicate that "Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work demonstrates that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day.".

In a recent development, as photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

Latest Update: Introducing Daggr: Chain apps programmatically, inspect visually

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR: Daggr is a new, open-source Python library for building AI workflows that connect Gradio apps, ML models, and custom functions.
  • If you've built AI applications that combine multiple models or processing steps, you know the pain: chaining API calls, debugging pipelines, and losing track of intermediate results.
  • Most developers either build fragile scripts that are hard to debug or turn to heavy orchestration platforms designed for production pipelines—not rapid experimentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR: Daggr is a new, open-source Python library for building AI workflows that connect Gradio apps, ML models, and custom functions. It automatically generates a visual canvas where you can inspect intermediate outputs, rerun individual steps, and manage state for complex pipelines, all in a few lines of Python code!

If you've built AI applications that combine multiple models or processing steps, you know the pain: chaining API calls, debugging pipelines, and losing track of intermediate results. When something goes wrong in step 5 of a 10-step workflow, you often have to re-run everything just to see what happened.

Most developers either build fragile scripts that are hard to debug or turn to heavy orchestration platforms designed for production pipelines—not rapid experimentation.

We've been working on Daggr to solve problems we kept running into when building AI demos and workflows:.

In a recent development, visualize your code flow: Unlike node-based GUI editors, where you drag and connect nodes visually, Daggr takes a code-first approach. You define workflows in Python, and a visual canvas is generated automatically. This means you get the best of both worlds: version-controllable code and visual inspection of intermediate outputs.

It has been revealed that inspect and Rerun Any Step: The visual canvas isn't just for show. You can inspect the output of any node, modify inputs, and rerun individual steps without executing the entire pipeline. This is invaluable when you're debugging a 10-step workflow and only step 7 is misbehaving. You can even provide “backup nodes” – replacing one model or Space with another – to build resilient workflows.

First-Class Gradio Integration: Since Daggr is built by the Gradio team, it works seamlessly with Gradio Spaces. Point to any public (or private) Space and you can use it as a node in your workflow. No adapters, no wrappers—just reference the Space name and API endpoint.

According to recent reports, state Persistence: Daggr automatically saves your workflow state, input values, cached results, canvas position—so you can pick up where you left off. Use "sheets" to maintain multiple workspaces within the same app.

Google Fi Wireless is rolling out a major update today with the return of network switching thanks to a “secondary” partner.

Google Fi is now bringing back a second partner as part of its newly introduced “super network.” Most people will be on the “Primary network,” but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the “Secondary network” if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called “smart thresholds” for doing so. Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android’s Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip.

It might be important to note that T-Mobile actually bought out Sprint, and added their towers to their network so its safe to say that Google Fi still works with the same coverage as before the merger.

It has been revealed that the Google Fi app gains a “Your super network” card in the Home tab that indicates whether you’re connected to the Primary or Secondary network. “See activity” lets you view switching history and when it last occurred. Google will also note if you’re in range of W+ networks.

It has been revealed that google today is also expanding its Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ network beyond Pixel phones to select Samsung Galaxy (S23, Fold/Flip 5, and newer) and modern Motorola phones. These premium Wi-Fi networks are available in millions of airports, malls, stores, and restaurants. The connection happens automatically, with the Google Fi Virtual Carrier Network encrypting data.

Recent findings suggest that the final patch today sees the companion app gain “Ask Fi.” This AI-powered chat is meant to quickly provide answers and guided troubleshooting for common concerns. You can request human support with seamless handoff that keeps the chat context.

These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability. This launch is accompanied by several deals:.

Why an answer isn’t always the answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1423 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I tried Googling “what is an answer,” I got: “Please provide the specific question, puzzle, or problem you are trying to solve so I can give you the right answer.” It seems answers are defined only in relation to their questions.
  • When I tried Googling “what is an answer,” I got: “Please provide the specific question, puzzle, or problem you are trying to solve so I can give you the right answer.”.
  • It has been revealed that it seems answers are defined only in relation to their questions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I tried Googling “what is an answer,” I got: “Please provide the specific question, puzzle, or problem you are trying to solve so I can give you the right answer.” It seems answers are defined only in relation to their questions. There is no definition of an “answer” on its own. I looked into this and found plenty of philosophy on “what is a question?” and far less on “what is an answer?” I came across mathematics papers on how to get to a solution, which is related, but still focused on the question. Searching for an answer on “answers” is a lot harder than it sounds. WHEN CONTEXT DILUTES THE ANSWER This becomes interesting in a world where answers are now delivered at scale. We’re getting extraordinarily good at producing them, but a gap remains. We don’t really know what an answer is. Basing an answer on the question is no longer enough. AI has dramatically increased our ability to find answers quickly and provide a wider aperture of information. Competition for this service has shifted into which tools can provide the best, fastest, and most accurate answers. We may be able to determine “fastest” and “most accurate,” but how do we determine “best?” Is it correct? Relevant? Complete? That works when a question has a definitive endpoint or when I am looking for a fact. I can ask, “How far is the moon from Earth?” get a number, and move on. Chatbots do this well. Often, the one-sentence answer is perfect, and adding too much context around the distance to the moon dilutes the information I need. Other times, the answer is the first thing I need, not the endpoint. “How far is the moon from Earth?” can lead to “How long does it take to get there?” Now the answer depends on how, who, and why. It gets more complex. It gives me enough context to ask the next question, compare sources, explore something I didn’t understand, form a point of view, or build something from it. If every answer is optimized to close the tab, what happens to the answers that are supposed to start something? A BUILDING PROCESS Building knowledge is a process. Sometimes it’s serendipitous discovery; other times, it’s methodical. A good answer depends on what you are trying to do with it. Correctness is necessary, but not always enough. It needs context, comparison, sources, or follow-up questions. So when is an answer best? Is it a human source? Is it longer? Does it have more citations? There still is no clear answer here. It depends on what I need. I view this as the pipeline: Information → answer → understanding → application. The answer is not the end goal; it’s merely the midpoint. Answers unlock deeper understanding and, ultimately, application. AI has made the first half of this pipeline wildly easier. That’s both a gift and a risk: it can dull the curiosity to dig deeper. Beyond a quick answer is how other people have approached the question before, what they asked next, and what they did with it. I find the back half much more interesting. But it’s more difficult, too. Understanding is subjective. Application is contextual. Both are much harder to measure than whether a system returned the correct answer. I think a lot about this at Scribd, Inc. We are a knowledge tech giant, and we want to help people get to the second half of that pipeline. But that does not mean we skip over the answer. You can’t get to application without it. I don’t know if anyone can “win” this. I don’t even think anyone can quite define it yet. Google was right in a way. It couldn’t tell me what an answer was without knowing what I wanted it for. The “best” answer is the one that meets your objective, whether that’s finding a fact or learning something upcoming. We’ve gotten very good at the answers that provide a fact. We are just scratching the surface on the ones that open something new.The next step is “beyond the answer”—what it allows someone to learn, create, or do. Tony Grimminck is CEO of Scribd, Inc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that malaysia aims to introduce a new law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail. The authorities also proposal to charge data center operators for unused electricity capacity they reserve. While the idea to use power consumption to detect potential GPU smuggling has merit, it also has flaws.

Malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations. To prevent such practices, Malaysia's Digital Ministry is now reviewing existing legislation to determine whether local authorities can take action against entities that re-export processors subject to U.S. export bans. The minister stressed that Malaysia wants AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically.

The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. The government intends to track data center operations throughout their lifetime rather than limit oversight to the project approval stage.

Meanwhile, data center operators will have to pay for all the electricity capacity they reserve, irrespective of their actual power consumption. For example, if a data center secures 100 MW of power capacity but only uses 50 MW, its operator will still have to pay for the remaining 50 MW. The measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving electricity capacity they may not need for another one to three years. As an added bonus, the measure will further discourage rerouting AI hardware to China while pretending it is used in Malaysia.

According to recent reports, while data on power consumption could help Malaysian authorities spot suspicious discrepancies between AI GPU imports and actual data center operations, it is virtually impossible to accurately determine the number of AI accelerators deployed at a facility based on power consumption alone. For example, Nvidia's H100 and H200 SXM GPUs are rated at 700W, whereas its B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, yet neither necessarily consumes its rated power under actual workloads.

Furthermore, without knowledge of server configurations, the power consumption of CPUs, memory, storage, and networking equipment, or the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of a particular facility, any estimates of the number of operational GPUs would be imprecise, to put it mildly. Also, there may be a considerable delay between GPU imports and their actual deployment. As a result, reliable verification would require physical inventory audits or other mechanisms to track individual processors.

Johari mentioned that Malaysian authorities were prepared to cooperate with their U.S. counterparts and provide information about facilities that house particular GPUs upon request. However, the minister did not specify whether the new legislation would require data center operators to disclose GPU models and serial numbers, or whether authorities would conduct on-site inspections.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, malaysia has emerged as a major destination for data center investments in Southeast Asia as cloud service providers and AI infrastructure companies expand their presence in the region. To date, Malaysian authorities have approved 117 data center projects, 55 of which are already operational, according to Johari. The proliferation of local AI data centers makes Malaysia a suitable venue for rerouting restricted hardware to countries like China, as it is easier to hide a needle in a pile of needles than in a haystack.

IP geolocation maps an IP address to a physical location & network details, letting you spot suspicious traffic before it reaches sensitive actions. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, after retiring a few years ago, my parents moved into a wooded retirement community in North Carolina.
  • Recent findings suggest that his solution: Get a Tesla.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After retiring a few years ago, my parents moved into a wooded retirement community in North Carolina. One of their neighbors is a former physician, now in his 90s, who sensed that his reflexes had deteriorated. He no longer trusted himself behind the wheel, but he valued the independence that a car can provide. His solution: Get a Tesla. He now relies on Full Self-Driving (Supervised), Tesla’s driver assistance system, to get around. That decision is a dubious one at best. Tesla’s driver assistance system is just that: technology that can make the act of driving less onerous, but cannot replace it. A person operating Full Self-Driving (Supervised)—let’s call it FSD—must be able to intervene immediately if the system makes a mistake, which does happen. If not, their use of FSD endangers themselves along with everyone else on the road. My parents’ neighbor is far from alone. A quick scan of Facebook or TikTok reveals numerous adults with declining health who depend on FSD to keep driving. And Tesla itself has amplified these narratives—despite officially claiming that drivers, not the tech giant, are responsible for the vehicle while FSD is in operation. A post on X earlier this year featured a 71-year-old man who bought a Cybertruck “because my eyes are getting bad.” Tesla’s North America X account shared the clip with a one-word comment: “Freedom.” Questions of whether and how older Americans can safely use driver assistance systems like FSD are devilishly tricky. Even if they avoid cognitive decline, Ehsani said, “older adults have reduced physical abilities like their reaction time, neck rotation, and ability to check blind spots.” Many seniors are excellent drivers: Overall, people in their 60s are less likely to be in a deadly collision than the general public, and those in their 70s are about on par with teenagers. But drivers in their 80s are significantly more prone to being involved in a fatal crash. Such resistance is understandable, given the general difficulty of doing errands or visiting friends without using an automobile. “In the United States, we take great pride in being able to be independent in our actions,” said Jennifer Crawley, deputy secretary at the Maryland Department of Aging. “The inability to continue to drive can impact people’s view of themselves and the ways they connect with their broader community.” Ehsani agreed, noting that losing the ability to drive can be mentally devastating. “Families often tell me stories of the day they took mom’s or dad’s keys, and how that was the beginning of their decline,” he said. To his point, researchers at Columbia University found that “older adults experienced faster declines in cognitive function and physical health” after they ceased driving. Given the stakes, the decision to stop using a car is often fraught. “There’s a grieving process that can occur when people give up the keys,” Crawley said. According to the AARP, its most-clicked site about driver safety is a free webinar, entitled “We Need to Talk,” offering suggestions to family members unsure how to broach the subject. The choice facing older Americans can be agonizing: Do they continue to drive, putting themselves and others road people at risk, or do they accept the loneliness and dependence that can follow the loss of a car? Presented with that dilemma, a third option involving a vehicle that safely drives itself would be cause for celebration. But no such option exists. The only autonomous trips at the moment available to consumers are from robotaxi companies like Waymo and Zoox. No senior—nor anyone else—can acquire their own self-driving car. Such systems can handle many driving tasks, including changing lanes, accelerating, braking, and turning. Convenient though they can be, Level 2 systems rely on active human oversight. In its public guidance, SAE warns that “you are driving whenever these driver support features are engaged—even if your feet are off the pedals and you are not steering.” Tesla owners can purchase a FSD subscription for $99 per month. Consistent with SAE’s guidance, Tesla’s manual gives owners bold-faced instructions: “You must remain attentive and be ready to take over at all times.” But in contrast to the manual’s clear messaging, Tesla’s marketing often exaggerates FSD’s capabilities. In May, the company posted a video on social media featuring a FSD-enabled car whose driver is making an espresso—an activity that would seemingly be impossible while focusing on the road. When asked if most Tesla owners read the manual, Birsen Donmez, an engineering professor at the University of Toronto who specializes in human factors, gave a short chuckle. “No, absolutely not,” she replied. “They don’t know the limitations of these systems.” (Tesla did not respond to a request for comment.) In fact, the very name Full Self-Driving could confuse consumers. In February, California regulators forced Tesla to append the parenthetical (Supervised) to the feature’s name, but Donmez does not think that move is sufficient. “It still indicates ‘full self-driving’,” she shrugged. “That could be misleading.” Tesla has spread misinformation in other ways, too. In September, CEO Elon Musk shared a viral in-car video about Larry, a 98-year-old who waxes euphoric about FSD. After his Tesla clears an intersection, Larry exclaims “Look, I didn’t have to look, you know! I don’t want to look, it’s just doing it.” But according to Tesla’s own manual, Larry does indeed have to look. As the automotive outlet Electrek noted at the time, “this is exactly what the terms forbid.” Musk’s resharing of Larry’s video is part of a pattern of boosterism. In July, Tesla posted a video on X about Lois, a 93-year-old woman who “noticed how tired she was on her daily drives,” before acquiring a Tesla that allows her to travel by car comfortably. Musk reshared that post, too, adding: “Tesla self-driving enables safer mobility for senior citizens.” Ehsani, the Johns Hopkins public health professor, was skeptical. If anything, the video led him to question whether Lois can safely use FSD. “Her feeling tired is a bit of a red flag,” he said. “She may not be awake while this [Tesla] is in operation.” And Tesla’s supercharged fan base has amplified the company’s messaging for seniors. On the TeslaModelY subreddit, plaudits poured in for a 90-year-old man who obtained a Model Y because “his kids thought it would be a good fit for him.” One poster called FSD “a digital chauffeur,” a sobriquet that implies self-driving capabilities that the system cannot deliver. A dearth of data The relative safety of Level 2 systems like FSD is highly contested. Tesla maintains that cars operating FSD are less crash prone, but Donmez noted that “it’s based on their analysis only” and lacks independent validation. She remains “very suspicious” of Tesla’s FSD claims, because most people struggle to remain vigilant without doing anything for long periods of time. Joseph Young, a spokesperson at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, said that specific features like automatic emergency braking can clearly reduce collisions, but it remains an open question whether combining many of them within a product like FSD provides additional upside. “Level 2 systems should be considered convenience features rather than safety systems,” he said. For seniors specifically, little is known about the safety of FSD or other Level 2 systems. Several high-profile crashes have involved older Tesla drivers, including a recent one in California, in which a 91-year-old driver killed one and injured five people in a Trader Joe’s parking lot. (Whether the driver was using FSD is unclear.) Credulous journalists have exacerbated public misunderstanding. A feature story in The Detroit News earlier this year declared that seniors are buying Teslas to “self-drive,” and claimed “FSD helps elderly drivers maintain a cocoon around their car as their confidence in reflexes and eyesight naturally deteriorate”—even though Tesla’s own manual makes clear that the company’s technology is reliant upon the driver, not the other way around. (The author of the Detroit News story did not respond to a request for comment.) Acknowledging a dearth of data, Ehsani said it is theoretically possible that a Level 2 system like FSD could reduce overall crashes among seniors, if the system—even with compromised oversight—is safer than the counterfactual of their driving themselves. On the other hand, it is also possible that seniors’ use of FSD increases total crashes. If this is the case, it could be because seniors drive more miles, each of which carries a degree of danger, or because they are unable to intervene in an emergency. Worryingly, research suggests that older drivers need more time to react when a Level 2 system’s mishap requires them to respond. Donmez, the University of Toronto engineering professor, proposed a simple rubric for seniors tempted by Tesla’s pitch. “If you can’t drive yourself,” she said, “you shouldn’t be driving with FSD.” A safer path forward A common-sense solution to help seniors—and everyone else—make better driving decisions would be to force Tesla and Musk to stop exaggerating FSD’s capabilities. European officials recently required Tesla to change the name of the system to Full Assisted Driving, after China had already made a similar move. The United States is “the last [massive car market] that doesn’t have a rule saying you can’t say that a system that isn’t self-driving is self-driving,” Ed Niedermeyer, the author of two books about Tesla, observed recently on the Autonocast podcast. “Why is it taking so long to say that up is up and down is down?” Ascendant leaders in Washington may be thinking along similar lines. Following the midterm election “bluenami,” Senator Ed Markey, Democrat of Massachusetts, vowed “to hold Musk and Tesla accountable for the risk their systems pose to our families and communities.” But reining in Tesla’s marketing would still leave millions of seniors struggling to maintain their quality of life as they become incapable of driving safely. If and when genuine autonomous vehicles go on sale, they could be a godsend. Crawley, the Maryland official, is optimistic about their long-term potential—she called autonomy a “new frontier” in elder care—provided that being affluent and tech savvy is not a prerequisite for using them. She also noted that fully autonomous vehicles may need modifications to serve seniors, such as the capability of loading a walker or wheelchair. (Disability advocates have called on robotaxi companies to speed the introduction of wheelchair-accessible robotaxis, which are not widely deployed.) Given the uncertainties about autonomy’s future, a more foolproof way to enhance senior mobility would be to enable more people to live in places where a car is unnecessary. As an example, the Atlanta exurb of Peachtree City features a separated golf cart network that enables residents to get practically anywhere without using an automobile. Peachtree City benefits from being master planned, but other cities like Long Beach, California, have envisioned roadway retrofits that enable people to travel by Low-Speed Vehicles that are slower and smaller than full-sized cars, and therefore pose less danger. Tech Report: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips.
  • Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem.
  • Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This demonstrates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an vital step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This demonstrates that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an vital step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

According to recent reports, the researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

Industry observers note that when the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

In a recent development, the team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

In a recent development, although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the latest technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A Upcoming Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

In a recent development, the findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," notes Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

It has been revealed that the broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Tech Report: Wyze’s new door lock has speedy fingerprint recognition and 12-month battery life

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (269 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wyze is today launching its latest “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.
  • Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock.
  • Industry observers note that the Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze states recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wyze is today launching its latest “Lever Lock,” a smart lock for your front door that has a year of battery life and fast fingerprint recognition, all for an affordable price tag.

Available starting today, the Wyze Level Lock is not your typical deadbolt smart lock. Rather, this is a smart lock designed for your standard single-bore latch, meaning it’s available for doors that other smart locks aren’t compatible with. You can still have a deadbolt, but you’ll need enough space for both (per Wyze’s guidelines below).

Industry observers note that the Lever Lock has a PIN entry and a fingerprint sensor, the latter of which Wyze states recognizes your fingerprint in about half a second. It uses local storage for biometric data and works to improve that data with each successful unlock.

According to recent reports, the PIN has a clever feature (though it’s presented in somewhat poor taste) that lets you input random digits before or after your actual code to prevent onlookers from being able to see your code. There’s also a physical key backup as well as a USB-C input on the outside in the case that the battery dies – Wyze states it lasts about 12 months on a charge using eight AA batteries.

The Wyze Lever Lock is available today for $99.98 and shipping immediately.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the second part of our series on training efficient text-to-image models from scratch.
  • In the first post of this series, we introduced our goal: training a competitive text-to-image foundation model entirely from scratch, in the open, and at scale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome back! This is the second part of our series on training efficient text-to-image models from scratch.

In the first post of this series, we introduced our goal: training a competitive text-to-image foundation model entirely from scratch, in the open, and at scale. We focused primarily on architectural choices and motivated the core design decisions behind our model PRX. We also released an early, small (1.2B parameters) version of the model as a preview of what we are building (go try it if you haven't already 😉).

According to recent reports, in this post, we shift our focus from architecture to training. The goal is to document what actually moved the needle for us when trying to make models train faster, converge more reliably, and learn better representations. The field is moving swiftly and the list of “training tricks” keeps growing, so rather than attempting an exhaustive survey, we structured this as an experimental logbook: we reproduce (or adapt) a set of recent ideas, implement them in a consistent setup, and report how they affect optimization and convergence in practice. Finally, we do not only report these techniques in isolation; we also explore which ones remain useful when combined.

According to recent reports, in the next post, we will publish the full training recipe as code, including the experiments in this post. We will also run and report on a public "speedrun" where we put the best pieces together into a single configuration and stress-test it end-to-end. This exercise will serve both as a stress test of our current training pipeline and as a concrete demonstration of how far careful training design can go under tight constraints. If you haven’t already, we invite you to join our Discord to continue the discussion. A significant part of this project has been shaped by exchanges with community members, and we place a high value on external feedback, ablations, and alternative interpretations of the results.

In a recent development, before introducing any training-efficiency techniques, we first establish a clean reference run. This baseline is intentionally simple. It uses standard components, avoids auxiliary objectives, and does not rely on architectural shortcuts or tricks to save compute resources. Its role is to serve as a stable point of comparison for all subsequent experiments.Concretely, this is a pure Flow Matching (Lipman et al., 2022) training setup (as introduced in Part 1) with no extra objectives and no architectural speed hacks. We will use the small PRX-1.2B model we presented in the first post of this series (single stream architecture with global attention for the image tokens and text tokens) as our baseline and train it in Flux VAE latent space, keeping the configuration fixed across all comparisons unless stated otherwise.

The baseline training setup is as follows:.

This baseline configuration provides a transparent and reproducible anchor. It allows us to attribute observed improvements and regressions to specific training interventions, rather than to shifting hyperparameters or hidden setup changes. Throughout the remainder of this post, every technique is evaluated against this reference with a single guiding question in mind:.

Does this modification improve convergence or training efficiency relative to the baseline?

Examples of baseline model generations after 100K training steps.

It has been revealed that to keep this post grounded, we rely on a small set of metrics to monitor checkpoints over time. None of them is a perfect proxy for perceived image quality, but together they provide a practical scoreboard while we iterate.

Fréchet Inception Distance (FID): (Heusel et al., 2017) Measures how close the distributions of generated and real images are, using Inception-v3 feature statistics (mean and covariance). Lower values typically correlate with higher sample fidelity.

CLIP Maximum Mean Discrepancy (CMMD): (Jayasumana et al., 2024) Measures the distance between real and generated image distributions using CLIP image embeddings and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). Unlike FID, CMMD does not assume Gaussian feature distributions and can be more sample-efficient; in practice it often tracks perceptual quality better than FID, though it is still an imperfect proxy.

DINOv2 Maximum Mean Discrepancy (DINO-MMD): Same MMD-based distance as CMMD, but computed on DINOv2 (Oquab et al. 2023) image embeddings instead of CLIP. This provides a complementary view of distribution shift under a self-supervised vision backbone.

Network throughput: Average number of samples processed per second (samples/s), as a measure of end-to-end training efficiency.

With the scoreboard defined, we can now dive into the methods we explored, grouped into four buckets: Representation Alignment, Training Objectives, Token Routing and Sparsification, and Data.

Industry observers note that diffusion and flow models are typically trained with a single objective: predict a noise-like target (or vector field) from a corrupted input. Early in training, that one objective is doing two jobs at once: it must build a useful internal representation and learn to denoise on top of it. Representation alignment makes this explicit by keeping the denoising objective and adding an auxiliary loss that directly supervises intermediate features using a strong, frozen vision encoder. This tends to speed up early learning and bring the model’s features closer to those of modern self-supervised encoders. As a result, you often need less compute to hit the same quality.

Recent findings suggest that A useful way to view it is to decompose the denoiser into an implicit encoder that produces intermediate hidden states, and a decoder that maps those states to the denoising target. The claim is that representation learning is the bottleneck: diffusion and flow transformers do learn discriminative features, but they lag behind foundation vision encoders when training is compute-limited. Therefore, borrowing a powerful representation space can make the denoising problem easier.

According to recent reports, REPA adds a representation matching term on top of the base flow-matching objective.Let x0∼pdatax_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}x0​∼pdata​ be a clean sample and x1∼ppriorx_1 \sim p_{\text{prior}}x1​∼pprior​ be the noise sample. The model is trained on an interpolated state xtx_txt​ (for t∈[0,1]t \in [0,1]t∈[0,1]) and predicts a vector field vθ(xt,t)v_\theta(x_t, t)vθ​(xt​,t). In REPA, a pretrained vision encoder fff processes the clean sample x0x_0x0​ to produce patch embeddings y0=f(x0)∈RN×Dy_0 = f(x_0) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}y0​=f(x0​)∈RN×D, where NNN is the number of patch tokens and DDD is the teacher embedding dimension. In parallel, the denoiser processes xtx_txt​ and produces intermediate hidden tokens hth_tht​ (one token per patch). A small projection head hϕh_\phihϕ​ maps these student hidden tokens into the teacher embedding space, and an auxiliary loss maximizes patch-wise similarity between corresponding teacher and student tokens: LREPA(θ,ϕ)=−Ex0,x1,t[1N∑n=1Nsim(y0,[n], hϕ(ht,[n]))] \mathcal{L}_{\text{REPA}}(\theta,\phi) = -\mathbb{E}_{x_0,x_1,t}\Big[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \text{sim}\big(y_{0,[n]},\, h_\phi(h_{t,[n]})\big)\Big] LREPA​(θ,ϕ)=−Ex0​,x1​,t​[N1​n=1∑N​sim(y0,[n]​,hϕ​(ht,[n]​))] Here n∈{1,…,N}n \in \{1,\dots,N\}n∈{1,…,N} indexes patch tokens, y0,[n]y_{0,[n]}y0,[n]​ is the teacher embedding for patch nnn, ht,[n]h_{t,[n]}ht,[n]​ is the corresponding student hidden token at time ttt, and sim(⋅,⋅)\text{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)sim(⋅,⋅) is typically cosine similarity.

This term is combined with the main flow-matching loss:.

L=LFM+λ LREPA \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} + \lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{REPA}} L=LFM​+λLREPA​.
