In practice, the student is trained to produce noise-robust, data-consistent patch representations from xtx_txt​, so later layers can focus on predicting the vector field and generating details rather than rediscovering a semantic scaffold from scratch.

According to recent reports, we ran REPA on top of our baseline PRX training, using two frozen teachers: DINOv2 and DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025). The pattern was very consistent: adding alignment improves quality metrics, and the stronger teacher helps more, at the cost of a bit of speed.

Industry observers note that on the quality metrics, both teachers improve over the baseline. The effect is strongest with DINOv3, which achieves the best overall numbers in this run.

According to recent reports, REPA is not free: we pay for an extra frozen teacher forward and the patch-level similarity loss, which shows up as a throughput drop from 3.95 batches/s to 3.66 (DINOv2) or 3.46 (DINOv3). In other words, DINOv3 prioritizes maximum representation quality at the cost of slower training, while DINOv2 offers a more efficient tradeoff, still delivering substantial gains with a smaller slowdown.

Our practical takeaway is that REPA is a strong lever for text-to-image training. In our setup, the throughput trade-off is real and the net speedup (time required to reach a given level of image quality) felt a bit less dramatic than what the authors of the paper report on ImageNet-style, class-conditioned generation. That mentioned, the quality gains are still clearly significant. Qualitatively, we also saw the difference early: after ~100K steps, samples trained with alignment tended to lock in cleaner global structure and more coherent layouts, which makes it easy to see why REPA (and alignment variants more broadly) have become a go-to ingredient in modern T2I training recipes.

According to recent reports, A natural follow-up to REPA is: what exactly should we be aligning? iREPA argues that the answer is spatial structure, not global semantics. Across a large sweep of 27 vision encoders, the authors find that ImageNet-style “global” quality (e.g., linear-probe accuracy on patch tokens) is only weakly predictive of downstream generation quality under REPA, while simple measures of patch-token spatial self-similarity correlate much more strongly with FID. Based on that diagnosis, iREPA makes two tiny but targeted changes to the REPA recipe to better preserve and transfer spatial information:.

Despite representing “less than 4 lines of code”, these tweaks consistently speed up convergence and improve quality across encoders, model sizes, and even REPA-adjacent training recipes.

In our setup, we observed a similar kind of boost when applying the iREPA spatial tweaks on top of DINOv2: convergence was a bit smoother and the metrics improved more steadily over the first 100K steps. Interestingly, the same changes did not transfer as cleanly when applied on top of a DINOv3 teacher and they tended to degrade performance rather than help. We do not want to over-interpret that result: this could easily be an interaction with our specific architecture, resolution/patching, loss weighting, or even small implementation details. Still, given this inconsistency across teachers, we will likely not include these tweaks in our default recipe, even if they remain an interesting option to revisit when tuning for a specific setup.

The paper REPA Works Until It Doesn't: Early-Stopped, Holistic Alignment Supercharges Diffusion Training (Wang et al., 2025) highlights a key caveat: REPA is a powerful early accelerator, but it can plateau or even become a brake later in training. The authors describe a capacity mismatch. Once the generative model starts fitting the full data distribution (especially high-frequency details), forcing it to stay close to a frozen recognition encoder’s lower-dimensional embedding manifold becomes constraining. Their practical takeaway is simple: keep alignment for the “burn-in” phase, then turn it off with a stage-wise schedule.

We observed the same qualitative pattern in our own runs. When training our preview model, removing REPA after ~200K steps noticeably improved the overall feel of image quality, textures, micro-contrast, and fine detail continued to sharpen instead of looking slightly muted. For that reason, we also recommend treating representation alignment as a transient scaffold. Use it to get fast early progress, then drop it after a while once the model’s own generative features have caught up.

So far, “alignment” meant regularizing the generator’s internal features against a frozen teacher while treating the tokenizer / latent space as fixed. A more direct lever is to shape the latent space itself so the representation presented to the flow backbone is intrinsically easier to model, without sacrificing the reconstruction fidelity needed for editing and downstream workflows.

It has been revealed that REPA-E (Leng et al., 2025) makes this concrete. Its starting point is a failure mode: if you simply backprop the diffusion / flow loss into the VAE, the tokenizer swiftly learns a pathologically easy latent for the denoiser, which can even degrade final generation quality. REPA-E’s fix is a two-signal training recipe:.

Thanks to these two tricks, the tokenizer is explicitly optimized to produce latents that yield higher alignment and empirically better generations.

In parallel, Black Forest Labs’ FLUX.2 AE work frames latent design as a trade-off between learnability, quality, and compression.Their core argument is that improving learnability requires injecting semantic structure into the representation, rather than treating the tokenizer as a pure compression module. This motivates retraining the latent space to explicitly target “better learnability and higher image quality at the same time". They do not share the full recipe, but they do clearly state the key idea: make the AE’s latent space more learnable by adding semantic or representation alignment, and explicitly point to REPA-style alignment with a frozen vision encoder as the mechanism they build on and integrate into the FLUX.2 AE.

Recent findings suggest that to probe alignment in the latent space, we compared two pretrained autoencoders as drop-in tokenizers for the same flow backbone: a REPA-E-VAE (where we do add the REPA alignment objective, as in the paper) and the Flux2-AE (where we do not add REPA, following their recommendation). The results were, honestly, extremely impressive, both quantitatively and qualitatively. In samples, the gap is immediately visible: generations show more coherent global structure and cleaner layouts, with far fewer “early training” artifacts.

Sources indicate that A first striking point is that both latent-space interventions lower the FID by ~6 points (18.20 to ~12.08), which is a much larger jump than what we typically get from “just” aligning intermediate features. This strongly supports the core idea: if the tokenizer produces a representation that is intrinsically more learnable, the flow model benefits everywhere.

According to recent reports, the two AEs then behave quite differently in the details. Flux2-AE dominates most metrics (very low CMMD and DINO_MMD, but it comes with a huge throughput penalty: batches/sec drops from 3.95 to 1.79. In our case this slowdown is explained by practical factors they also emphasize: the model is simply heavier, and it also produces a larger latent (32 channels), which increases the amount of work the diffusion backbone has to do per step.

REPA-E-VAE is the “balanced” option: it reaches essentially the same FID as Flux2-AE while keeping throughput much closer to the baseline (3.39 batches/sec).

Recent findings suggest that architecture gets you capacity, but the training objective is what decides how that capacity is used. In practice, small changes to the loss often have outsized effects on convergence speed, conditional fidelity, and how quickly a model “locks in” global structure. In the sections below, we will go through the objectives we tested on top of our baseline rectified flow setup, starting with a simple but surprisingly effective modification: Contrastive Flow Matching.

It has been revealed that flow matching has a nice property in the unconditional case: trajectories are implicitly encouraged to be unique (flows should not intersect). But once we move to conditional generation (class- or text-conditioned), different conditions can still induce overlapping flows, which empirically demonstrates up as “averaging” behavior: weaker conditional specificity, and muddier global structure. Contrastive flow matching addresses this directly by adding a contrastive term that pushes conditional flows away from other flows in the batch.

Recent findings suggest that for a given training triplet (x,y,ε)(x, y, \varepsilon)(x,y,ε), standard conditional flow matching trains the model velocity vθ(xt,t,y)v_\theta(x_t,t,y)vθ​(xt​,t,y) to match the target transport direction. Contrastive flow matching keeps that positive term, but additionally samples a negative pair (x~,y~,ε~)(\tilde{x}, \tilde{y}, \tilde{\varepsilon})(x~,y~​,ε~) from the batch and penalizes the model if its predicted flow is also compatible with that other trajectory. In the paper’s notation, this becomes:.

LΔFM(θ)=E[∥vθ(xt,t,y)−(α˙tx+σ˙tε)∥2  −  λ∥vθ(xt,t,y)−(α˙tx~+σ˙tε~)∥2] \mathcal{L}_{\Delta \text{FM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\Big[ \|v_\theta(x_t,t,y)-(\dot{\alpha}_t x+\dot{\sigma}_t\varepsilon)\|^2 \;-\; \lambda \|v_\theta(x_t,t,y)-(\dot{\alpha}_t \tilde{x}+\dot{\sigma}_t\tilde{\varepsilon})\|^2 \Big] LΔFM​(θ)=E[∥vθ​(xt​,t,y)−(α˙t​x+σ˙t​ε)∥2−λ∥vθ​(xt​,t,y)−(α˙t​x~+σ˙t​ε~)∥2].

Industry observers note that where λ∈[0,1)\lambda\in[0,1)λ∈[0,1) controls the strength of the “push-away” term. Intuitively: match your own trajectory, and be incompatible with someone else’s.

According to recent reports, the authors show that contrastive flow matching produces more discriminative trajectories and that this translates into both quality and efficiency gains: faster convergence (reported up to 9× fewer training iterations to reach similar FID) and fewer sampling steps (reported up to 5× fewer denoising steps) on ImageNet (Deng et al. 2009) and CC3M(Sharma et al., 2018) experiments.

A key advantage is that the objective is almost a drop-in replacement: you keep the usual flow-matching loss, then add a single contrastive “push-away” term using other samples in the same batch as negatives which provides the extra supervision without introducing additional model passes.

Sources indicate that on this run, contrastive flow matching yields a small but measurable improvement on the representation-driven metrics: CMMD goes from 0.41 → 0.40 and DINO-MMD from 0.39 → 0.36. The magnitude of the gain is smaller than what the paper reports on ImageNet, which is not too surprising: text conditioning is much more complex than discrete classes, and the training data distribution is likely less “separable” than ImageNet, making the contrastive signal harder to exploit.

Sources indicate that we do not see an improvement in FID in this specific experiment (it slightly worsens), but the throughput cost is negligible in practice (3.95 → 3.75 batches/sec). Given the simplicity of the change and the consistent movement in the right direction for the conditioning/representation metrics, we will likely still keep contrastive flow matching in our training pipeline as a low-cost regularizer.

Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise is probably one of our favorite recent papers in the diffusion space because it is not a new trick but a reset: stop asking the network to predict off-manifold quantities (noise or velocity) and just let it denoise. Most modern diffusion and flow models train the network to predict noise ε\varepsilonε or a mixed quantity like velocity vvv. Under the manifold assumption, natural images live on a low-dimensional manifold, while ε\varepsilonε and vvv are inherently off-manifold, so predicting them can be a harder learning problem than it looks.

According to recent reports, the authors frame the problem with the standard linear interpolation between the clean image xxx and the noise ε\varepsilonε: zt=t x+(1−t) ε, z_t = t\,x + (1-t)\,\varepsilon, zt​=tx+(1−t)ε, and the corresponding flow velocity: v=dztdt=x−ε. v = \frac{d z_t}{dt} = x - \varepsilon. v=dtdzt​​=x−ε.

It has been revealed that instead of outputting vθv_\thetavθ​ directly, the model predicts a clean image estimate: xθ(zt,t):=netθ(zt,t), x_\theta(z_t,t) := \mathrm{net}_\theta(z_t,t), xθ​(zt​,t):=netθ​(zt​,t), and we convert it to a velocity prediction via: vθ(zt,t)=xθ(zt,t)−zt1−t. v_\theta(z_t,t) = \frac{x_\theta(z_t,t) - z_t}{1-t}. vθ​(zt​,t)=1−txθ​(zt​,t)−zt​​.

Then we can keep the exact same flow-style objective in v-space: Lv=Et,x,ε[∥vθ(zt,t)−v∥22]withv=x−ε. \mathcal{L}_{v} = \mathbb{E}_{t,x,\varepsilon}\left[\left\|v_\theta(z_t,t) - v\right\|_2^2\right] \quad\text{with}\quad v = x-\varepsilon. Lv​=Et,x,ε​[∥vθ​(zt​,t)−v∥22​]withv=x−ε.

According to recent reports, this formulation makes the learning problem substantially easier in high dimensions: instead of predicting noise or velocity (which are essentially unconstrained in pixel space), the network predicts the clean image xxx, i.e., something that lies on the data manifold. In practice, this makes it feasible to train large-patch Transformers directly on pixels without a VAE or tokenizer while keeping optimization stable and the total number of tokens manageable.

We first evaluated x-prediction in the same setting as the rest of our objective experiments, namely training in the FLUX latent space at 256×256 resolution.

In this regime, the benefit of x-prediction is unclear. While FID improves slightly compared to the baseline, both CMMD and DINO-MMD degrade noticeably, and throughput is unchanged. This suggests that, when working in an already well-structured latent space, predicting clean images instead of velocity does not consistently dominate the baseline objective, and can even hurt representation-level alignment.

That said, this experiment is not where x-prediction really shines.

The exciting part is that x-prediction stabilizes high-dimensional training, making it feasible to use larger patches and denoise directly in pixel space, without a VAE, at much higher resolutions. Using JiT, we trained a model directly on 1024×1024 images with 32×32 patches, instead of operating in a compressed latent space. Despite the much higher resolution and the absence of a tokenizer, optimization remained stable and fast. We reached FID 17.42, DINO_MMD 0.56, and CMMD 0.71 with a throughput of 1.33 batches/sec.

These results are remarkable: training directly on 1024×1024 images is only about 3× slower than training in a 256×256 latent space, while operating on raw pixels. This strongly supports the core claim of Back to Basics: letting the model predict clean images makes the learning problem significantly easier, and opens the door to high-resolution, tokenizer-free text-to-image training without prohibitive compute costs.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, we initiative to use this formulation as the backbone of our upcoming speedrun experiments, to see how far we can push it when combined with the other efficiency and sparsification techniques discussed above. The main downside for now is that this approach does not let us benefit from the very nice properties of the FLUX.2 VAE; exploring whether some form of alignment or hybrid training could make these two worlds compatible is an open direction we plan to investigate further.

Recent findings suggest that so far, most of the techniques we discussed focus on making each training step more effective: improving the objective, shaping the representations, or accelerating convergence. The next lever is orthogonal: make each step cheaper.

For diffusion and flow transformers, the dominant cost is running deep transformer stacks over a large set of image/latent tokens where attention scales poorly with sequence length. Token sparsification methods target this directly by ensuring that only a subset of tokens pays the full compute price in the expensive parts of the network, while still preserving enough information flow to keep quality high.Most masking approaches accelerate training by removing tokens from the forward pass, then asking the model to hallucinate the missing content from learned placeholders. That works surprisingly well, but it violates the spirit of iterative denoising. Instead of refining all the content in each step, we are reconstructing parts from scratch.

Recent findings suggest that two recent papers illustrate a cleaner alternative: instead of deleting information, they reorganize where compute is spent. TREAD and SPRINT share the same high-level objective of avoiding full-depth computation for every token at every layer, but they pursue it through complementary strategies.

In a recent development, TREAD's (Krause et al., 2025) core idea is to replace compute reduction through information loss, such as dropping or masking tokens, with compute reduction through information transport using token routing. It introduces a route: for each training sample, it randomly selects a fraction of tokens and temporarily bypasses a contiguous chunk of layers, then re-injects those tokens later. Tokens are not discarded. Instead, they avoid paying the cost of full depth. Concretely, for a denoiser with a stack of blocks L0,…,LB−1L_0, \dots, L_{B-1}L0​,…,LB−1​, TREAD defines a route ritojr_{i\\to j}ritoj​ (start layer iii, end layer jjj). A subset of tokens follows the cheap path (identity) across Li,…,LjL_i,\dots,L_jLi​,…,Lj​, while the rest follows the normal full computation. Then both streams merge again at LjL_jLj​. In practice, the paper shows that routing up to 50% of tokens remains effective, while higher rates begin to degrade quality.

Industry observers note that SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) extends this approach by introducing sparsity in the most computationally expensive parts of the network, while preserving a dense information pathway. Its recipe is intentionally structured: run dense early layers over all tokens to build reliable low-level features, then keep only a subset of tokens through the sparse middle layers where compute is heaviest, and finally go dense again by re-expanding and fusing sparse deep features with a dense residual stream from the early layers, before producing the output. The key distinction from TREAD is where robustness comes from: TREAD keeps tokens “present” but shallower (routing), whereas SPRINT allows many tokens to be absent in the middle blocks, relying on the dense residual path to preserve full-resolution information. This is what enables more aggressive sparsification in practice. The paper explores drop ratios around 75%, versus ~50% for TREAD.

In a recent development, under our standard 256×256 latent setup, both methods deliver the primary benefit we were targeting. TREAD goes from 3.95 → 4.11 batches/sec, and SPRINT pushes it a bit further to 4.20 batches/sec. The cost is that under our evaluation protocol, this extra throughput comes with a clear loss in quality: FID rises from 18.20 to 21.61 (TREAD) and 22.56 (SPRINT), with the same pattern observed in CMMD and DINO-MMD.

Taken at face value, routing yields a modest ~7–9% throughput gain, but it comes with worse metrics in this benchmark, with SPRINT (the more aggressive scheme) degrading quality slightly more than TREAD.

It has been revealed that one key caveat is that token-sparse / routed models tend to score worse under vanilla Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG), and this effect is likely amplified here because these runs are still relatively undertrained in our setting. The authors of Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025) argue this is partly an evaluation mismatch: routing changes the model’s effective capacity, and plain “conditional vs. unconditional” CFG often becomes less effective, which can artificially reduce quality. We deliberately did not use specialized guidance schemes to keep our benchmark consistent across methods, and at this stage it would also not be very meaningful to treat the sparse model as a “bad version of itself” for guidance. As a result, we consider these numbers directionally useful, but still pessimistic and worth interpreting with caution.

Industry observers note that at 256×256, routing only gave modest gains because the model processes relatively few tokens. At 1024×1024, the picture changes completely. With 1024 tokens, routing finally targets the dominant cost, and the results are striking.

Industry observers note that both TREAD and SPRINT deliver large throughput gains over the dense baseline, with SPRINT pushing speed the furthest. More importantly, this time the gains do not come at the expense of quality but quite the opposite. TREAD in particular stands out, with a dramatic drop in FID (17.42 → 14.10) alongside strong improvements in CMMD and DINO-MMD. SPRINT is slightly more aggressive and a bit noisier in quality, but still clearly improves over the baseline while being the fastest option.

It has been revealed that in short, this is the regime where token routing really shines: high resolution, many tokens, and JiT-style pixel-space training. Here, routing is no longer a marginal optimization—it’s a major lever that improves both how fast and how well the model trains.

It has been revealed that after covering representation alignment, the core training objective, and token routing, we turned to the fourth axis that kept constantly mattered in practice: data. We found that the choice of training data, including how it is described through captions, can influence the trajectory of a training run as much as optimization techniques. Below are three concrete data experiments that consistently moved the needle in our setup.

Recent findings suggest that captions are an essential part of the training set: for a text-to-image model, they are not just metadata, they are the supervision. The DALL·E 3 (Betker et al., 2023) research paper showed that richer captions can be one of the strongest levers for improving training signal and prompt-following. To isolate the effect in our setup, we kept everything else fixed and changed only the caption style to compare:.

Long, descriptive captions (our baseline): multi-clause captions that mention composition, attributes, lighting, materials, and relationships.

Example "A photograph depicts a fluffy lop-eared rabbit sitting on a weathered wooden surface outdoors. The rabbit is predominantly white with patches of light brown and tan fur, particularly on its head and ears. Its ears droop noticeably, and its fur appears soft and thick. The rabbit's eyes are dark and expressive. It is positioned slightly off-center, facing towards the left of the frame. Behind the rabbit, slightly out of focus, is a miniature dark red metal wheelbarrow. A partially visible orange apple sits to the left of the rabbit. Fallen autumn leaves, predominantly reddish-brown, are scattered around the rabbit and apple on the wooden surface. The background is a blurred but visible expanse of green grass, suggesting an outdoor setting. The lighting is soft and natural, likely diffused daylight, casting no harsh shadows. The overall atmosphere is calm, peaceful, and autumnal. The aesthetic is rustic and charming, with a focus on the rabbit as the main subject. The color palette is muted and natural, consisting mainly of whites, browns, oranges, and greens. The style is naturalistic and straightforward, without any overt artistic manipulation. The vibe is gentle and heartwarming.".

Short, one-line captions: minimal descriptions with much less structure.

Example "A rabbit sitting on top of a wooden table.".

The outcome was unambiguous: switching to short captions severely hurt convergence across all metrics. Long captions provide a richer supervision signal: beyond prompt adherence, there is a very practical optimization reason. More tokens usually means more information, and therefore more learning signal for the denoiser. When the conditioning text specifies composition, attributes, lighting, materials, and relationships, the model gets a sharper “target” for what the denoising trajectory should preserve and refine, especially early in training.

Recent findings suggest that the fun paradox is that this extra detail often makes the learning problem easier, not harder: intuitively, one might expect longer prompts, with more attributes, constraints, and relationships, to increase complexity and burden the model. In practice, the opposite happens. Short captions leave many degrees of freedom unspecified, forcing the model to learn under ambiguity and implicitly average across multiple plausible interpretations. Long captions collapse that uncertainty by turning implicit choices into explicit constraints, allowing the denoiser to focus its capacity on refining a well-posed solution instead of guessing what matters.

Industry observers note that long captions are a strong training-time accelerator, but we still want the model to behave well on short prompts because that is how people actually use these systems. A simple workaround is to end training with a short fine-tuning stage on a mixture of long and short captions. That keeps the benefits of rich supervision early, while teaching the model to stay robust when conditioning is sparse.

Sources indicate that another data-related research question we explore is whether a low-cost synthetic corpus can accelerate early training compared to a real corpus of similar size. For this benchmark, we trained a model on a dataset of real images collected from Pexels and compared it with our Baseline which was trained on synthetic data generated with MidjourneyV6, both of which have around 1M images. We evaluated both runs against the same Unsplash reference set, composed exclusively of real images.

The synthetic-trained model scores better on CMMD and DINO-MMD, while the model trained on real images achieves a lower FID. Rather than a contradiction, this split mostly reflects what these metrics emphasize.

It has been revealed that FID is particularly sensitive to low-level image statistics: fine textures, high-frequency detail, noise patterns, and the subtle irregularities of real photography. Since our evaluation reference is composed of real images, a model trained on real photos naturally matches those statistics more closely, which translates into a better FID. Synthetic images, by contrast, often exhibit slightly different high-frequency signatures, cleaner edges, smoother micro-textures, more uniform noise, which are barely noticeable qualitatively but still get penalized by distributional metrics like FID.

Sources indicate that qualitatively, this difference is easy to spot. Models trained on synthetic data tend to produce images with cleaner global structure and stronger compositional and object coherence, but also exhibit a more synthetic appearance, characterized by smoother textures and reduced photographic noise. In contrast, models trained on real images better capture the irregular, fine-grained textures typical of natural photographs, though they often require more training to achieve comparable global structure.

One plausible explanation synthetic data remains so effective early on is that it exposes the model to a wider range of compositional collisions: unusual pairings of objects, attributes, styles, and viewpoints that rarely co-occur in natural datasets. While this can hurt realism at the texture level, it forces the model to explain a broader space of combinations, which appears to help with early disentanglement and structure learning.

Considered jointly, this suggests a simple but practical strategy: synthetic data is an efficient way to bootstrap training and lock in global structure quickly, while real images remain important later on if matching photographic texture statistics is the priority.

Industry observers note that finally, we experimented with a targeted Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) pass using Alchemist (Startsev et al., 2025), a compact dataset explicitly curated for high-impact. Alchemist is small by design (3,350 image–text pairs), but is constructed through a sophisticated curation pipeline that starts from a web-scale pool and progressively distills it down to visually exceptional samples.

In our setup, we fine-tuned our preview models for 20K steps on Alchemist. Despite the dataset’s small size, it had an outsized effect: it adds a distinct “style layer” with better composition, more photographic polish, and richer scenes without a clear impact on generalization.

The samples below show a side-by-side comparison of generations from the same base model, before and after the Alchemist fine-tuning pass.

Last but not least, we will briefly cover two practical training details that turned out to matter more than we expected. These factors are easily overlooked and in our case they had a clear impact on convergence and final image quality.

We generally default to AdamW for our benchmarks because it’s predictable and easy to compare across runs. However, lately, we have seen a renewed interest in optimizers that try to behave more like a good preconditioner without the full overhead of second-order methods. One recent example is Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), which, at a high level, tries to improve optimization by applying a better-conditioned update step, often translating into faster convergence and cleaner progress early in training.

In our setup, Muon was one of the rare cases in which a change of optimizer produced an immediately observable effect on the metrics.

For this experiment, we used the official PyTorch implementation of Muon, which at the moment supports Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) training only. If you’re running Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), there are community variants available; for example here.

While we refrain from broad conclusions based on a single benchmark, these results indicate that optimizer choice extends beyond stability considerations and can yield tangible gains in time-to-quality.

We eventually identified an error in our setup, where the denoiser weights were mistakenly stored in bfloat16 for a period of time.

Industry observers note that to be clear, using the BF16 autocast is great. Running the forward and backward passes in BF16 or mixed precision is standard and usually what you want for speed and memory. The problem arises from keeping the parameters in BF16 precision, which negatively impacts numerically sensitive operations.

In practice, some layers and operations are much less tolerant to reduced parameter precision:.

So the rule we now follow very strictly is: use BF16 autocast for compute, but keep weights (and optimizer state) in FP32 or at least ensure numerically sensitive modules stay FP32.

It is not a glamorous trick but it is exactly the kind of “silent” detail that can cost you multiple days of work if you do not notice it early.

We ran a systematic set of ablations on PRX training, comparing a range of optimization, representation, efficiency, and data choices against a clean flow-matching baseline using both quality metrics and throughput.

It has been revealed that the biggest gains came from alignment: REPA boosts early convergence (best used as a burn-in, then turned off), and better latents/tokenizers (REPA-E/FLUX2-AE) give a large jump in quality with clear speed trade-offs. Objective tweaks were mixed—contrastive FM helped slightly, while x-prediction mattered most by enabling stable 1024² pixel training. Token routing (TREAD/SPRINT) is minor at 256² but becomes a major win at high resolution. Data and practical details also mattered: long captions are critical, synthetic vs. real data shifts texture vs. structure, small SFT adds polish, Muon helped, and BF16-stored weights quietly hurt training.

In a recent development, that’s it for Part 2! If you want to play with an earlier public checkpoint from this series, the PRX-1024 T2I beta is still available here.

We are really excited about what’s next: in the coming weeks we will release the full source code of the PRX training framework, and we will do a public 24-hour “speedrun” where we combine the best ideas from this post into a single run and see how far the full recipe can go in one day.

If you made it this far, first of all thank you very much for your interest. Furthermore, we would love to have you join our Discord community where we discuss PRX progress and results, along with everything related to diffusion and text-to-image models.

It has been revealed that amazing work ! Super nice to see you work on this !

#11309. Industry News: 23 ways to handle tasks that trigger dread

Industry News: 23 ways to handle tasks that trigger dread

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, everyone has them: Tasks they dread.
  • Everyone has them: Tasks they dread.
  • Recent findings suggest that we asked members of the Fast Company Impact Council how they handle tasks they dread.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, everyone has them: Tasks they dread. They can range from mundane or routine items that clog the calendar to difficult conversations and meetings that cause stress. Avoiding them doesn’t make them go away. It just makes the dread heavier. Figuring out how to get through them frees up the time and headspace they take up. We asked members of the Fast Organization Impact Council how they handle tasks they dread. Here, 23 of them provide their best tips for getting them off your to-do list. 1. BODY-DOUBLE THE TASK I don’t tackle them alone. We call it body doubling: pulling in a teammate for a focused session to knock out the task neither of us wants to face solo. It depends on the task at hand too! My default is our incredible chief of staff. She’s the left brain to my right brain. From there it’s our executive team if the task requires finance, operations, technology, etc. Consistently routing the task with the right team members keeps the business moving forward. — Cody Barbo, Trust & Will 2. JUST DO IT AND DO IT NOW Dread is what you feel when you aren’t just doing it. Just do it. And when you do, more often than not you enter flow state, and you just keep doing stuff. — Eric Simons, Bolt.new 3. APPROACH IT LIKE AN ATHLETE When I face a task I’d rather avoid, I try to tackle it right away, before I give myself a hundred reasons to postpone it. I approach these situations like an athlete: Discomfort is part of progress, not a reason to stop. Whether it’s a challenging negotiation or a difficult decision, I’ve learned to take action even when I don’t feel ready. Years of daily training and building at my company have taught me that motivation comes and goes, and discipline is the key to keeping you moving forward. You can’t always control how you feel about a task, but you can train yourself to show up and get it done anyway. — Victoria Repa, BetterMe 4. TAKE ONE SMALL STEP In my mind, most dread comes from a task that has no clear definition or parameter. I’ve found it helpful to jump on the first physical step, small enough to finish in a few minutes (e.g., open the file, draft the subject line, pull last month’s numbers) and physically stop there to build next steps. This creates a sense of internal accountability. Once the task has a shape, the rest usually goes faster than the dread predicted. Also, if it still sits there after a week, that’s useful information: It may belong to someone else, or it may not need doing at all. — James Chester, WVN 5. CHIP AWAY EACH DAY Momentum beats motivation. I start small and chip away a little each day. Procrastinating doesn’t buy you time, it just weighs you down, and eventually it crowds out the work you love. — Tami Rosen, executive board and advisor to technology and finance companies 6. TACKLE THEM FIRST, EARLY IN THE DAY I do them first, and I make them smaller. Dread grows in the gap between knowing a task needs doing and starting it. So I close that gap early in the day, before anything else competes for my attention. If it’s major, I commit only to the first part. Momentum handles the rest. I’ve also learned to ask what the dread is telling me. Sometimes it’s a sign the task needs a conversation, not more effort, and the fastest way through is a call to the right person. — Megan Noel, Covista 7. NAME WHAT YOU DREAD AND WHY Usually, people dread something because it is uncomfortable, ambiguous, or carries some sort of emotional weight. I try to name what I dread and why, instead of pretending the task itself is the problem. If it matters, do it and do it now, because avoidance compounds just like progress does. The things we put off usually get heavier, not lighter. — Ethan Braden, Texas A&M University 8. TAKE OUT THE TRASH DAY A colleague once inspired me with her “take out the trash day,” dedicating a chunk of time each week to knock through dreaded tasks. With all the noise on Slack, texts, and email, I block an hour at the end of the week, mute my notifications, and cruise through. It’s how I take care of budgets, expenses, and the general paperwork, so I can get back to the creative work where I’m in my flow. Sometimes there’s a snack reward waiting at the end. — Courtney Brigham, Typeface 9. SET A REWARD FOR YOURSELF I break it down into chunks, set a target date and time to complete each chunk, and then block out time and get it done. I also set a reward for myself after doing it. For example, I’ll get to have this great lunch after I finish it. It sounds silly, but it’s nice to have rewards after doing a project that is not enjoyable! — Felicia Curcuru, Binti 10. RELY ON PREPARATION During dreaded high-stakes situations like meetings with multiple stakeholders or delivering sensitive performance-based feedback, I rely on preparation. Coming armed with a brief outline of mission-critical points ensures you stay on track and helps you recover if the conversation gets derailed. If I’m ruminating on a complex problem that I just can’t seem to crack, I put everything down and do something completely unrelated. Taking a walk, listening to a podcast, or even washing the dishes allows my brain to marinate, discover hidden connections, and eventually the solution becomes clear. — Celia Jones, FINN Partners 11. PRIORITIZE ACCORDINGLY Tasks I dread are rarely the most key for our business, so I prioritize them accordingly. However, they tend to bubble up to the higher end of the list of less critical tasks. The longer they remain on my to-do list, the more days they get to impact my morale, so I’m motivated to get them done. — Brad Weber, InspiringApps 12. CONNECT IT TO OUTCOME I try to stay positive by focusing on the value the task will create once it’s completed. I put it in the broader context of the goal it supports and the impact it will have. As a big-picture person, details can be challenging, but connecting the work to a meaningful outcome helps me stay motivated and push through with a positive mindset. — Chris K Bailey, Bailey Brand Consulting 13. TAKE THE MEDICINE ALL AT ONCE I put them off. Then I bundle them up and take care of them all at once. Like medicine. It tastes bad but works. Sort of like Buckley’s cough and cold medicine. — Phillip Haid, Public Inc. 14. STOP AND MAP IT OUT If I catch myself spending real time on something where I’m just going through the motions, I stop and map it out. What are the inputs, what am I doing with them, and what does the output need to look like? Once the process is clearly mapped, it’s usually pretty obvious that a lot of it doesn’t need me. Then I build an automation around it. I still get the result; I just skip the mundane part. — Mike Sewell, Gresham Smith 15. ASK WHETHER YOU’RE THE RIGHT PERSON TO DO IT I try not to spend too much time negotiating with myself. If something needs to be done, I focus on the next step and start. Usually, the anticipation is worse than the task itself. As a CEO, I’ve also learned to ask whether I’m the right person to do it. There are many things I can do, but I don’t need to do all of them. Sometimes leadership means taking something on yourself. Other times it means trusting someone else to own it. What I try to avoid is letting something I don’t enjoy become something the organization has to wait for. — Yuping Huang, Quantum Computing Inc. 16. CARVE UP YOUR DAY Technology marketing is constant context switching and rapid decision-making. If you’re not careful, a whole day passes without a minute of real thought or creativity. You give in to the “critical” transactions, and eventually the work that’s most critical to your job disappears entirely. So I carve up my day. Mornings are for content, strategy, and creative problem-solving. Midday is the transactional work. The last couple of hours go to administration and anything that wasn’t urgent. And if something that needs real creativity slips through until late in the day, it gets the first look the next morning, with fresh eyes. — Colby Proffitt, Seekr 17. DIVIDE IT INTO MANAGEABLE STEPS When I face a task I dread, I focus on understanding what makes it difficult and what depends on completing it. This matters because postponing an uncomfortable responsibility does not remove it. It can affect decisions, relationships, and other people’s work. I divide the task into manageable steps, establish a clear deadline, and begin with the first action. For me, discipline is not about enjoying every responsibility. It is about addressing what needs to be done before hesitation becomes a larger problem. — Manuel Freire-Garabal, Gioya HEI 18. DO THE WORST THING FIRST Do it first. I was told once that you should always do the worst thing on your to-do list first because the day then only gets better. Have stuck to it ever since. And never overlook the power of reward: For every annoying task give yourself a little treat in return. The promise of a future good thing coming your way works every time. — Helen Andrews, Johannes Leonardo 19. AUTOMATE THE MUNDANE Recently, I’ve unlocked a new cheat code in chipping away at those dreaded tasks. When walking to work, I’ll start talking with my favorite large language model of the moment and we can hammer out 10 open items from unanswered Slack messages and emails to meeting recaps and other nagging tasks that can rapidly pile up. When all the right connectors are in place, the efficiency unlock is tremendous and has been a game changer for knocking out those dreaded to-dos. — Matt Conlin, Fluent 20. KNOW WHEN THE TASK BELONGS TO SOMEONE ELSE I like to understand every aspect of my business, even the things that don’t come naturally to me. I’m always open to learning something new, but I also recognize when something falls outside my skill set. I believe in knowing your strengths and surrounding yourself with people who bring expertise you don’t have. If it’s something I can tackle, I get it done. If someone else can do it better, I delegate. My time is best spent where I can make the greatest impact. — Kim Wileman, No Makeup Makeup 21. USE THE HEADWIND AS A TAILWIND I once heard Jimmy Iovine, co-founder of Beats, talk about using a headwind as a tailwind, and it’s stuck with me ever since. If there’s something you hate doing, run towards it, not away from it. Delay is a false economy because it just extends the dread. Then I break it into tiny actions and get the first one done. Momentum beats motivation every time, and most tasks are never as bad as the story you’ve told yourself about them. — Emily Kortlang, Meaco 22. MEET IT AT YOUR COGNITIVE PEAK I use power hours. I know my brain is sharpest late in the evening or early in the morning, so I save the tasks I would normally procrastinate on for that window. I don’t do it every day. The idea is simple: Dreaded work takes far less energy when you meet it at your cognitive peak, so an hour or two of focus can clear what would otherwise linger for weeks. — Muneer Panjwani, Engage for Good | The Halo Awards 23. ATTACK THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES I try to attack the first five minutes rather than the whole task. Dread grows in the space between knowing you have to do something and starting it. Once I take action, the task usually gets a lot less intimidating. — Ran Mullins, Psympl.

#11308. Tech Report: We tested the RAM-saving storage tech in Gears of War: E-Day

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1115 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: We tested the RAM-saving storage tech in Gears of War: E-Day

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase.
  • However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally crucial role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage.
  • Industry observers note that we’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gears of War: E-Day delivers an impressive visual and technical showcase. The game brings together several advanced graphics technologies, including Unreal Engine 5’s Nanite and Lumen, MegaLights, and RTX Mega Geometry for more accurate ray-traced shadows and reflections, alongside a range of upscaling and frame generation technologies.

However, today we’re focusing on a less-discussed technology that plays an equally crucial role in bringing this visually rich, densely detailed world to systems with more limited hardware resources: storage technology designed to reduce RAM usage.

Industry observers note that we’ll begin by examining its behavior on a high-end system with plenty of resources to spare, before moving to a more modest configuration that better represents the hardware available to the average PC gamer. This will allow us to see how much of a difference the technology makes, particularly on lower-end systems.

In an interview with Digital Foundry, The Coalition explained how they leveraged the Xbox Series S’s fast SSD to bring the dense world of Gears of War: E-Day to a memory-limited system. By effectively using the NVMe SSD as an extension of system memory, they can dynamically load and offload complex city data in real time. This approach allows the game to stream the necessary assets for each scene just in time, overcoming the console’s limited RAM.

Digital Foundry notes that the true “special sauce” lies in The Coalition’s smart data management. The team employs advanced heuristics to determine which assets are fetched from the SSD and when, carefully balancing performance. Overusing this technique could harm frame rates, so the system is tuned to swap data only when it benefits the experience.

Gears of War: E-Day also supports DirectStorage, although based on our previous testing, this alone does not always result in high SSD activity or read rates.

YouTuber Mostly Positive Reviews shared his findings in a recent post on X, where he found higher-than-usual SSD activity in Task Manager when playing the game.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that gears of War E-Day is visually very impressive, but something has to be done with how the game either compiles shaders or streams data. My 14400F is constantly sitting at 80% CPU usage, 16GB RAM is maxed out, and disk read is sitting at a constant 120 MBps, with spikes up to 500 MBps. Will test this with the 9060 XT as well. These are settings I chose to maintain 60 fps, which it does, except for the massive shader compilation stutters every so often.October 7, 2026.

Based on his findings, we decided to investigate further.

According to recent reports, task Manager does not use a low enough polling period to measure SSD activity accurately, so we used HWInfo with the polling period set to 20 milliseconds. We tested SSD activity across all of the game’s graphics presets at 4K using DLSS Quality.

It has been revealed that in our previous tests of games that relied heavily on the SSD, none came close to sustaining 1 GB/s of average bandwidth. The highest we recorded was 366 MB/s in Forspoken at 4K with maximum settings, while many titles stayed well under 100 MB/s. Some games did show higher peak bandwidths, but these spikes lasted only a few milliseconds. For our purposes, it’s the sustained throughput – reflected in the average bandwidth – that truly matters.

In Gears of War: E-Day at higher settings, we essentially have a steady stream of a little over 1 GB/s at all times, indicating that the disk is indeed being utilized as an extension of system memory. As you can see, peaks hit up to 3.7 GB/s of throughput.

We measured RAM usage on our high-end system to see how much the game will use across each generation of SSD tested.

The game uses a significant amount of system memory, but having the game installed on an NVMe SSD – regardless of generation – saves about 2GB of RAM. The storage technology seems to be working as expected.

Since the game’s average read bandwidth far exceeds the limits of a SATA SSD, we expect that installing the game on one would lead to visual issues – and that is exactly what we observe.

In the first comparison, textures are slow to load, which noticeably reduces image quality. In the second comparison, lighting and shadows take some time to appear. While everything eventually loads correctly, running the game on a SATA SSD does hurt immersion.

It has been revealed that we tested the game across four generations of SSDs to evaluate any impact on performance. Using a high-end system with ample memory, we aim to determine the behavior of the storage technology on a system that is not resource-constrained. We will then compare the performance of our laptop’s internal PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with that of a SATA SSD.

In a recent development, on a system with sufficient memory, installing the game on a SATA SSD has no measurable performance impact. The only drawback is the aforementioned visual degradation.

Now, we focused on our lower-end system with only 16GB of DDR5.

Now we start to see the benefit of installing the game on an NVMe SSD, especially on higher settings.

In a recent development, although the average frame rate remains virtually identical on both the NVMe and SATA SSDs, increasing the graphics preset impacts the 1% lows. The NVMe SSD delivers smoother frametimes, resulting in a more responsive and fluid gaming experience.

While the concept isn’t entirely upcoming – Windows already uses virtual memory to page data to disk when physical memory is exhausted – The Coalition has fine-tuned this technology specifically for their game. Their approach ensures that the data being paged out won’t noticeably slow down gameplay as it’s read from disk. In our testing, this technology successfully reduces RAM usage when the game is installed on an NVMe SSD.

Placing the game on an NVMe SSD also enables near-instant asset loading. For systems with 16GB of RAM or less, an NVMe SSD can deliver higher 1% lows, resulting in smoother performance. With RAM prices climbing and many players using machines with 16GB – or even 8GB – of memory, it’s reasonable to wonder if other developers will adopt similar techniques. For titles striving to create visually dense, richly detailed worlds, leveraging fast storage could be a practical way to preserve their vision on lower-end systems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a newly introduced generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • Recent findings suggest that A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a newly introduced generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an vital role in how computers store and process data.

Recent findings suggest that A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

In a recent development, rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

In a recent development, skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the newly introduced study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

Sources indicate that "For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A Newly introduced Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a fresh way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us fresh insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," noted Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling upcoming computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

The Future of the Global Open-Source AI Ecosystem: From DeepSeek to AI+

📅 03 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this third article, we examine paths and trajectories of prominent Chinese AI organizations, and posit future directions for open source.
  • In a recent development, for AI researchers and developers contributing to and relying on the open source ecosystem and for policymakers understanding the rapidly changing environment, due to intraorganizational and global community gains, open source is the dominant and popular approach for Chinese AI organizations for the near future.
  • Sources indicate that having examined strategic and architectural changes since DeepSeek's R1, we get a glimpse for the first time at how an organic open source AI ecosystem is taking shape in China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this third article, we examine paths and trajectories of prominent Chinese AI organizations, and posit future directions for open source.

In a recent development, for AI researchers and developers contributing to and relying on the open source ecosystem and for policymakers understanding the rapidly changing environment, due to intraorganizational and global community gains, open source is the dominant and popular approach for Chinese AI organizations for the near future. Openly sharing artifacts from models to papers to deployment infrastructure maps to a strategy with the goal of large-scale deployment and integration.

Sources indicate that having examined strategic and architectural changes since DeepSeek's R1, we get a glimpse for the first time at how an organic open source AI ecosystem is taking shape in China. A culmination of powerful players, some established in open source, some new players, and some changing course entirely to contribute to the new open culture, signal that the open collaborative approach is mutually beneficial.

This collaboration is reaching beyond national boundaries; the most followed organization on Hugging Face is DeepSeek, and the fourth most followed is Qwen.

In a recent development, in addition to models, openly sharing science and techniques has not only informed other AI organizations, but also the entire open source community. The most popular papers on Hugging Face largely come from Chinese organizations, namely ByteDance, DeepSeek, Tencent, and Qwen.

source: https://huggingface.co/spaces/evijit/PaperVerse.

Recent findings suggest that alibaba positioned open source as an ecosystem and infrastructure strategy. Qwen was not shaped as a single flagship model, but continuously expanded into a family covering multiple sizes, tasks, and modalities, with frequent updates on Hugging Face and their own platform ModelScope. Its influence did not concentrate on any single version. Instead, it was repeatedly reused as a component across different scenarios, gradually taking on the role of a general AI foundation. By mid-2025, Qwen became the model with most derivatives on Hugging Face, with over 113k models using Qwen as a base, and over 200k model repositories tagging Qwen, far exceeding Meta's Llama's 27k or DeepSeek's 6k. Organization-wide, Alibaba boasts the most derivatives almost as much as both Google and Meta combined.

At the same time, Alibaba aligned model development with cloud and hardware infrastructure, integrating models, chips, platforms, and applications into a single engineering stack.

Industry observers note that tencent also made a significant move from borrowing to building. As one of the first major companies to integrate DeepSeek into core consumer-facing products after R1's release, Tencent did not initially frame open source as a public narrative. Instead, it brought mature models in through plug-in style integration, ran large-scale internal validation, and only later began to release its own capabilities. From May 2025 onward, Tencent accelerated open releases in areas where it already had strengths, such as vision, video, and 3D with its own brand named Tencent Hunyuan (it's now Tencent HY), and these models quickly gained adoption in the community.

ByteDance, by following its "AI application factory" approach, starts selectively open sourcing high value components while keeping its competitive focus on product entry points and large scale usage. In this context, the ByteDance Seed team has contributed several notable open-source artifacts, including UI-TARS-1.5 for multimodal UI understanding, **Seed-Coder **for data-centric code modeling, and the SuperGPQA dataset for systematic reasoning evaluation. Despite a relatively low-profile open-source presence, ByteDance has achieved significant scale in China's AI market, with its AI application Doubao surpassing 100 million DAU in December 2025.

The most notable change within Baidu, whose CEO openly calls short on open source, also started its shift: after years of prioritizing closed models, it re-entered the ecosystem through free access and open release, such as the Ernie 4.5 series. This shift was accompanied by renewed investment in its open-source framework, PaddlePaddle, as well as its own AI chip Kunlunxin, which announced an IPO on January 1, 2026. By connecting models, chips, and PaddlePaddle within a more open system, Baidu can lower costs, attract developers, and influence standards, while maintaining strategic control under shared constraints of compute, cost, and regulation.

Among startups, Moonshot, Z.ai, and MiniMax adjusted rapidly and brought new momentum to the open-source community within months after R1. Models such as Kimi K2, GLM-4.5, and MiniMax M2 all earned places on AI-World's open-model milestone rankings.At the end of 2025, Z.ai and MiniMax released their most advanced open-source models to date and subsequently confirmed their IPO intends in close succession.

The open-sourcing of Kimi K2 was widely described as a "Another DeepSeek moment" for the community. Although Moonshot has not unveiled an IPO, market reports indicate that the tech giant raised approximately $500M in funding by the end of 2025, with AGI and agent-based systems positioned as its primary commercialization objectives.

Those application-first companies such as Xiaohongshu, Bilibili, Xiaomi, and Meituan, previously focused only on the application layer, began training and releasing their own models. With their native advantage in real usage scenarios and domain data, once strong reasoning became available at low cost through open source, building in-house models became practical. It tunes AI around their specific businesses, rather than being constrained by the cost structures or limits of external providers.

If the business world seized the ROI positive opportunity for growth, research institutions and the broader community welcomed the shift even more willingly. Organizations such as BAAI and Shanghai AI Lab redirected more effort toward toolchains, evaluation systems, data platforms, and deployment infrastructure, projects like FlagOpen, OpenDataLab, and OpenCompass. These efforts did not chase single-model performance, but instead strengthened the long-term foundations of the ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that the defining feature of the latest ecosystem is not that there are more models, but that an entire chain has formed. Models can be open-sourced and extended; deployments can be reused and scaled; software and hardware can be coordinated and swapped; and governance capabilities can be embedded and audited. This is a shift from isolated breakthroughs to a system that can actually run in the real world.

Industry observers note that this ecosystem did not appear overnight. It is built on years of accumulated infrastructure "tailwind" since 2017. Over the past several years, China has periodically invested in data centers and compute centers, gradually forming a nationwide, integrated compute layout centered on the "East Data, West Compute" strategy. The national plan established 8 major compute hubs and 10 data center clusters, guiding compute demand from the east toward the central and western regions.

According to recent reports, public information suggests China intends to invest in continual growth in energy capacity. China's total compute capacity is around 1590 EFLOPS as of the year 2025, ranking among the top globally. Sources in China assert that intelligent compute capacity, tailored for AI training and deployment, is expected to grow by roughly 43% year over year, far outpacing general-purpose compute. At the same time,the average data center power usage effectiveness (PUE) fell to around 1.46, indicating better effectiveness and providing a solid hardware foundation for AI at scale. Energy is a clear key focus.

If the 2017 "Newly introduced Generation AI Development Strategy" was mainly about setting direction and building foundations, then the August 2025 "AI+" action plan clearly shifted focus toward large-scale deployment and deep integration. This marks a directionally different pursuit from AGI. The emergence of R1 provided the missing "lift" at the engineering and ecosystem level. It was the catalyst that systematically activated compute, energy, and data infrastructure that had already been built.

Sources indicate that as a result, in the year following R1's release, China's AI development accelerated along two main paths. First, AI became more deeply embedded in industrial processes, moving beyond chatbots toward agents and workflows. Second, greater emphasis was placed on autonomous and controllable AI systems, reflected in more flexible training pathways and increasingly localized deployment strategies.

Industry observers note that looking back, the real turning point was not the growth in the number of models, but a fundamental change in how open-source models are used. Open source moved from an optional choice to a default assumption in system design. Models became reusable and composable components within larger engineering systems.

Industry observers note that from DeepSeek to "AI+", China's path in 2025 was not about chasing peak performance. It was about building a practical path organized around open source, engineering efficiency, and scalable delivery, a path that has already begun to run on its own.

In a recent development, resource constraints did not limit China's AI development. In some respects, they reshaped its trajectory. The release of DeepSeek R1 acted as a catalytic event, triggering a chain of responses across the domestic industry and accelerating the formation of a more organically structured ecosystem. At the same time, this shift created a critical window for continued domestic research and development. As this ecosystem matures, its longer-term impact---and how the global AI community may engage with an increasingly self-sustaining AI ecosystem in China---will become vital questions for future discussion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury Secretary, admitted that the U.S. export controls cannot prevent all the restricted hardware from reaching China or other adversaries, which is why the country allegedly obtained millions of restricted AI GPUs from Nvidia. At the same time, he questioned the efficiency of Nvidia's internal controls. called for accountability at Nvidia, criticized the firm's general counsel, but stressed that it was unclear whether Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang knew about the potentially illicit practices.

"I think that there is a lot of leakage in the system, and we are constantly working to close that down," in an interview with CNBC (via @siliconmemes). "One thing here is that the story has been thus far on Jensen Huang's personal foibles. The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client? And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies? And I think it is key that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.".

Bessent admitted that despite strict U.S. export controls that prohibit sales of advanced AI GPUs to China, considerable quantities of restricted hardware may still make their way to the country. However, the Treasury Secretary does not believe that the U.S. needs to introduce more stringent export restrictions or grant government agencies additional powers to prevent GPU smuggling. Instead, the authorities should properly enforce existing regulations, according to Bessent.

Recent findings suggest that bessent also criticized Nvidia's general counsel Timothy Teter, who reportedly contacted the U.S. Department of Commerce to inquire whether U.S. authorities were behind the detention of Megaspeed's Alice Wong in Singapore. However, the Treasury Secretary declined to speculate about potential consequences for Nvidia if it turned out that some of its executives knew that their customers acted as intermediaries for Chinese entities. Meanwhile, Bessent expressed confidence that Nvidia's board of directors would conduct a thorough investigation into the matter.

In a recent development, "But let us just say, if this was happening, then there were not robust controls at the manufacturer," Bessent said. "We do not know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this. The [general council] seems to have been very involved here, probably should have done more oversight rather than the haranguing [government officials at the U.S. DoC].".

Bessent also revealed that the Departments of the Treasury, War, and State, as well as the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), had supported the addition of Megaspeed to the Entity List for months. However, the authority to impose such export restrictions belongs to the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which reportedly stalled efforts to blacklist Megaspeed for months as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick feared that the move could worsen trade tensions with China.

Industry News: Nike spent years reinventing Air. Meet the upcoming Tuned Air (exclusive)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that for half a century, Nike has been synonymous with Air.
  • It has been revealed that for half a century, Nike has been synonymous with Air.
  • Today, a day before it reveals its financial results, Nike is unveiling Tuned Air, a high-tech evolution of Air that has been in the works for years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for half a century, Nike has been synonymous with Air. The cushioning—developed at NASA, then incorporated inside a 1978 running shoe and the Air Max 1—came to represent Nike’s commitment to cutting-edge innovation. Now, with Nike on its back foot after several years of missteps, the tech giant is counting on a new version of Air to help pull it out of its slump. Today, a day before it announces its financial results, Nike is unveiling Tuned Air, a high-tech evolution of Air that has been in the works for years. It’s debuting this technology in a running sneaker that will come out within a year. But Nike sees Tuned Air as a broader platform that can be incorporated into other sports and even its apparel lines. [Video: Nike] It’s one way Nike hopes to restore its credibility as an innovator and win back runners who have drifted to rivals. Given how much ground Nike has lost in recent years, it’s unclear whether this strategy will work. But the company is optimistic. “There’s no better innovation that speaks to our formula than Air,” states Phil McCartney, Nike’s chief innovation, design, and product officer. McCartney has spent three decades at Nike, where he ran the footwear business from 2016 until last year, when CEO Elliott Hill put him in charge of innovation, design and product across Nike, Jordan, and Converse. Speaking to me from the LeBron James Innovation Center at Nike’s campus in Beaverton, Oregon, McCartney explained that his team has a motto borrowed from two Nike legends: “Create epic shit. Make athletes better.” (The first comes from Kobe Bryant, the second from Nike’s cofounder, Bill Bowerman.) McCartney says Nike is translating that slogan into a formula, “athlete, science, solution,” that will guide the company’s approach to innovation. His teams gather insights from athletes, then tests ideas at the Nike Sports Research Lab in Beaverton and through field teams in Eldoret, Kenya; London, and Shanghai. [Photo: Nike] Introducing Nike Tuned Air The original Air technology created tough pockets of nitrogen using two sheets of plastic. In that case, the air was evenly distributed, creating cushioning throughout the pocket. With Tuned Air, Nike adds nuance. Before the plastic sheets are pressed together, Nike adds a chemical that allows it to create a pattern; it can now fine-tune where the gas is located and how much air is in each pocket. In doing so, it can make one part of the cushion soft and springy, and another part firm and stable. “It allows us to completely change the relationship between cushioning and support, and precision-tune the experience,” says McCartney. Nike has given this technology to runners over the last few years. “The feedback that we’ve had from the runners who have been trying this for a couple of years now is it feels like no other cushioning system out there,” he says. “Incredibly well cushioned, but also has stability. That’s the sort of holy grail that we’ve been trying to unlock in Air.” While Nike’s approach to achieving this balance might be distinct, many other running brands are also trying to balance cushioning with structure with their own innovations. Brooks’s DNA Tuned foam uses a dual-cell construction, with large cells in the heel to cushion landings and smaller cells in the front to make the toes more responsive. Hoka’s H-Frame features a firm strip of foam in the midsole, surrounded by softer cushioning. On’s CloudTec technology uses hollow tubes of foam molded to the bottom of the sole to absorb impact, along with a steel plate in the midsole. With this newfound ability to modulate how much air is in each pocket, Nike can now explore “wildly different expressions” of the technology, McCartney says. Besides running, Tuned Air will be incorporated into other sports, like soccer, and into clothing like the Air Milano jacket, creating air pockets that improve temperature regulation. Nike can even integrate Tuned Air into lifestyle shoes, like vintage sneakers, creating more comfort. “How could we make an Air Force 1 using a sock liner that is Tuned Air, so you get comfort and support?” McCartney says. Nike has streamlined the manufacturing of Tuned Air so that it can move 70% faster than it typically does from idea to product. This is crucial to allowing Nike to be nimble as it seeks to compete with the many rivals that are also spinning out innovative new products quickly. [Video: Nike] Nike Needs a Win Nike needs this innovation to resonate with consumers. Last quarter, revenue declined 4% to $11.2 billion, and the company expects full-year sales to fall by a high single digit percentage. Sportswear, which accounts for nearly half the business, fell by double digits. Sales in China dropped 26% and Converse sank 28%. Nike has declared a restructuring strategy that will cut more jobs after several rounds of layoffs in recent years. Nike’s rivals have been closely observing its missteps, and taken advantage of the opportunity to steal market share. In running, a category Nike once dominated, it’s now in third place, trailing Brooks and Hoka. In the lifestyle sphere, Adidas has had hit after hit by bringing back its classic Samba and Gazelle, and New Balance has turned its retro styles like the 550 into bestsellers. Meanwhile, Nike hasn’t had a lifestyle sneaker hit in years. Nike’s running business is starting to recover. It’s grown by double digits for more than a year, helped by the successful Vomero line. “We’re seeing market share gains almost daily right now,” says McCartney. Historically, Nike has built running technology for elite athletes that tries to shave seconds off on their race times. But that technology takes a long time to trickle down into running shoes that the average person can lace up. Nike doesn’t have the luxury of time anymore. That’s why its Tuned Air is designed for the everyday runner. “The entry point will be that everyday run,” McCartney says. “When you’re just trying to log your Tuesday morning run, you want the maximum amount of running with precision-tuned support.” Nike is making a big bet on Tuned Air. But whether enough consumers get excited about the technology—and the forthcoming sneakers—to boost Nike’s fortunes is unclear. Tomorrow, when Nike lays out its long-term financial prepares, we’ll get a better glimpse into how much ground it has yet to make up.
