#11300. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2315 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • According to recent reports, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

According to recent reports, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

It has been revealed that conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

Recent findings suggest that "In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

Industry observers note that to minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

Industry observers note that the term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Sources indicate that although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

According to recent reports, the proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the latest approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

In a recent development, "Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

It has been revealed that this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

According to recent reports, the researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

It has been revealed that "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

Industry observers note that this behavior is notable because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

It has been revealed that the nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

In a recent development, the weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

Industry observers note that the proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

Recent findings suggest that "Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

Recent findings suggest that the approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

Industry observers note that these calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

In a recent development, the results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

Industry observers note that this makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely fresh materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain vital challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

Sources indicate that from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

Industry observers note that from a technological perspective, the study indicates how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

Industry observers note that if future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after more than five decades in Hollywood, Arnold Schwarzenegger finally feels fit to play his most iconic role yet. And he’s taking the reins just in time for the holiday season. The Terminator and Total Recall actor is suiting up in bright red and white for Amazon Prime’s upcoming holiday creative campaign, “Santa Schwarzenegger,” which debuts on Monday. The advertising spot begins with Schwarzenegger looking a little forlorn as the paparazzi chase him around New York. He then orders a Santa suit from Prime, allowing for anonymity as Schwarzenegger donates snacks to a dog rescue center, watches a basketball game, and heaves a Christmas tree onto the roof of a car. “I’m at that age now and it’s believeable” Throughout his career, Schwarzenegger has played plenty of iconic roles. He’s portrayed a killing machine from the future, Batman’s nemesis Mr. Freeze, both Hercules and his father, Zeus, and an undercover cop teaching kindergarteners. But Schwarzenegger states no role he has ever played has been as worldwide as this one. [Photo: Amazon] “This is the perfect time for me to play Santa, because I’m at that age now and it’s more believable,” Schwarzenegger tells Fast Company. “With all the interesting characters that I played in my career—from Conan to Terminator—I thought that Santa is the ultimate.” For Amazon, the Schwarzenegger spot fits neatly into two goals: driving sales and attention to Prime, a core pillar of the online retail giant’s Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and other holiday sales events throughout the season. But it also ties in neatly with Amazon Prime’s The Man with the Bag, an upcoming holiday film that debuts on December 2, starring Schwarzenegger as Santa for a second time. Alan Ritchson, Awkwafina, and Ken Jeong are also featured in the film’s cast. The film also ties into Amazon’s 2026 holiday campaign, which is called “Joy Delivered.” “Arnold is the king of the kids, we saw that when he made Kindergarten Cop,” Jo Shoesmith, Amazon’s vice president and global chief brand officer, tells Fast Company. “There is a warmth and charm to him that lives outside of the character of Santa.” Santa “has to be in shape” “Santa Schwarzenegger” will run through December 23 across several channels including television, digital, social, and streaming audio. Yet another component of the campaign that Amazon is promoting is Schwarzenegger’s curated holiday gift guide, which includes plush dog toys, supplements, toys intended for children and grandchildren, and dumbbells. “Think about it, Santa has to fly all the way from the North Pole, he has to be in shape to hand out the gifts at every single continent to go to every single house,” says Schwarzenegger. “It is a lot of work. He has to be in shape.”  [Photo: Amazon] There are also two books: Better Every Day, a self-help book penned by Schwarzenegger that’s due to be published in January, and Arnold, which is written about him. There’s also a cigar lighter, which may seem counterintuitive for the fitness enthusiast, but apparently he’s smoked them for over 40 years, including during his interview with Fast Company. “We never want to twist the arm of the personality to put something in their mouth that doesn’t come across as authentic,” says Shoesmith. “It’s very driven by his holiday ordering list.”  As an Austrian, Schwarzenegger says his holiday traditions differed from how he raised his children in America. The holiday is celebrated on December 24 and the gift giver is a baby Jesus called Christkind, not Santa, though Schwarzenegger says the latter has become more popular there in recent years. “I always question with every script I get: is this something that would just be good for America, or just good for Europe, or is this something that can play in every continent,” says Schwarzenegger. Santa, he says, is a role that can “entertain the whole world.” [Photo: Amazon] The rise of star-powered Santas While Santa has been “the face” of the Christmas holiday for marketers for more than a century, the celebrity angle has been a more recent development. John Travolta has played the role in multiple ad spots for Capital One, while Jon Hamm did so for Fox Sports, Steve Carell for Comcast, and Brent Bailey for Target. “He’s kind of just this joyous, universally loved figure,” adds Shoesmith. To be clear, Shoesmith was talking about Schwarzenegger at this moment, not Santa, though she says both have cross-generational appeal. Schwarzenegger is also a safe casting choice for the retailer at a time when the American consumer isn’t optimistic. Unease about the economy was a central theme in the recent midterm elections, and the sales projection forecasts for the upcoming holiday season look fairly mixed. Research firm Circana says average holiday spending will total $779 this year, down from $796 in 2025. The trade association the National Retail Federation is more bullish, expecting retail sales in November and December to increase 4.2% to about $1 trillion, compared to a year ago. “We’re a brand whose logo is a smile, so joy is inherently part of who we are as a brand,” says Shoesmith of the tone approach for Amazon Prime’s campaign. “We really make sure that we have a great selection of brands at a really great price, and that’s really crucial for customers right now . . . they’re very price conscious.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Besides a significant update for phones, there’s also a sizable Pixel Watch Drop today, but it’s mostly a preview of what’s to come.

In a recent development, on the Pixel Watch 3 and newer (Wear OS 7+), step-by-step workouts are rolling out starting today. In addition to instructions, you can log reps and weights, as well as track metrics. Make sure you’re on Google Health 4.12+ on your Pixel Watch and version 5.12+ on Android.

The other four features previewed today will be available in the next few weeks.

Phone-to-Watch unlock is such a welcome addition!

Recent findings suggest that as for "workouts on watch", that's something I was expecting when I first purchased the Pixel Watch 2 about 6 months ago. Since then I moved to PW3, and while I was super disappointed such a basic feature wasn't available (what's the point of all custom workouts on the phone app if they can't be run on the watch!?), I'm super glad that this feature they've announced at the release of Pixel Watch 5 is now being rolled out also to Pixel Watch 3 and 4!

With the Wear OS 7.1 update, the Pixel Watch 3 and newer will summarize “extensive” notification clusters and multi-message chats into overviews. This requires a paired Pixel 9 (excluding the A-Series) or newer.

Like on phones and Googlebooks, Create My Widget lets you create custom displays of information on the Pixel Watch 4 and newer.

Recent findings suggest that manual Call Screen is becoming Gemini Call Screen on the Pixel Watch 5. This “proactive, agentic feature” will filter incoming calls on demand and generate key details in US English.

The final feature lets your nearby phone unlock the Pixel Watch instead of having to manually enter the PIN or pattern on a small screen. After unlocking your phone, a prompt (“Unlocking your watch”) appears at the top of the screen with a button to “Cancel.” Your watch must be on your wrist to unlock. This will be available on the Pixel Watch 3 and newer, with UWB playing a role in the process.

Seismic appears to set the tone for this week's events in the hardware industry, and we've covered the biggest beats, including deeper dives on hardware and AI topics over on Tom's Hardware Premium. Stories this week are colored by the fact that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has stepped away from his post as CEO. The ramifications are wide and far-reaching, as the company transformed from a gaming GPU manufacturer to an AI business over the past five years.

First up, it's not only hyperscalers and neoclouds that have their eyes on AI. An increasingly popular segment among enthusiasts is PCs dedicated to running local AI models. With so many choices on the market presently, from the recently released RTX Spark to AMD's Strix Halo platform, we take a look at two unlikely contenders that are now going head-to-head: Nvidia's DGX Spark and Apple's Mac Studio. We ran a suite of real-world and synthetic benchmarks across both devices and tested large models on both machines. With prices at eye-watering levels, it's more crucial than ever that you make the correct choice for your intended workloads.

DRAM capacity constraints have been an industry-wide sticking point as the AI buildout accelerates demand for dies. With costs spiraling across both client and enterprise hardware, AMD has shared further detail about MEXT, a predictive memory engine which aims to offer 99% of a server's performance while running on half the DRAM. Powered by a transformer model and clever use of flash storage, AMD is already running 145 servers with the system in place, with a view to expand that figure to 2,000 next year.

According to recent reports, next, we sat down with Cognichip's Chief Product Officer in an extensive interview to explore how the company is rolling out AI-powered chip design tools. Back in September, the company revealed a suite of proprietary AI models, named Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), which are specifically developed for semiconductor engineering. While the tools have yet to be used in a shipping product, it could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks.

The Jensen Huang scandal deepens, as the now-former Nvidia CEO has become embroiled in a series of alleged extramarital affairs and has since resigned from Nvidia. While much of the past week's stories have centered on his relationship with alleged Chinese Spy Alice Huang, we explored the former CEO's unlikely relationship with Kang Wei, Ms. Huang's husband, who recently landed in hot water with China's Securities Regulatory Commission.

Nvidia-based compute remains difficult to find in China, especially as AI labs line up to order racks and newer cards like the RTX 5500 Pro, with over 6 million units reportedly ordered for the export-compliant GB202-based AI accelerator. But the Chinese AI labs that are chasing after Nvidia's tech may still have to pay a premium and ensure that they're running enough homegrown silicon to not fall afoul of Beijing's rules. We explore how some companies have now moved to renting compute in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore in an attempt to get around export controls.

Google's one of the biggest competitors to Nvidia, especially in the AI domain. The company's 8th-gen TPU lineup has now expanded even further, with two upcoming chips designed for long-context agentic AI and security. These two new chips, TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, signal a further diversification across Google's eighth-generation TPU stack. While TPU 8i Max doubles the specs of the original TPU 8i, TPU 8tx makes a more interesting change to AMD's EPYC to serve its use in specialized security workloads.

For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

In a recent development, this article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

Sources indicate that we reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

Sources indicate that AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

In a recent development, vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

It has been revealed that kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

It has been revealed that hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects quickly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

In a recent development, “Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

Recent findings suggest that it depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

It has been revealed that treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”.

Recent findings suggest that scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

According to recent reports, developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

In a recent development, the script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below reveals the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Industry observers note that most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Industry observers note that usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Industry observers note that thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

In a recent development, for short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

Industry observers note that it depends on the tool and plan. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

Recent findings suggest that AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two months since releasing our first batch of Holo2 models, H Company is back with our largest UI localization model yet: Holo2-235B-A22B Preview. This model achieves a newly introduced State-of-the-Art (SOTA) record of 78.5% on Screenspot-Pro and 79.0% on OSWorld G.

Available on Hugging Face, Holo2-235B-A22B Preview is a research release focused on UI element localization.

It has been revealed that high-resolution 4K interfaces are challenging for localization models. Small UI elements can be difficult to pinpoint on a large display. With agentic localization, however, Holo2 can iteratively refine its predictions, improving accuracy with each step and unlocking 10-20% relative gains across all Holo2 model sizes.

Holo2-235B-A22B's Performance on ScreenSpot-Pro.

According to recent reports, holo2-235B-A22B Preview reaches 70.6% accuracy on ScreenSpot-Pro in a single step. In agent mode, it achieves 78.5% within 3 steps, setting a new state-of-the-art on the most challenging GUI grounding benchmark.

It has been revealed that training Holo2 models at scale requires coordinating workloads across multiple cloud providers. H Organization uses SkyPilot as a unified interface for launching training jobs on our clusters with Kubernetes (k8s). By abstracting away infrastructure complexity, SkyPilot lets researchers focus on model development instead of managing k8s manifests or maintaining separate deployment scripts.

What is the FAA’s SMART AI system? Officials are denying a link to the nationwide ground stop

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence firm behind the technology.But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.
  • The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology.But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems.
  • It has been revealed that the SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence firm behind the technology.But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems. Officials say no connection to ground stop The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated Friday there’s no indication the communications challenges that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday.The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails.“Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.”SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so. What is the SMART system? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories.The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise.The FAA claims that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations.So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop.According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals.SMART is also supposed to help with weather-related issues faster.Currently, the FAA blocks off portions of airspace affected by weather as “large, rectangular boxes,” according to the fact sheet, which doesn’t reflect how weather actually looks, with quick-moving thunderstorms and storm systems that are “often irregular in shape, with narrow gaps or corridors that aircraft could safely fly through.”To help with this, SMART gives the FAA and airspace operators a “clearer picture of how weather will affect air traffic over time,” allowing air traffic controllers to plan around storms and use available airspace instead of unnecessarily shutting down large areas.No other country has a working AI air traffic tool like the SMART system, according to Michael McCormick, a former FAA airspace manager and an associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority, has a system in testing and several manufacturers are prototyping similar tools. Concerns around relying on AI While government officials and ASI, the company behind SMART, have stressed that its AI system is designed to assist humans and not run flight control, its deployment has raised concerns about relying on artificial intelligence when human lives are at stake, given that even the most advanced models are prone to hallucinations — when models fabricate false information and present it as fact.Mike O’Donnell, a former top FAA official who worked for the agency for 17 years and now does aviation safety consulting work, said the agency “has got to make sure that this is just a tool in the toolbox and not the actual machine that’s doing the work.”The FAA, he said, “cannot afford to be wrong on this.”“It’s good to use it with the proper guardrails and backstops to ensure that they’re not giving wrong information to controllers based on what (AI) has come up with,” O’Donnell said. “There’s got to be a way to verify and validate what it’s doing to make sure that it’s not the wrong information.”He cautioned against putting too much trust in AI “until we know for sure that it’s proven itself time and time again. And that’s going to take a while.”The AI system’s launch comes amid a longstanding shortage of air traffic controllers around the country. The National Air Traffic Controllers Association has been raising concerns about this for more than a decade, telling Congress in 2015 that the shortage was at a crisis level. It said then that the FAA had missed its hiring targets for five years in a row. The union represents about 14,000 controllers, roughly 3,000 of them trainees. That said, experts say no AI system can replace the human air traffic controllers who spend years training for this highly demanding and stressful job.In an October interview with NPR, ASI co-founder and CEO Phillip Buckendorf said the SMART tool is designed for traffic managers who manage the entire U.S. airspace.“The AI does the math, the AI does the computation,” Buckendorf told NPR, but it’s ultimately up to the human operator whether to take the system’s recommendation. “They make the decision, they are the decider, they are the judge.” —Barbara Ortutay and Josh Funk, Associated Press.

#11292. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • Sources indicate that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a latest form of computer memory.

Sources indicate that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

In a recent development, the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an crucial role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

In a recent development, chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Industry observers note that quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

It has been revealed that one of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

It has been revealed that in the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

In a recent development, many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Fresh Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

It has been revealed that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

According to recent reports, to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

According to recent reports, "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the fresh architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

In a recent development, one of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

Industry observers note that however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

It has been revealed that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Recent findings suggest that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising fresh route toward making those machines a reality.

Community Evals: Because we're done trusting black-box leaderboards over the community

📅 04 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, TL;DR: Benchmark datasets on Hugging Face can now host leaderboards.
  • Let's be real about where we are with evals in 2026.
  • Furthermore, there is another gap within reported benchmark scores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, TL;DR: Benchmark datasets on Hugging Face can now host leaderboards. Models store their own eval scores. Everything links together. The community can submit results via PR. Verified badges prove that the results can be reproduced.

Let's be real about where we are with evals in 2026. MMLU is saturated above 91%. GSM8K hit 94%+. HumanEval is conquered. Yet some models that ace benchmarks still can't reliably browse the web, write production code, or handle multi-step tasks without hallucinating, based on usage reports. There is a clear gap between benchmark scores and real-world performance.

Furthermore, there is another gap within reported benchmark scores. Multiple sources report different results. From Model Cards, to papers, to evaluation platforms, there is no alignment in reported scores. The result is that the community lacks a single source of truth.

Decentralized and transparent evaluation reporting.

In a recent development, we are going to take evaluations on the Hugging Face Hub in a newly introduced direction by decentralizing reporting and allowing the entire community to openly report scores for benchmarks. At first, we will start with a shortlist of 4 benchmarks and over time we’ll expand to the most relevant benchmarks.

For Benchmarks: Dataset repos can now register as benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE are already live). They automatically aggregate reported results from across the Hub and display leaderboards in the dataset card. The benchmark defines the eval spec via eval.yaml, based on the Inspect AI format, so anyone can reproduce it. The reported results need to align with the task definition.

According to recent reports, for Models: Eval scores live in .eval_results/*.yaml in the model repo. They appear on the model card and are fed into benchmark datasets. Both the model author’s results and open pull requests for results will be aggregated. Model authors will be able to close score PR and hide results.

Industry observers note that for the Community: Any user can submit evaluation results for any model via a PR. Results get shown as "community", without waiting for model authors to merge or close. The community can link to sources like a paper, Model Card, third-party evaluation platform, or inspect eval logs. The community can discuss scores like any PR. Since the Hub is Git based, there is a history of when evals were added, when changes were made, etc. The sources look like below.

To learn more about evaluation results, check out the docs.

It has been revealed that decentralizing evaluation will expose scores that already exist across the community in sources like model cards and papers. By exposing these scores, the community can build on top of them to aggregate, track, and understand scores across the field. Also, all scores will be exposed via Hub APIs, making it easy to aggregate and build curated leaderboards, dashboards, etc.

Community evals do not replace benchmarks so leaderboards and closed evals with published results are still crucial. However, we believe it's vital to contribute to the field with open eval results based on reproducible eval specs.

In a recent development, this won't solve benchmark saturation or close the benchmark-reality gap. Nor will it stop training on test sets. But it makes the game visible by exposing what is evaluated, how, when, and by whom.

It has been revealed that mostly, we hope to make the Hub an active place to build and share reproducible benchmarks. Particularly focusing on new tasks and domains that challenge SOTA models more.

Read the docs: To learn more about evaluation results, check out the docs.

Add eval results: Publish the evals you conducted as YAML files in .eval_results/ on any model repo.

Check out the scores on the benchmark dataset.

Register a upcoming benchmark: Add eval.yaml to your dataset repo and contact us to be included in the shortlist.

Recent findings suggest that the feature is in beta. We're building in the open. Feedback welcome.

Great initiative, aggregating multiple signals is the way to go!

Although such a measure has not solved the problems encountered in the current evaluation, at least it is indeed a very good measure in terms of decentralization and mobilizing the power of the community for co-construction.

Will there be the integration with existing huggingface lighteval?

It has been revealed that hi @naufalso ! Lighteval now suport inspect-ai as a backend, so everything supported by inspect is integrrated in lighteval 🔥.

It has been revealed that this is a very important and timely initiative. It’s easy to get lost in the sea of leaderboards, each with its own format and reporting style. The Inspect AI log format brings much‑needed standardization, and having Hugging Face host evaluation logs is a real game changer. One reason many valuable benchmarks fade away is that original contributors often lack the resources to continuously maintain leaderboards. The Community Evals initiative has tremendous potential to address this gap, and I truly appreciate the effort behind it.

We’re hoping to include our planning benchmark, ACPBench, as part of this ecosystem—it's fully compatible with Inspect AI, the evaluation scripts are available on our GitHub.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging.
  • The Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller.
  • Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging. That remarked, the Samsung 990 SSD is currently available at a discounted price of $189.99, against its original list price of $229.99 on Amazon. Although the $40 saving might not seem that impressive, deals on high-performance internal SSDs are becoming harder to come by amid the ongoing NAND and DRAM crisis. If you've been holding off on a storage upgrade, this could be a good opportunity to pick up a reliable, high-speed SSD.

The Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller. It was introduced earlier this year with MSRPs of $269.99 for the 1TB model and $529.99 for the 2TB model. The 1TB model offers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and 6,450 MB/s, making it an excellent option for everyday computing, gaming, and handling large files. Samsung rates the drive for up to 400TB of written data, although it offers just three years of warranty. It features a single-sided M.2 2280 design, which should make it compatible with a wide range of desktop motherboards, laptops, and even mini-PCs.

Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications.

In our testing of the 2TB variant, we found that the Samsung 990 delivers reasonably good all-around performance, particularly for gaming and everyday applications. It offered similar performance to the Samsung 990 EVO Plus in some tests. However, it fell behind competing drives such as the Crucial P310 and WD Blue SN5100 in others, particularly during file transfers. One of its biggest advantages is its large write cache, which allows it to maintain speeds of nearly 6,100 MB/s for more than 57 seconds before performance drops once the cache is exhausted. Its power efficiency may not be the best, but overall it is a competent budget PCIe 4.0 SSD.

For anyone upgrading from an older SATA SSD or a traditional hard drive, the Samsung 990 should offer a noticeable improvement in boot times, application loading, and overall system responsiveness. At its current price of $189.99, it is also a suitable option for expanding game storage without spending a fortune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for months, Democrats on the campaign trail hammered President Donald Trump’s unpopular tariffs, arguing that the taxes on imports drive up prices for American families already frustrated by the high cost of living.James Talarico, a Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, blamed Trump’s tariff on Mexican tomatoes for pushing up the price of a popular appetizer: “Chips and salsa,” he mentioned, “are sacred in Texas.”Targeting tariffs proved to be a winning message nationwide, contributing to the Democrats’ stunning gains in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. And in Texas? Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1988.“Americans don’t like tariffs,” said Scott Lincicome at the Cato Institute’s Center for Trade Policy Studies. “They connect them to the cost of living.”But when the Democrats take full control of Congress, they are likely to find that reversing Trump’s tariffs won’t be easy.The president will still have power to veto any legislation that repeals his import taxes or reins in his legal authority to impose them. And it’s unclear — probably doubtful — that enough Republicans would defy Trump and join Democrats in overriding his veto.Moreover, Democrats themselves are divided over trade policy. Some want to move back toward low-tariff trade policies that Trump demolished. Other Democrats want to see the United States continue using tariffs to fight other countries’ unfair trade policies and to sanction U.S. adversaries such as China.“There’s going to be a major debate over what should the Democrats’ tariff and trade policy be,” said Ryan Majerus, a former U.S. trade official during Trump’s first term and in the Biden administration. “It can’t just be: We don’t like what Trump’s doing.”Complicating matters is the fact that Trump’s tariffs are delivering significant amounts of revenue to the U.S. Treasury — nearly $370 billion in the last two budget years — at a time when the federal government is sitting on a staggering $40 trillion in debt.Democrats have “just been elected to come in and address concerns about affordability,” said Sally Laing, former chief trade counsel for the Senate Finance Committee and now a partner at the law firm Akin Gump. “It’s not as easy as people may think.” Trump’s tariffs pinched family budgets The U.S. Constitution gives the power to levy taxes — including tariffs — to Congress. But over the years, lawmakers have relinquished tariff-setting authority to the president.Trump swept into the vacuum. In his first term, he started a trade war with China and slapped taxes on steel and aluminum imports, saying they posed a threat to U.S. national security. All that was just a warmup for his second term. Although the Supreme Court rejected his most ambitious tariffs in February, he has still managed to build a high protective wall around the U.S. economy, sometimes relying on the expansive use of the legal authority Congress gave up.His use of tariffs also has proven erratic. Last year, for instance, he suddenly imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil because its government had prosecuted his friend, former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro. (The Supreme Court decision struck down that tariff, among others.)“Trade policy has sort of gone off the rails and has lost a strategic focus,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. “Now, we’re just using tariffs as a blunt cudgel instead of addressing real challenges.”Trump’s tariff frenzy has lifted the average U.S. tariff from around 2.5% when he returned to the White House in January 2025 to 11.2% now, according to Yale University’s Budget Lab. Tariffs are paid by importers in the United States. And they often pass along the burden to consumers via higher prices. Yale’s Budget Lab estimates that tariffs cost the average U.S. household about $900 a year.That burden comes at a time when elevated inflation is already pinching family budgets, even more so because Trump’s war with Iran has driven up gasoline prices.But the Republicans who controlled Congress did nothing to reassert their authority and push back against the president’s aggressive use of tariffs.Voters largely turned against Trump’s tariffs as they voted in the midterm elections. About two-thirds of U.S. voters said Trump’s tariffs had hurt the national economy or the economy in their area, while only about 2 in 10 said they’d helped, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. Voters who saw a negative impact from the tariffs overwhelmingly supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.Trump, meanwhile, remains committed to his protectionist agenda.“President Trump will never waver from putting Americans and America First, whether in trade negotiations or through an economic agenda of tax cuts and deregulation,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to questions from The Associated Press. Democrats must round up Republican votes to repeal Trump tariffs As they campaigned this fall, Democrats vowed to cancel some Trump tariffs and curb his legal authority to impose others. Their proposals include repealing the tariffs he levied in July on 60 U.S. trading partners for allegedly failing to do enough to crack down on trade in products made by forced labor. Another would require Congress to approve his tariffs.Turning their ideas into law will require overcoming a daunting obstacle: Trump’s veto power. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress. Even if Democrats win all the congressional races that are still undecided this year, they won’t have enough votes to override a Trump veto on their own. They will need Republican support.Can they get it? Their resounding midterms victory makes “a veto-proof vote more possible,” said Majerus, the former trade official and now a partner at King & Spalding. “Are Republicans willing to break with Trump? I’m still skeptical.”Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, sees one issue that could draw Republican support: ending the 50% tariffs that Trump imposed in August on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports.“That’s what we’re focused on, figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto,” said Wyden, who will be Senate Finance chair when the Democrats take over.The levies damaged relations with America’s neighbor and longstanding ally, drew retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa and hurt U.S. companies that depend on trade with Canada. “The Canadian tariffs, these tariffs on our allies, are wildly unpopular,” Laing said.Gellert Global Group, a food importer based in Elizabeth, New Jersey, is contending with Trump tariffs on Canadian cheese.“We are paying millions of dollars in additional costs and tariffs to maintain our distribution and have our products on the shelf,” said co-CEO Thomas Gellert. “We’re absorbing that today. It’s not sustainable for our business.” The company, represented by the libertarian advocacy group Liberty Justice Center, has sued the Trump administration over the Canada tariffs.Furor over the Canada tariffs contributed to longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ loss in Maine — even after Trump exempted products from the levies to aid her reelection bid.Republicans, Wyden said, face a choice: They can “help lower costs for American families or they can continue to defend Trump’s tariffs and make clear whose side they’re on.” AP Polling Editor Amelia Thomson-Deveaux contributed to this story. —Paul Wiseman, AP Economics Writer.

Industry News: Harvard study: Hyperscale data centers collectively power through more electricity than some U.S. states

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hyperscale data centers across the country are using as much electricity as entire states over the course of one year, according to a latest study.
  • Hyperscale data centers across the country are using as much electricity as entire states over the course of one year, according to a new study.
  • Industry observers note that and with the majority of that power coming from fossil fuels, those data centers produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2024 to 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hyperscale data centers across the country are using as much electricity as entire states over the course of one year, according to a latest study. And with the majority of that power coming from fossil fuels, those data centers produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2024 to 2025. That’s about three times higher than the emissions from the country’s hyperscale data centers in 2018. The research adds to a growing understanding of just how much the expansion of AI infrastructure and cloud computing has ramped up both electricity use and fossil fuel production across the country. Hyperscale data center secrecy Though the electricity use and pollution from data centers have come under public scrutiny recently, there has been little peer-reviewed science about data center emissions, says Francesca Dominici, an author of the study, published in Nature Sustainability, and director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative. To her knowledge, Dominici says, the only peer-reviewed study on greenhouse gas emissions and electricity consumption of hyperscaler data centers is from 2018, years before AI caused data center development to skyrocket. Dominici and her co-researchers spent two years investigating hyperscale data centers, which often aren’t publicly transparent about their emissions. The researchers used satellite imagery to compile a list of 403 hyperscale data centers, scraped the web for information filed in permits, used remote sensing, and relied on Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) data to calculate emissions based on the mix of power plants around the data centers. That effort “tells you about the fact that there is a lot of secrecy about these facilities,” Dominici notes. “Why can’t we just have a database which would tell us where are the facilities, how substantial they are, what’s the total capacity?” An underestimate on electricity use The study found that the country’s hyperscale data centers together used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity, in just one year. One terawatt hour can power approximately 90,000 homes. That means the hyperscale data center fleet uses as much or more electricity than entire states. Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee each use about 100 terawatt-hours of electricity a year. Some states use far less, like South Carolina (around 84 Twh), Oregon (60 Twh), and Maine (11 Twh). (States like Texas, California, and Florida use much more electricity; 475, 251, and 248 TWh respectively.) Those figures surprised Dominici. “It’s something so much bigger that I was actually not even expecting myself,” she says. And they’re also likely an underestimate, she adds. The paper focused on electricity use from 2024 to 2025, already making the data a year old. “So much more construction and development of hyperscaler data centers has been happening just in the last year,” she says. Data centers use dirty grids To supply all that electricity, these hyperscale data centers are relying mostly on fossil fuels, which make up about 54% of the power mix. That includes natural gas (38%) and coal (15%). About a quarter of this electricity also came from grid regions that are dirtier than average, researchers say, where coal-fired power plants dominate. The grids on which these data centers rely “really matter” to their overall impact, Dominici says. The research also makes clear, she adds, that “there has been no attention on renewable sources,” Dominici says. Though wind and solar are the cheapest power sources to build, they still don’t offer the same stability without battery storage. Fossil fuels are still the easiest way to get quick, constant, high power. Alongside the paper, the researchers are also publishing a website, neverjustabuilding.org, that illustrates the findings. Through that website, the researchers hope to reach those involved in some way in data center development, from the communities where data centers are being built to policymakers to utilities to developers themselves. [Screenshot: neverjustabuilding.org] This study is just the first step in a series of research efforts to better understand the AI data center boom and its impacts, including not only emissions and energy use but noise, water consumption, and the health impacts of that pollution. (The website allows people to sign up for updates on forthcoming research.) “This gives us now a framework . . . to start not only tracking,” Dominici says, “but also to really start identifying what we can do and where we should build and how to build, so [data centers] will have less of an impact.”.

Update 11/11: Right on schedule, Google has opened up Pixel Tag sales through the Google Store and Amazon.

Announced in August, the Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker directly from Google, and it’s been worth the wait. In our initial review earlier today, we found it to be a solid option with polish not found on third-party alternatives. It doesn’t magically make Find Hub a perfect tracking network, but it’s as good as it gets, at least based on our brief experience so far.

But the Pixel Tag isn’t available to buy just yet.

I think (at least for me) part of the confusion is from Damien's review video that is/was featured on the site... He notes the Pixel Tag is available to be purchased right now within the first few seconds of the video. And mentioned it again that you can buy them today later on.

Rather, the official Pixel Tag release date is November 11. As it stands today, the Google Store is not accepting orders, nor are any third-party retailers that you may have seen linked in posts around Pixel Tag availability today. Pricing is still set for $29.99 for a 1-pack and $99.99 for a 4-pack.

Google explicitly noted in a blog post just this morning:.

Pixel Tag offers peace of mind so you always know where your most key things are — and it’s available November 11.

We’re eager to get our hands on more of these trackers too, but we’ve got just a bit longer to wait.
