Industry observers note that syGra 2.0.0 introduces Studio, an interactive environment that turns synthetic data generation into a transparent, visual craft. Instead of juggling YAML files and terminals, you compose flows directly on the canvas, preview datasets before committing, tune prompts with inline variable hints, and watch executions stream live—all from a single pane. Under the hood it’s the same platform, so everything you do visually generates the corresponding SyGra compatible graph config and task executor scripts.

Let’s walk through this experience step by step.

Industry observers note that open Studio, click Create Flow, and Start/End nodes appear automatically. Before adding anything else:.

Once validated, Studio keeps the configuration in sync and pipes those variables throughout the flow—no manual wiring or guesswork.

Drag the blocks you need from the palette. For a story-generation pipeline:.

Studio’s detail panel keeps everything in context—model parameters, prompt editor, tool configuration, pre/post-process code, and even multi-LLM settings if you want parallel generations. Typing { inside a prompt surfaces every available state variable instantly.

According to recent reports, open the Code Panel to inspect the exact YAML/JSON Studio is generating. This is the same artifact written to tasks/examples/, so what you see is what gets committed.

After the run, download outputs, compare against prior executions, get metadata of latency and usage details.

SyGra Studio can also execute existing workflow in the tasks. For example, in the tasks/examples/glaive_code_assistant/ workflow — it ingests the glaiveai/glaive-code-assistant-v2 dataset, drafts answers, critiques them, and loops until the critique returns “NO MORE FEEDBACK.”.

It has been revealed that syGra Studio turns synthetic data workflows into a visual, user friendly experience. Configure once, build with confidence, run with full observability, generate the data without ever leaving the canvas.

Sources indicate that syGra Studio looks like a powerful platform for synthetic data generation workflows! For teams working with complex data pipelines like this, clear system documentation is essential. I've been using InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) to document our ML infrastructure—you describe your system architecture in plain English and it generates diagrams that you can refine conversationally. It's been really helpful for onboarding new team members and creating design docs that actually stay current with our evolving architecture.

SyGra Studio is a legit unlock: visual graph workflows that remove the pain of hand-editing YAML. Good work!

#11283. Four ways work was better in the ’90s

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2259 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Four ways work was better in the ’90s

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the fundamentals of work remain remarkably stable over time.
  • According to recent reports, the fundamentals of work remain remarkably stable over time.
  • But the specific cultural forces shaping what we do and how we do it can change dramatically, even within a few decades.Take the 1990s, which many living humans today would not have experienced because they were too young.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the fundamentals of work remain remarkably stable over time. For both our hunter-gatherer ancestors and modern chief AI ethicists, work was, and still is, a critical way to translate skill, effort, and time into food and safety—and being good at it enhances status as well as lubricating our self-esteem. But the specific cultural forces shaping what we do and how we do it can change dramatically, even within a few decades.Take the 1990s, which many living humans today would not have experienced because they were too young. In the scheme of things, three decades isn’t that much time. Yet the differences between then and now are almost comically dramatic. In the ‘90s, work was dominated by fax machines, pagers, bulky early mobile phones, and painfully slow dial-up internet connections that occupied the telephone line. Email was only emerging, to the point that your exchanges were largely limited to other early adopters, and the content of messages was often less interesting than the process of exchanging electronic mail itself. Being online was something you actively did, rather than a permanent state of existence, and work took place almost entirely at work, with the office encapsulating our professional selves and much of life unfolding outside it. Leaving the office generally meant leaving work behind, and being unreachable was the norm rather than a sign of negligence, indulgence, or power. Technology was an add-on—a secondary part of work rather than something we ought to supervise by bot-sitting, being a meat proxy, or calling ourselves the “human in the loop.” Since there were few apps or websites through which our personal lives could infiltrate working hours, digital distractions and multitasking were relatively rare: no Amazon shopping, Expedia travel planning, LinkedIn humblebragging, or keeping up with what our neighbor’s cat had for breakfast on Facebook or Instagram. So, was all of that better or worse? Here are four ways in which it was arguably the former—and four in which it was perhaps the latter. Four things that were arguably better about work in the 1990s 1. More genuine human connection. Work was a fundamentally more social, in-person experience, with more face-to-face interactions, spontaneous conversations, and opportunities to build relationships beyond scheduled meetings. We lacked digital personas and our reputations were the result of what we actually do in the physical world. 2. Greater focus and fewer distractions. With fewer digital interruptions and less pressure to respond instantly, people had more opportunities for sustained attention, deep work, and uninterrupted concentration. Or at least, our distractions were purely human—which meant that you could actually withdraw from others by staring at your computer (as opposed to the reverse). 3. More independent thinking and intellectual effort. Knowledge workers had to rely more heavily on their own memory, reasoning, creativity, and problem-solving skills, rather than outsourcing cognitive tasks to algorithms or AI. General knowledge, as demonstrated by the art of storytelling and argumentation, as well as engaging others in deep thinking and logical reasoning, all occupied a more central role in our daily working days than they do today. 4. Greater psychological separation between work and life. Work had clearer temporal and physical boundaries, and employees were less likely to feel permanently connected, constantly monitored, or threatened by technologies capable of making their skills obsolete. There were few discussions about “bringing your whole self to work” and employers didn’t need to monitor our social media footprint to alleviate any concerns about reputation management or brand compromising. Oh, and work did not occupy the central part of our identity, unless you were a workaholic: someone who resembles the average worker today in the sense of never disconnecting and always thinking about work and their professional self. Four things that were arguably worse about work in the 1990s 1. Less flexibility and autonomy. Work was tied to specific locations and fixed schedules, with little opportunity for remote or hybrid working, even when physical presence added little value. This may sound great today to people who miss or like structure and demarcation, but there is a reason why online and hybrid work have become so popular, namely that people enjoy freedom and flexibility—and especially their employers’ trust—vis-à-vis how their work is done. 2. More rigid hierarchies and organizational bureaucracy. Authority was more concentrated, communication more top-down, and employees generally had less freedom to challenge decisions or influence how work was organized. Organizational designs are more fluid, agile, and networked, which has persuaded employers to shift beyond formal org charts and try to evaluate the value each individual brings to their teams and organizations. In essence, this is good news for those who work hard and have talent, and bad news for those who simply pretend to work. 3. Less access to information and expertise. Knowledge was harder to find, slower to circulate, and more dependent on formal education, organizational status, and proximity to influential people. In theory, any novice could produce much more proficient, competent, and high-quality output in any area of the knowledge economy—which of course doesn’t guarantee they will!—because there is no longer any distance or separation between any question and any answer. And the ability to learn and acquire a decent level of expertise in any topic has increased dramatically with AI. 4. Fewer opportunities for inclusion and global collaboration. Geographic barriers, traditional career paths, and less inclusive workplace norms limited opportunities for women, minorities, people with disabilities, and talent outside major economic centers. This means opportunities to thrive and succeed because of your social capital (a euphemism for privilege or “who you know”) were far more common than today. In essence, work has been evolving towards a more meritocratic and talent-centric model, though there’s still a great deal of progress to make. Does it matter? In short, there is an interesting paradox in that work in the 1990s offered less freedom over where and when we worked, but arguably more freedom from work when we weren’t working. And while today’s technologies have liberated us from many tedious tasks, they have also made it harder to escape work, focus on it, or feel valued, not least since our professional identity is being rewritten by AI’s impact on our jobs, roles, and skills, and the impact of that is yet to be determined. Importantly, since employee engagement levels tend to fluctuate very little across the years, it is safe to conclude that people were no more or less happy then than they are today. Which points to the idea that any objective changes or improvements in working conditions and habits are promptly absorbed by our expectations. We adjust very quickly to normalizing changes, which leaves roughly the same proportion of people happy, indifferent, and miserable at work.Maybe the more work changes, the more it remains the same.

According to recent reports, the fundamentals of work remain remarkably stable over time. For both our hunter-gatherer ancestors and modern chief AI ethicists, work was, and still is, a critical way to translate skill, effort, and time into food and safety—and being good at it enhances status as well as lubricating our self-esteem.

But the specific cultural forces shaping what we do and how we do it can change dramatically, even within a few decades.Take the 1990s, which many living humans today would not have experienced because they were too young. In the scheme of things, three decades isn’t that much time. Yet the differences between then and now are almost comically dramatic.

Recent findings suggest that in the ‘90s, work was dominated by fax machines, pagers, bulky early mobile phones, and painfully slow dial-up internet connections that occupied the telephone line. Email was only emerging, to the point that your exchanges were largely limited to other early adopters, and the content of messages was often less interesting than the process of exchanging electronic mail itself.

According to recent reports, being online was something you actively did, rather than a permanent state of existence, and work took place almost entirely at work, with the office encapsulating our professional selves and much of life unfolding outside it. Leaving the office generally meant leaving work behind, and being unreachable was the norm rather than a sign of negligence, indulgence, or power.

Technology was an add-on—a secondary part of work rather than something we ought to supervise by bot-sitting, being a meat proxy, or calling ourselves the “human in the loop.” Since there were few apps or websites through which our personal lives could infiltrate working hours, digital distractions and multitasking were relatively rare: no Amazon shopping, Expedia travel planning, LinkedIn humblebragging, or keeping up with what our neighbor’s cat had for breakfast on Facebook or Instagram.

In a recent development, so, was all of that better or worse? Here are four ways in which it was arguably the former—and four in which it was perhaps the latter.

1. More genuine human connection. Work was a fundamentally more social, in-person experience, with more face-to-face interactions, spontaneous conversations, and opportunities to build relationships beyond scheduled meetings. We lacked digital personas and our reputations were the result of what we actually do in the physical world.

2. Greater focus and fewer distractions. With fewer digital interruptions and less pressure to respond instantly, people had more opportunities for sustained attention, deep work, and uninterrupted concentration. Or at least, our distractions were purely human—which meant that you could actually withdraw from others by staring at your computer (as opposed to the reverse).

3. More independent thinking and intellectual effort. Knowledge workers had to rely more heavily on their own memory, reasoning, creativity, and problem-solving skills, rather than outsourcing cognitive tasks to algorithms or AI. General knowledge, as demonstrated by the art of storytelling and argumentation, as well as engaging others in deep thinking and logical reasoning, all occupied a more central role in our daily working days than they do today.

4. Greater psychological separation between work and life. Work had clearer temporal and physical boundaries, and employees were less likely to feel permanently connected, constantly monitored, or threatened by technologies capable of making their skills obsolete. There were few discussions about “bringing your whole self to work” and employers didn’t need to monitor our social media footprint to alleviate any concerns about reputation management or brand compromising. Oh, and work did not occupy the central part of our identity, unless you were a workaholic: someone who resembles the average worker today in the sense of never disconnecting and always thinking about work and their professional self.

In a recent development, 1. Less flexibility and autonomy. Work was tied to specific locations and fixed schedules, with little opportunity for remote or hybrid working, even when physical presence added little value. This may sound great today to people who miss or like structure and demarcation, but there is a reason why online and hybrid work have become so popular, namely that people enjoy freedom and flexibility—and especially their employers’ trust—vis-à-vis how their work is done.

2. More rigid hierarchies and organizational bureaucracy. Authority was more concentrated, communication more top-down, and employees generally had less freedom to challenge decisions or influence how work was organized. Organizational designs are more fluid, agile, and networked, which has persuaded employers to shift beyond formal org charts and try to evaluate the value each individual brings to their teams and organizations. In essence, this is good news for those who work hard and have talent, and bad news for those who simply pretend to work.

3. Less access to information and expertise. Knowledge was harder to find, slower to circulate, and more dependent on formal education, organizational status, and proximity to influential people. In theory, any novice could produce much more proficient, competent, and high-quality output in any area of the knowledge economy—which of course doesn’t guarantee they will!—because there is no longer any distance or separation between any question and any answer. And the ability to learn and acquire a decent level of expertise in any topic has increased dramatically with AI.

It has been revealed that 4. Fewer opportunities for inclusion and global collaboration. Geographic barriers, traditional career paths, and less inclusive workplace norms limited opportunities for women, minorities, people with disabilities, and talent outside major economic centers. This means opportunities to thrive and succeed because of your social capital (a euphemism for privilege or “who you know”) were far more common than today. In essence, work has been evolving towards a more meritocratic and talent-centric model, though there’s still a great deal of progress to make.

In short, there is an interesting paradox in that work in the 1990s offered less freedom over where and when we worked, but arguably more freedom from work when we weren’t working. And while today’s technologies have liberated us from many tedious tasks, they have also made it harder to escape work, focus on it, or feel valued, not least since our professional identity is being rewritten by AI’s impact on our jobs, roles, and skills, and the impact of that is yet to be determined.

Importantly, since employee engagement levels tend to fluctuate very little across the years, it is safe to conclude that people were no more or less happy then than they are today. Which points to the idea that any objective changes or improvements in working conditions and habits are promptly absorbed by our expectations. We adjust very quickly to normalizing changes, which leaves roughly the same proportion of people happy, indifferent, and miserable at work.Maybe the more work changes, the more it remains the same.

Ahead of its IPO filing, Anthropic pledges to prioritize humanity’s benefit. Here’s how

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the latest pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it notes will protect the organization’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests.
  • It has been revealed that when Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the upcoming pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the organization’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests.
  • Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the latest pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it notes will protect the organization’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it’s benefiting society, experts say.Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, noted Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI. “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80% of their wealth. A pledge to do good is baked into corporate structure Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind.Elon Musk’s takeover of Twitter in 2021 highlights how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law.“Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.”Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company.There aren’t many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and OpenAI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the insurance company Lemonade and software developer Veeva Systems, which had a conventional corporate structure when it went public in 2013 and converted to a public benefit corporation in 2021.Anthropic’s idealistic ambitions for how it develops AI could run up against competitive pressure, such as from China, Kreps said.Anthropic and OpenAI’s models have gone from answering almost any question, even if it was dangerous, to becoming much more circumspect. But as they face more competition, including from open-source Chinese models that likely will tell you whatever you want, she said, “will they start to rethink some of those guardrails? And what happens then?”The setup generally is not preferred by shareholders because it gives more power to the company’s board than it does to shareholders.Whatever a company decides as its public benefit mission, it will likely be much more difficult to measure than profits. That’s particularly true for AI companies, whose leaders have exalted AI as the solution to many of humanity’s problems — from curing cancer to creating economic prosperity.“There are these echo chambers, the Silicon Valley bubble where they really think that what they’re doing is for the good of humanity,” Kreps said. And someone immersed in that environment, she added, might not even ask the right questions or understand how “public benefit” should be measured. A trust aims to hold Anthropic accountable A Long-Term Benefit Trust created by Anthropic is intended to operate as an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.Through a special Class T common stock, the trust “generally has the authority to elect and remove” Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of Anthropic’s board of directors, according to the IPO filing. The Class T common stock is a single share that allows the five trustees to vote as a unit. It has no economic rights — meaning they get to vote but they don’t see any financial benefit or losses from the share and can’t sell it.“The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately,” the filing said.Three of the company’s board directors are elected by the trust directly, and another three are elected by other shareholders, which include the company founders with a 50.1% voting majority. A seventh director, with a potentially tie-breaking vote, is nominated by the trust and the holders of the Class T shares, but cannot be appointed or removed without consent from the board’s nominating committee, which is expected to be controlled by the founders.Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on challenges such as AI safety and the company’s broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said.The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company,” he said. “If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.”As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly.The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic’s corporate structure, Gadinis said.“I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community,” he said. —Barbara Ortutay, AP Technology Writer.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Transformers.js v4: Now Available on NPM!

📅 09 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM!
  • Recent findings suggest that the biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a fresh WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++.
  • In addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this latest WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM! After a year of development (we started in March 2025 🤯), we're finally ready for you to use it.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a fresh WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++. We've worked closely with the ONNX Runtime team to thoroughly test this runtime across our ~200 supported model architectures, as well as many new v4-exclusive architectures.

In addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this latest WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications. That's right, you can now run WebGPU-accelerated models directly in Node, Bun, and Deno!

We've proven that it's possible to run state-of-the-art AI models 100% locally in the browser, and now we're focused on performance: making these models run as fast as possible, even in resource-constrained environments. This required completely rethinking our export strategy, especially for large language models. We achieve this by re-implementing latest models operation by operation, leveraging specialized ONNX Runtime Contrib Operators like com.microsoft.GroupQueryAttention, com.microsoft.MatMulNBits, or com.microsoft.QMoE to maximize performance.

For example, adopting the com.microsoft.MultiHeadAttention operator, we were able to achieve a ~4x speedup for BERT-based embedding models.

Developing a new major version gave us the opportunity to invest in the codebase and tackle long-overdue refactoring efforts.

Until now, the GitHub repository served as our npm package. This worked well as long as the repository only exposed a single library. However, looking to the future, we saw the need for various sub-packages that depend heavily on the Transformers.js core while addressing different use cases, like library-specific implementations, or smaller utilities that most customers don't need but are essential for some.

It has been revealed that that's why we converted the repository to a monorepo using pnpm workspaces. This allows us to ship smaller packages that depend on @huggingface/transformers without the overhead of maintaining separate repositories.

Another major refactoring effort targeted the ever-growing models.js file. In v3, all available models were defined in a single file spanning over 8,000 lines, becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. For v4, we split this into smaller, focused modules with a clear distinction between utility functions, core logic, and model-specific implementations. This upcoming structure improves readability and makes it much easier to add new models. Developers can now focus on model-specific logic without navigating through thousands of lines of unrelated code.

In v3, many Transformers.js example projects lived directly in the main repository. For v4, we've moved them to a dedicated repository, allowing us to maintain a cleaner codebase focused on the core library. This also makes it easier for customers to find and contribute to examples without sifting through the main repository.

In a recent development, we updated the Prettier configuration and reformatted all files in the repository. This ensures consistent formatting throughout the codebase, with all future PRs automatically following the same style. No more debates about formatting... Prettier handles it all, keeping the code clean and readable for everyone.

It has been revealed that thanks to our newly introduced export strategy and ONNX Runtime's expanding support for custom operators, we've been able to add many new models and architectures to Transformers.js v4. These include popular models like GPT-OSS, Chatterbox, GraniteMoeHybrid, LFM2-MoE, HunYuanDenseV1, Apertus, Olmo3, FalconH1, and Youtu-LLM. Many of these required us to implement support for advanced architectural patterns, including Mamba (state-space models), Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and Mixture of Experts (MoE). Perhaps most importantly, these models are all compatible with WebGPU, allowing people to run them directly in the browser or server-side JavaScript environments with hardware acceleration. We've released several Transformers.js v4 demos so far... and we'll continue to release more!

Sources indicate that we've migrated our build system from Webpack to esbuild, and the results have been incredible. Build times dropped from 2 seconds to just 200 milliseconds, a 10x improvement that makes development iteration significantly faster. Speed isn't the only benefit, though: bundle sizes also decreased by an average of 10% across all builds. The most notable improvement is in transformers.web.js, our default export, which is now 53% smaller, meaning faster downloads and quicker startup times for users.

Version 4 also adds new library features that make it easier to build robust, production-ready applications.

The newly introduced ModelRegistry API is designed for production workflows. It provides explicit visibility into pipeline assets before loading anything: list required files with get_pipeline_files, inspect per-file metadata with get_file_metadata (quite useful to calculate total download size), check cache status with is_pipeline_cached, and clear cached artifacts with clear_pipeline_cache. You can also query available precision types for a model with get_available_dtypes. Based on this new API, progress_callback now includes a progress_total event, making it easy to render end-to-end loading progress without manually aggregating per-file updates.

We also added newly introduced environment controls for model loading. env.useWasmCache enables caching of WASM runtime files (when cache storage is available), allowing applications to work fully offline after the initial load.

env.fetch lets you provide a custom fetch implementation for use cases such as authenticated model access, custom headers, and abortable requests.

Sources indicate that finally, logging is easier to manage in real-world deployments. ONNX Runtime WebGPU warnings are now hidden by default, and you can set explicit verbosity levels for both Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. This update, also driven by community feedback, keeps console output focused on actionable signals rather than low-value noise.

Recent findings suggest that A frequent request from users was to extract the tokenization logic into a separate library, and with v4, that's exactly what we've done. @huggingface/tokenizers is a complete refactor of the tokenization logic, designed to work seamlessly across browsers and server-side runtimes. At just 8.8kB (gzipped) with zero dependencies, it's incredibly lightweight while remaining fully type-safe.

This separation keeps the core of Transformers.js focused and lean while offering a versatile, standalone tool that any WebML project can use independently.

Industry observers note that we've made several quality-of-life improvements across the library. The type system has been enhanced with dynamic pipeline types that adapt based on inputs, providing better developer experience and type safety.

Additionally, we've added support for larger models exceeding 8B parameters. In our tests, we've been able to run GPT-OSS 20B (q4f16) at ~60 tokens per second on an M4 Pro Max.

We want to extend our heartfelt thanks to everyone who contributed to this major release, especially the ONNX Runtime team for their incredible work on the fresh WebGPU runtime and their support throughout development, as well as all external contributors and early testers.

#11280. I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1271 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

I’ve waited a long time for the Boox Picco, and I’m not disappointed

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, at around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get.
  • There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track.
  • But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, at around $100, the Boox Picco offers one of the most portable e-reader experiences you can get. You add MagSafe-like capability with a refreshingly simple UI, and you have a delightful way to read, literally wherever you are.

There is an argument to be made for every single shape and size e-readers come in, and they come in so many different sizes it’s hard to keep track. I love the idea of having a 10-inch display that I can skim, but even if it’s perfect for sitting at home and reading anything from novels to comics, I don’t think it provides a very good travel experience.

But even smaller devices like the Boox Palma make you choose between bringing a second device or sticking with your phone. Most often, the phone wins out – especially when you have a flexible approach with a foldable like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using daily.

In a recent development, unlike the other phone-sized e-readers from Boox, the Picco stands at just 4.15 inches tall. The screen measures at just under that – 3.97 inches. It’s essentially the size of a MagSafe or Qi2 wallet – just small enough to fit on the back of your phone with the included magnetic case.

It’s thin, too. A 5.5mm side profile means it slips anywhere a minimal wallet would without concern. That goes for pockets just as well as crossbody bags; perfect for travel.

And that’s where I think I find so much more joy in using this over what would otherwise be considered a small e-reader, like the Palma. I don’t have a lot of excuses not to carry it around when I’m on the go. I’ll throw it in my Bellroy bag when I’m carrying what I’d considered my minimal EDC. It slides into any internal pocket, and it weighs next to nothing.

The back of the Boox Picco isn’t magnetic, but the included case is. If you want the thinnest possible footprint, forego the case. But adding it lets you do one of the coolest – and slightly copium-inducing – things with your phone: attach the e-ink device directly to your OLED-laden phone.

Industry observers note that it does not work well with an unconventional device like my Galaxy Z Fold 8, but if you have nearly any other device like the Pixel 11, you should get a rather perfect fit. The Picco squares up to the back of any slab phone with Qi2 magnets, whether internal or via a case.

But, why? Why slap another device and add weight/thickness to your phone when it’s perfectly capable of displaying e-books?

According to recent reports, because it’s cool! That’s the driving reason. You can make the argument that it doubles your phone’s usability or that it gives you an easy place to store the tiny e-reader. The truth is that it does add extra thickness to your phone, and using your phone with the Picco piggybacking along can be uncomfortable, since your fingers now rest on another display and not a case or phone backing.

You can get used to it, and, as unnecessary as it may seem, it’s a fun way to carry around a much more eye-friendly screen.

Recent findings suggest that the Picco diverts from other Boox devices in another way. It doesn’t run Android, which means you have no access to third-party apps like Google Play Books, Amazon Kindle, or any other store/library. Instead, the Picco uses a companion app to transfer EPUBs from your phone to the tiny e-reader.

I initially opposed this idea when I got a sneak peek during IFA in Berlin this year. But after using it for a few weeks, I’ll admit I’ve come around. But that all comes down to how you consume your media.

In a recent development, I try to source EPUBs no matter what device I use. On Android-powered e-readers, that means downloading Google Play Books and reading from there; I have my EPUBs uploaded to my own Google Play Books library, so they’re available universally.

Sources indicate that on the Picco, my approach hasn’t changed much. I take those same EPUBs I have in storage and transfer them from the companion app.

According to recent reports, I can understand how the lack of third-party libraries would make the Boox Picco moot. Still, I’ve been a proponent of buying digital books I can store in my own drives, so I can read them wherever, whether that’s the Google Play Books library or from a device like the Picco.

All of that is a roundabout way of saying the Picco, though it doesn’t let you use apps to read, makes it easy to get digital copies loaded and ready to flip through.

It has been revealed that it uses a handshake connection that requires you to open the companion app on your phone, hit connect, and do the same on the Picco. Once connected, transferring EPUB files is as easy as selecting them from your phone’s physical or cloud storage and queueing them up. The process takes seconds, and the only matter I’ve had was solved by a force stop and trying again.

Industry observers note that the homescreen is simply a carousel of your library, with a delightful little progress bar under each title as they’re sorted. You can access and manage the bookshelf from that page, as well as the minimal “apps” and settings. I appreciate the focus app and reading stats, but the countdown and to-do options require using the companion app. I don’t see the point of those.

It doesn’t even have a control panel. Swiping down from the top surfaces screen brightness and color controls. Even though this little guy is just over $100, it still has a front light controlled by a physical switch on the side. Compare that to e-readers at much higher price points without that game-changing feature.

It has been revealed that the buttons opposite don’t control volume. Instead, they’re there for page turning.

Recent findings suggest that it’s just simple and well-designed. Features are there to make reading a better experience, down to granular text controls for your digital books. It does exactly what it needs to do – nothing more, nothing less.

Sources indicate that as far as battery goes, it meets my expectations. It’s not massive, so the battery is small in comparison to a smartphone. It still holds its own easily, with an easy week of use if you’re reading for an hour or two a day. Beyond that, it takes little time to charge and does great on idle, which is perfect for such a passive device.

The Picco will hit home for you if you want an ultra-portable option for your e-books. The same goes for those who don’t mind the smaller screen and lack of Android or third-party app support.

I get genuine joy every time I pick it up to read where I left off, and I think that’s because it’s so simple and nothing about it feels bloated, even the companion app, which is also straight to the point.

It has been revealed that I think it’s been a while since a device has offered that experience for me. Adding the form factor, optional magnetic attachment for your phone, and price tag just gets me to that conclusion sooner.

The Boox Picco is the most adorable e-reader I’ve used, and it’s $109 on Amazon.

It has been revealed that not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and prepares, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

Industry observers note that openArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

Recent findings suggest that the direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

According to recent reports, pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid intends add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

Sources indicate that for developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free initiative includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid intends start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Pricing: Free initiative with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Recent findings suggest that murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

It has been revealed that murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

It has been revealed that speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

Sources indicate that the use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid looks are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

According to recent reports, pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:.

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

In a recent development, treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

It has been revealed that newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that states to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free plans or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free plan, which has no commercial licence.

Can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid prepares, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

What is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

It has been revealed that AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

The original Xbox was released 25 years ago today

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that microsoft’s first games console hit North America 25 years ago today.
  • The Xbox arrived on Nov 15, 2001, during the sixth generation of consoles, facing stiff opposition from the legendary Sony PlayStation 2, Nintendo GameCube, and Sega Dreamcast.
  • Recent findings suggest that it is interesting to weigh up the performance hardware that was a massive reason behind the OG Xbox’s success.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that microsoft’s first games console hit North America 25 years ago today. Effectively a PC in a box, the original Xbox was powered by an Intel Pentium III CPU and an Nvidia GPU inside a bulky black and green case. This first-gen device would sell 24 million units and be succeeded by the sleek PowerPC/ATI-powered Xbox 360 in late 2005.

The Xbox arrived on Nov 15, 2001, during the sixth generation of consoles, facing stiff opposition from the legendary Sony PlayStation 2, Nintendo GameCube, and Sega Dreamcast. However, it established a very respectable foothold in the console market thanks to its formidable hardware and a killer app in the shape of Halo: Combat Evolved. It would end up outselling Nintendo and Sega rivals, only living in the shadow of the PS2.

Recent findings suggest that it is interesting to weigh up the performance hardware that was a massive reason behind the OG Xbox’s success. Though the contemporary PC parts it used probably made it one of the biggest and ugliest consoles ever, powerful hardware is a great foundation for cutting-edge gaming experiences. The key components behind the Xbox were the Intel Pentium III 733 MHz CPU and an Nvidia NV2A 233 MHz GPU. Systems came with 64MB of DDR SDRAM and accessed games via optical media through its DVD drive. Perhaps most unusual for the time, the system included a built-in HDD (8GB), as well as offering 8MB memory cards for removable storage.

Another hardware advantage of the Xbox and key to connected gaming fun during the early broadband proliferation era was the inclusion of an Ethernet jack as standard. Xbox Live online gaming would launch in 2002. Microsoft used a heavily modified controller-friendly version of Windows 2000 for the system’s OS.

Recent findings suggest that setting the foundation for the next 25 years of Xbox, the original console was clearly a success. However, as the games industry prepares for a latest generation of hardware, Microsoft’s strategy looks less certain than ever before. Even more so than with Sony, it seems less clear where the Xbox business is headed.

In a recent development, microsoft couldn’t pass such an important anniversary without a celebratory promotion, and it looks like a very attractive one. If you are buying a new pre-built PC for gaming, you should keep an eye out for the 25-year Xbox bundle. This bestows new system purchasers with “25 fan-favorite Xbox games.” You’ll find the following games in your Microsoft Store Library, under the ‘Included with device’ tab on qualifying machines:.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition.

Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition.

Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition.

Rise of Nations: Extended Edition.

Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire.

Zoo Tycoon: Ultimate Animal Collection.

Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge.

In a recent development, those who aren’t getting a upcoming gaming PC can still harvest a few commemorative freebies from Microsoft. On the dedicated page about the 25th anniversary, I spied free wallpapers, free in-game anniversary items for various titles, and an Xbox account badge. Fans are asked to check back at the linked page for “updates, freebies, exclusive experiences and the latest news throughout the year.”.

Lastly, Microsoft is offering a limited-edition Xbox Series X25 ($899 at Best Buy) in translucent OG Green with 1TB SSD storage and a matching controller.

Family Dollar has to pay $40 million back to customers in an FTC lawsuit settlement: How to claim your payout

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 17 states that it charged customers more at the register than the prices shown on shelves, product tags, its website, and its mobile app.
  • Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 17 states that it charged customers more at the register than the prices shown on shelves, product tags, its website, and its mobile app.
  • According to the complaint, Family Dollar overcharged its customers “millions of dollars” since January 2023, including in low-income communities where residents had limited access to full-service grocery stores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 17 states that it charged customers more at the register than the prices shown on shelves, product tags, its website, and its mobile app. According to the complaint, Family Dollar overcharged its customers “millions of dollars” since January 2023, including in low-income communities where residents had limited access to full-service grocery stores. Family Dollar did not respond to Fast Manufacturer’s request for comment as of publication. Here’s what to know about the settlement and whether you qualify for a payout: When was the settlement revealed? The settlement was announced on November 12, the same day that the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia filed an order that requires Family Dollar to implement a pricing accuracy program that must be independently certified annually. While Family Dollar agreed to the settlement, it did not admit to or deny any of the allegations in the complaint, according to the order. “Today’s order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in the announcement. How much money will customers get? Of the $63 million, $40 million will be distributed as payments to customers, and $20 million will take the form of a discount program. The discount program would be a single event: a 15% reduction on most items for at least two consecutive days, excluding alcohol, tobacco and gift cards. Who is eligible for a payout? Shoppers who made at least one purchase at a Family Dollar store between January 1, 2023, and October 1, 2026, are eligible to qualify for Family Dollar’s payouts. How can I submit a claim? Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said an online claim portal will be posted on Family Dollar’s website within 14 days of the final court order. The order does not specify how much each customer would receive. Payments would then be issued on a rolling basis until the $40 million is spent. What kinds of items did Family Dollar allegedly overcharge for? The complaint alleges that customers have reported Family Dollar’s pricing inconsistencies for years. Common household supplies such as eggs, milk, diapers, cleaning products and toilet paper were named among the household items for which customers were overcharged. Family Dollar has also faced scrutiny in the past over its inaccurate pricing, according to the complaint. Over the last two years, Family Dollar reached settlements with three state attorneys general and consumer protection agencies, including a $400,000 settlement in Ohio in February 2024, a $113,960 settlement with Wisconsin in January 2025, and a $300,000 settlement with Arizona in May 2025. Family Dollar is not the only company accused of deceptive pricing practices. In a related complaint filed on October 26, the FTC and state partners sued Dollar General Corporation over similar pricing tactics that resulted in overcharging consumers. The litigation is still ongoing. Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

OpenEnv in Practice: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents in Real-World Environments

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.
  • In a recent development, openEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments.
  • In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

In a recent development, openEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

It has been revealed that openEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

It has been revealed that openEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

Recent findings suggest that the environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?".

Recent findings suggest that calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple people, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

To ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across customers and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

According to recent reports, below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

Below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

According to recent reports, evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

According to recent reports, multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

In a recent development, correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

Recent findings suggest that these challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

It has been revealed that for a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

It has been revealed that in practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring issues.

Below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

In a recent development, the agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

Industry observers note that we can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

We can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

We can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

Industry News: Stressful jobs do, in fact, pay more. But there’s a catch

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, do more stressful jobs come with a bigger paycheck?
  • Do more stressful jobs come with a bigger paycheck?
  • According to a recent study conducted by online resume building platform Resume Genius, the most stressful jobs pay an average of 62% more than the least stressful jobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, do more stressful jobs come with a bigger paycheck? It depends. According to a recent study conducted by online resume building platform Resume Genius, the most stressful jobs pay an average of 62% more than the least stressful jobs. And yet, not everyone is enjoying a high-pressure premium. Workers with a high school diploma or postsecondary certificate typically see a 24% pay premium for taking on a more stressful job; those with a Master’s earn 27% more in high-stress roles, while those with a doctoral or professional degree earn a whopping 78% more. Among bachelor’s degree holders, however, higher work stress doesn’t pay. In fact, bachelor’s degree holders in high-pressure roles earn 1% less on average than bachelor-holding colleagues in lower-pressure positions. “Not all forms of workplace stress are rewarded equally,” indicates Resume Genius career expert Nathan Soto. “The data we found suggests that a stress premium exists, but it’s concentrated in particular educational and occupational groups, rather than being a universal feature of the labor market.” The study is consistent with other research that suggests workers are less willing to take on more stressful jobs, even if they come with a higher salary. A survey of 14,000 workers by emotional insight platform Hint App, for example, found that 58% would reject a promotion that required them to be available after hours. Putting a price on workplace pressure Soto says Resume Genius developed a “Stress Index” to help quantify workplace pressure across 754 occupations. One-third of that 100-point scale is based on the role’s “Stress Tolerance” level, according to the U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational Information Network (or O*NET) database. The agency defines “Stress Tolerance” as “a tendency to cope and function effectively in stressful situations at work.” The remaining two-thirds were based on seven stressful job attributes: time pressure, workplace conflicts, dealing with unpleasant or angry people, the consequence of errors, responsibility for others’ health and safety, competition and long working hours. Stress Index scores were then compared against the latest pay data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. “Among six-figure occupations, workers in high-stress jobs were much more likely to deal with unpleasant or angry people, handle conflict regularly and face time pressure every day,” Soto says. “Responsibility for other people’s health and safety and the seriousness of potential mistakes were also major factors.” Soto explains that high-paying, highly stressful jobs that don’t require a bachelor’s degree often involve physical risk, demanding work conditions or significant responsibility. For example, electrical power-line installers earn an average of $95,320 and have a Stress Index level of 97. Detectives and criminal investigators, who also aren’t required to earn a bachelor’s, scored 100 on the stress index and earned an average of $93,790. High-paying jobs that require a professional or doctorate degree, meanwhile, often require specialized training or expertise, come with greater responsibility as well as higher stakes. For example, anesthesiologists scored 100 on the Stress Index and earned an average of $391,490 per year. But: “Jobs that require bachelor’s degrees follow a different pattern,” Soto says. “Many of them pay high salaries without necessarily rewarding additional workplace stress with higher pay.” More than half of the six-figure jobs included in the study scored above 67 on the Stress Index, but the researchers did identify 19 high-paying low-stress jobs. They include electronics engineer, software developer, statistician, data scientist, computer and information research scientist and actuary. A high tolerance for stress has a dollar value Many workers look to avoid stress, and are even willing to take a pay cut for it. But those who can take the heat can often earn more. According to a 2025 study conducted by researchers at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg in Germany, workers are willing to take a 9.6% wage cut to avoid frequent, tight deadlines, and earn about 6% less to avoid having to multitask often. “Avoiding pressure comes at a price. So you have to think whether you’re willing to pay that price,” explains economics professor Markus Nagler, who co-authored the study. Swapping a low-pressure job for a high-pressure job within the same occupation, according to the study, came with a 12% earnings premium on average, though half of that raise was due to an increase in working hours. The researchers, however, also found that those who didn’t mind certain stressful job aspects were more likely to find jobs that paid them for that sacrifice. For example, those who take on jobs with tight deadlines may be able to stomach the pressure more than the average worker. “The kind of people who select into these jobs and remain in these jobs typically are those who have the highest tolerance for these kinds of working conditions,” Nagler says. “The problem is that you choose a job, but you don’t get to choose specific aspects of the job.” Not everyone gets to choose a lower-stress job The research suggests that workers in higher-stress jobs tend to earn more. But other research finds that workers in low-wage jobs are more likely to face harsher working conditions. According to a 2023 study published in the American Economic Review, workers earning lower wages were less willing to give up part of their earnings to enjoy non-work amenities like schedule flexibility, more paid time off and less heavy lifting. The study also found that higher-wage workers are more likely to enjoy those additional perks than workers in lower-wage jobs. “The people that are getting paid more are also getting better working conditions,” explains one of the study’s co-authors and an associate professor at Penn Medicine, David Powell. “People who are compensated better want a combination of higher wages and better amenities, so when you look at disparities, and you include amenities, they typically widen.” That is not to say that high earners aren’t dealing with difficult working conditions. However, Powell’s research suggests those with higher earnings are in a better position to sacrifice some of their earnings for a lower-stress role. Those struggling to make ends meet, however, are typically less willing to forfeit some of their pay for better working conditions. As a result, lower earners tend to enjoy fewer of the amenities that make work less stressful, while higher earners can more easily swap a high-stress job for a more laid-back alternative, even if it pays less.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It looks like AMD is trying to get back into the good graces of gamers, with its CEO, Dr. Lisa Su, joining the grand opening of Micro Center Austin. The firm shared official photos of AMD’s chief executive cutting the ribbon to mark the store’s opening on its Instagram page, while a Redditor shared a short clip showing her making the rounds among the people waiting to get inside the shop and signing a Gigabyte Radeon RX 9070 XT GPU, one of the best gaming GPUs you can buy today.

AMD has been saying that it is a data-center-first company repeatedly since 2024. Dr. Su reiterated the stance in an interview earlier this month, at which point some in the press finally decided to notice. The reporting naturally enraged gamers who supported AMD and Nvidia for decades and are now feeling left behind as these companies pivoted towards more lucrative AI hardware. This has become apparent with the paper launches of Nvidia’s latest RTX 50-series chips in 2025 and the purported production cuts of powerful RTX 5080 and RTX 5090 GPUs, even as demand for Nvidia’s AI GPUs continues to rise.

A post shared by Micro Center (@microcenter).

However, it seems that this outrage has been drowned out by the unfolding scandal at Nvidia, which saw the dramatic fall from grace of the tech giant’s legendary founder. It’s unclear if this initiative to have the AMD chief at the Micro Center Austin’s grand opening has been in place for some time or if it was an attempt to smooth the ruffled feathers of the gaming community, but Austin is home to one of AMD's largest hubs, so it's likely an organic and planned event. But whatever the case, it was a treat to the people who were on the ground during the event — Micro Center remarked that AMD gave away 300 swag bags and had a couple of prizes for the people in the store.

The opening of Micro Center’s Austin brick-and-mortar store is actually a good sign for the people in the area, especially now that we’re at the age where almost everything can be bought online. While the AI shortage has made RAM, GPU, and many other things more expensive, physical retailers remain one of the best places where PC builders can find deals on parts and components. We even saw Walmart honor a $2,299 CyberPowerPC mistakenly displayed for $1,099 each, allowing a Redditor to secure two relatively powerful gaming PCs for more than half off.

Your marketing approval process is spending your budget
