📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Can we get one more person to weigh in?” If you work in marketing, you know where this can lead.
  • Industry observers note that if you work in marketing, you know where this can lead.
  • New copy, updated graphics, another round of approvals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Can we get one more person to weigh in?” If you work in marketing, you know where this can lead. The campaign is ready, the team has worked through the feedback, and the launch date is approaching. Then another reviewer joins the conversation and questions a decision everyone thought was already settled. Back it goes. Newly introduced copy, updated graphics, another round of approvals. Meanwhile, the next project is waiting. No one approved a bigger budget. But the team is spending more time on the same work. In June 2026 research from Bloomberg Media and Lippincott, nearly eight in 10 CMOs said bureaucracy frequently interferes with decision-making. Corporate leadership was the primary source of delays for major marketing initiatives. As leaders, we need to look at our part in that. We expect teams to deliver on time, but every additional review affects their ability to do it. “ONE MORE REVIEW” IS MORE WORK THAN IT SOUNDS Changing a headline might take a few minutes. Updating it across a landing page, emails, ads, and a sales deck takes longer. Someone also has to check those changes and send the updated materials back for approval. That rework has to fit somewhere, and it’s rarely planned for in the workback schedule. So it takes time from a campaign already in production. It forces the creative department to stay late (again), or pushes the deadline to next week. Your team feels overworked and stressed, so it may appear to be a resource problem. But the real problem is in the process. The solution is to take a hard look at your marketing workflow, both documented and unspoken. START WITH APPROVALS If you find your campaigns are consistently missing deadlines, look at how many review rounds you typically have, and how many stakeholders must sign off. Understand who is involved, why they are involved, and how you can make sure they’re providing that value at the right time. Is the CMO signing off on the campaign messaging before any creative is designed, or are they seeing the campaign messaging the night before launch? Is legal being asked to approve photos from the expensive product shoot without being asked to provide any legal guardrails in the brief? Carefully sequencing sign-offs based on dependencies, and allotting time in your workback schedule for their review, will ensure you’re setting your team up for success from day one. GIVE REVIEWERS CLEAR EXPECTATIONS Often, the root of friction is in how we request feedback. Send a draft with “Let me know your thoughts,” and you may get a rewrite when you just needed someone to check the facts. Be specific about each person’s role. Product experts review accuracy. Legal reviews claims. The marketing lead evaluates whether the message speaks to the audience and aligns with the campaign goal. Establish who makes the final call when those perspectives conflict. A project manager can gather comments and chase responses, but someone with decision-making authority needs to resolve any disagreement. Asking the team to satisfy incompatible feedback just sends it around again. RANK FEEDBACK BY ITS IMPACT There are good reasons to reopen approved work. A product feature changes, a claim turns out to be inaccurate, or legal identifies a concern. If someone wants a late change, bring the conversation back to the campaign’s goal. Will it help the audience understand the message or correct something important? If it doesn’t clear one of those hurdles, stick with the approved version. As a reviewer, before requesting a change, find out what that change will impact. That includes who must review it again and what will have to move or be sacrificed to accommodate it. You need to understand its impact on the schedule, the team capacity, and ultimately the budget. Make sure it’s worth the cost. As leaders, we need to trust our team to make the right decisions. But when there are too many decision-makers on a project, nothing gets resolved. Before asking your marketing team to move faster, look at how approvals are handled in your organization. Every review has a cost, and those review cycles may be eating up your budget. Lisa Larson-Kelley is president and CEO of Quantious.

Sources indicate that as leaders, we need to look at our part in that. We expect teams to deliver on time, but every additional review affects their ability to do it.

In a recent development, changing a headline might take a few minutes. Updating it across a landing page, emails, ads, and a sales deck takes longer. Someone also has to check those changes and send the updated materials back for approval.

That rework has to fit somewhere, and it’s rarely planned for in the workback schedule. So it takes time from a campaign already in production. It forces the creative department to stay late (again), or pushes the deadline to next week. Your team feels overworked and stressed, so it may appear to be a resource problem. But the real problem is in the process.

The solution is to take a hard look at your marketing workflow, both documented and unspoken.

If you find your campaigns are consistently missing deadlines, look at how many review rounds you typically have, and how many stakeholders must sign off. Understand who is involved, why they are involved, and how you can make sure they’re providing that value at the right time.

Is the CMO signing off on the campaign messaging before any creative is designed, or are they seeing the campaign messaging the night before launch? Is legal being asked to approve photos from the expensive product shoot without being asked to provide any legal guardrails in the brief?

Carefully sequencing sign-offs based on dependencies, and allotting time in your workback schedule for their review, will ensure you’re setting your team up for success from day one.

Often, the root of friction is in how we request feedback. Send a draft with “Let me know your thoughts,” and you may get a rewrite when you just needed someone to check the facts.

Be specific about each person’s role. Product experts review accuracy. Legal reviews claims. The marketing lead evaluates whether the message speaks to the audience and aligns with the campaign goal.

It has been revealed that establish who makes the final call when those perspectives conflict. A project manager can gather comments and chase responses, but someone with decision-making authority needs to resolve any disagreement. Asking the team to satisfy incompatible feedback just sends it around again.

Sources indicate that there are good reasons to reopen approved work. A product feature changes, a claim turns out to be inaccurate, or legal identifies a concern.

In a recent development, if someone wants a late change, bring the conversation back to the campaign’s goal. Will it help the audience understand the message or correct something key? If it doesn’t clear one of those hurdles, stick with the approved version.

Recent findings suggest that as a reviewer, before requesting a change, find out what that change will impact. That includes who must review it again and what will have to move or be sacrificed to accommodate it. You need to understand its impact on the schedule, the team capacity, and ultimately the budget. Make sure it’s worth the cost.

According to recent reports, as leaders, we need to trust our team to make the right decisions. But when there are too many decision-makers on a project, nothing gets resolved. Before asking your marketing team to move faster, look at how approvals are handled in your organization. Every review has a cost, and those review cycles may be eating up your budget.

Lisa Larson-Kelley is president and CEO of Quantious.

It has been revealed that writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

The Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

According to recent reports, speedup scales with sequence length: 1.58x at 128 tokens, 2.47x at 8192 tokens. For long-context inference, the custom kernel roughly halves RMSNorm latency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Sources indicate that every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site debuted. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot update itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

It has been revealed that freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

It has been revealed that A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination consumers might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

Sources indicate that the example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

According to recent reports, quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand plan. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

Industry observers note that what is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

According to recent reports, is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for users. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

How often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

According to recent reports, do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

How many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and owners engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

In a recent development, the sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even Realities is making its first big push into the enterprise business world with a new Enterprise SDK release.

Even Realities’ G2 glasses have been a hit for the company, making up 11% of the AR glasses market as of September. Now that consumers are clearly interested in what they can do, Even Realities is branching out to the business world with the release of the company’s first Enterprise SDK (software development kit).

It has been revealed that the SDK works well with Even Realities’ app-based software, which lets users browse a bespoke app store filled with games, utilities, and more, all of which are designed to be used on the Even Realities G2’s in-lens displays. In our Even Realities G2 review, reviewer Andrew Romero said the glasses are “for the tech minimalist who wants to stay connected to notifications, while keeping a healthy distance away.”.

In the business world, that actually makes a lot of sense. XR glasses and other types of smart glasses with displays are used in fields where you might need more information in front of you but can’t be on a device like a phone. Even Realities glasses are also extremely useful for keeping up with notifications when they come through, something that would be very handy on a job site.

“We built Even G2 to help people access useful information while staying present in their everyday lives, and we believe that principle matters just as much at work. With the Enterprise SDK, we’re giving companies the flexibility to build around the way their teams already work, rather than asking them to change their workflows to fit the technology,”– Will Wang, Founder and CEO of Even Realities.

The ‘recession indicators’ visible at your workplace

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, people all over the U.S.
  • In a recent development, people all over the U.S.
  • According to employment attorney Craig Levey, a partner at Bennett & Belfort, there are recession indicators at your workplace, too—you just have to take a look around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, people all over the U.S. have been sharing their “personal recession indicators” in recent months, from only being able to afford Goldfish crackers and water for lunch to filling up their cars with a few dollars’ worth of gas at a time. According to employment attorney Craig Levey, a partner at Bennett & Belfort, there are recession indicators at your workplace, too—you just have to take a look around. And they could be a sign that bigger cutbacks, or even layoffs, could be around the corner. Levey makes content on TikTok, where he tracks patterns in his comments and feed that highlight how people feel about the world of work. “Over the last few months, I noticed that a lot of companies were suffering financial complications. There was a downturn in their numbers,” he tells Fast Company. “People were trying to assess whether a recession was happening in the United States.” Levey posted a video about workplace recession indicators that employees should look out for, including companies slashing expenses on business trips, bonuses, holiday parties, and even office snacks. Companies often start with the little things when tightening their belts, he indicates, and these cuts could be an early signal that a business is preparing for tougher economic conditions. “Upper management and leadership, they probably get together and they say, ‘Okay, we need to cut costs. What can we do? Let’s cut the low-hanging fruit,’” he says. Cutting now to save later Companies do this, Levey says, because they’re looking six, 12, or even 18 months ahead, and taking preemptive steps to put themselves in a better position for the next fiscal year. These cuts may seem trivial to some. But for other employees, they can be incredibly notable. Levey says he regularly hears from people who have full-time jobs but have to live in their cars because they can no longer afford rent. “A lot of employees are really struggling because the day-to-day costs are so high that they can’t pay their bills,” Levey says. “If you’re somebody who can’t pay their rent, trying to figure out how you’re going to get your next meal, and you can go into your company’s kitchen and get a snack—that makes a substantial difference.” According to Chris Marvel Davis, cofounder of Pivot, a training and development provider that runs workshops on wellness, burnout, and leadership, snacks may be what people notice first. But there are other, less obvious signs that a company is becoming more cautious with its spending. Travel and conference requests getting denied or delayed may not be immediately apparent, he tells Fast Company. Other signs include open roles staying unfilled, job postings disappearing, backfills for departed employees being paused, and contractors being let go before full-time employees. “Small purchases need bigger approvals,” he adds. “When a $200 expense suddenly needs a director’s sign-off, someone in finance is watching cash closely.” Is it routine or a sign of something bigger? Companies make these kinds of cuts first because they’re easier to reverse, Davis says. On their own, they may simply suggest that leadership is being careful. “They buy leadership time to see how bad things might get without alarming employees or customers,” he says. “One sign by itself doesn’t tell you much, but several at once are worth taking seriously.” People should also pay attention to what happens the next time someone leaves, Chiquita Hall-Jackson, an employment attorney at Hall-Jackson & Associates, tells Fast Company. “If the company leaves the position vacant, divides the work among the remaining team, and still expects the same output, that tells you more about its staffing looks than a cut to the travel budget,” she says. “When that pattern shows up across teams, it’s worth asking whether leadership is planning to operate with fewer people.” According to Hall-Jackson, it’s also a good idea to look at what’s being cut and how long the cuts last. A canceled off-site meeting may save money once, but a hiring freeze changes how the business operates. “One budget decision can have plenty of explanations,” she says. “Several decisions that consistently reduce staffing or hours are more meaningful.” Another potential warning sign is a change in the company’s management structure. If there are fewer middle managers than there used to be, and larger teams are now reporting to more senior supervisors, that could suggest the company is looking to operate with fewer people, Levey says. It’s more important than ever to have leverage Of course, many of these signs could just mean that an individual company isn’t doing well and may not indicate a wider, looming recession. But in this tough economy and job market, employees should consider being more sensitive to changes at work that may hint at something bigger happening, Levey says. He adds that it’s important to maintain a sense of where you stand within the company, how secure your position is, and what the general temperature is when it comes to potential layoffs. “You want to pay attention to messages from the CEO or upper management. Because if you think that your job is in jeopardy, then while you’re still employed there and making a wage, you’ve got to start looking elsewhere to see what your other options are,” Levey says. The worst thing is being blindsided, so it’s always a good idea to make sure you have some leverage, he notes. “It doesn’t mean you need to microanalyze every single thing that happens with the company. But be a realist. Keep your eyes open, really understand what’s going on. That way, you’re less surprised if these things happen.”.

Of course, many of these signs could just mean that an individual company isn’t doing well and may not indicate a wider, looming recession.

But in this tough economy and job market, employees should consider being more sensitive to changes at work that may hint at something bigger happening, Levey says. He adds that it’s key to maintain a sense of where you stand within the firm, how secure your position is, and what the general temperature is when it comes to potential layoffs.

“You want to pay attention to messages from the CEO or upper management. Because if you think that your job is in jeopardy, then while you’re still employed there and making a wage, you’ve got to start looking elsewhere to see what your other options are,” Levey says.

Sources indicate that the worst thing is being blindsided, so it’s always a good idea to make sure you have some leverage, he notes. “It doesn’t mean you need to microanalyze every single thing that happens with the firm. But be a realist. Keep your eyes open, really understand what’s going on. That way, you’re less surprised if these things happen.”.

Make money or make a difference

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that early in your career, you’ve probably been told you have to choose: Make money, or make a difference. Do well first. Then, once you’ve earned it, do good through philanthropy. I believed that for most of my career. I spent decades on Wall Street, eventually becoming a partner in one of the country’s leading alternative investment firms, where I oversaw its real estate business. Simultaneously, I spent years as a philanthropist. Both paths left me unsatisfied. Growing net worth felt hollow, and many of the charities I funded treated symptoms without “curing the disease.” A FALSE CHOICE What I’ve learned since is that the choice is false. Some of the best investment opportunities for the next generation sit inside society’s hardest problems. They start with the foundations every community depends on: housing, education, and healthcare. That’s where my firm invests, because when those foundations are strong, everything built on them gets stronger too. The investors who see this opportunity first will do well, and they’ll help reshape our world. They will build economic success and solve societal problems at the same time. When Magic Johnson and I launched our first urban real estate fund in 1998, I thought raising the capital would take six months. It took two-and-a-half years. Investors believed then, as many still do, that attaching a social goal to an investment means sacrificing returns. We proved them wrong. Over 15 years, those funds raised $2 billion, facilitated $6 billion in urban revitalization, and created tens of thousands of jobs while generating strong returns. Potential investors also didn’t believe that an athlete could be a financial success of this scale. Yet today, Magic is a billionaire and proved those doubters wrong. WHAT IMPACT INVESTING LOOKS LIKE Done right, impact investing can deliver better risk-adjusted returns than traditional strategies. This type of investing targets large, growing, unmet needs in markets less tied to the broader economy, where government and philanthropy have historically been the only players. Take workforce housing. In 2023, over 21 million renter households (49.7 percent of renter households) spent at least 30 percent of their income on housing. Households spending more than 50 percent are considered severely cost-burdened. I’m talking about teachers, police officers, firefighters, and healthcare workers who earn too much for subsidized housing but not enough to buy a home. They don’t need a handout. They need housing that’s within reach. Building new affordable housing at market-rate returns without public incentives is nearly impossible. Meanwhile, existing affordable units keep disappearing as investors buy them, renovate, and raise rents on the people who can least afford it. We flipped the model by buying existing properties and keeping rents affordable. Then we offer reduced rent to teachers, law enforcement officers, and healthcare workers who live on-site and provide tutoring, community safety, and health programs in return. The result is pride in rentership. When residents feel invested in where they live, they stay longer and treat the property better. In our first housing fund, lease terms increased 32%, crime fell 48%, and economic loss dropped 37%. Net operating income grew 13%, and the fund delivered a 25% internal rate of return, all without raising rents. The social outcome drove the financial outcome. IMPACT MARKETING As impact investing grows, so does impact marketing. Plenty of funds now put “impact” on the label without changing anything underneath. Here are four things to look for. 1. Ask where the impact indicates up in the financials. If the social goal could be cut without touching returns, it’s an add-on, and it will be the first thing cut when times get tight. Real impact drives the business. In our housing, the community programs are why tenants stay longer, which is why the numbers work. 2. Look for measured outcomes, not good intentions. Lease duration, crime rates, graduation rates, patient outcomes. If a fund can’t show you the data, the impact is a story, not a strategy. 3. Follow the demand. Durable impact investments meet an existing and growing need. Be wary of anything that depends on creating demand or on a single subsidy that could disappear. 4. Look at who’s on the team. Ask whether the people making decisions understand the problem firsthand. Our team includes former teachers, physicians, law enforcement officers, and frontline workers alongside recovering bankers. That expertise is how we spot financial and social risk before it costs anyone. FINAL THOUGHTS Too many Americans have their health, education, and economic outcomes determined by where they were born. That isn’t sustainable, and government and philanthropy can’t solve it alone. If you’re early in your career, you have something my generation didn’t: proof that you don’t have to choose. You can build a career and a portfolio around solving the problems that matter most, and get paid for doing it. That’s the conversation I want to have with the next generation of investors. Impact investing has never been more critical, and it has never been more rewarding. Bobby Turner is founder of Turner Impact Capital.
